right.text: Site of T-cell education (positive and negative selection)
Site of B-cell development and T-cell precursor origin
T-cell zone where dendritic cells present antigen to naive T cells
Site of rapid B-cell proliferation and antibody refinement after activation

questions.explanation: Bone marrow and thymus are the primary organs where lymphocytes are made and educated; the paracortex and germinal center are secondary-organ structures where mature lymphocytes actually respond to antigen.

questions.prompt: Which vessels do naive lymphocytes use to enter a lymph node directly from the bloodstream?

options.text: Afferent lymphatics
High endothelial venules
Efferent lymphatics
The thoracic duct

explanations.a: Afferent lymphatics carry antigen and dendritic cells into the node from peripheral tissue, not lymphocytes arriving from blood.
explanations.b: Correct — high endothelial venules are specialized blood vessels within the node that let naive lymphocytes cross directly from the bloodstream into the node tissue.
explanations.c: Efferent lymphatics carry lymphocytes and lymph out of the node, not in from blood.
explanations.d: The thoracic duct returns lymph (and recirculating lymphocytes) to the bloodstream after they exit a node, not the entry route.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a naive lymphocyte's continuous recirculation through the body, starting from the bloodstream.

items.text: Enters a lymph node from blood via a high endothelial venule
Patrols the node's zones for a matching antigen
Exits via efferent lymphatics if no match is found
Returns to the bloodstream through the thoracic duct to repeat the cycle

questions.explanation: This closed loop, demonstrated by Gowans (1959), is what lets a rare antigen-specific lymphocyte cover the whole body instead of relying on chance to be in the right node once.

questions.prompt: How does the spleen's basic organizing logic compare to a lymph node's?

options.text: The spleen has no B-cell or T-cell zones at all
The spleen uses the same B-zone/T-zone organization around central arterioles but filters blood instead of lymph
The spleen only contains T cells, never B cells
The spleen is a primary lymphoid organ like the thymus

explanations.a: The spleen's white pulp is organized into B-cell and T-cell zones just as a lymph node is, arranged around central arterioles instead of afferent lymphatics.
explanations.b: Correct — the spleen mirrors lymph-node zoning but samples blood-borne antigen rather than antigen arriving through lymphatic vessels.
explanations.c: The spleen's white pulp contains B-cell follicles as well as T-cell zones.
explanations.d: The spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ where responses happen, not a primary organ where lymphocytes are generated.

lessons.label: What Makes an Antigen

sections.heading: Antigen, immunogen, hapten: three related but different words
sections.body: An antigen is, strictly, anything that can be bound by an antibody or lymphocyte receptor — the word says nothing about whether it provokes a response by itself. An immunogen is a molecule that actually triggers an adaptive immune response when introduced into the body; every immunogen is an antigen, but not every antigen is an immunogen. A hapten is the clearest illustration of that gap: a small molecule that antibodies can bind (so it qualifies as an antigen) but that is too small on its own to activate B cells or trigger T-cell help, and therefore is not immunogenic unless it is chemically attached to a larger 'carrier' molecule.

sections.heading: Landsteiner's hapten-carrier work defined immunological specificity
sections.body: Karl Landsteiner's experiments in the 1920s and 1930s turned this distinction into the operational foundation of immunology. He attached small synthetic chemical groups to carrier proteins, immunized animals, and then tested the resulting antisera against haptens with tiny structural variations — moving a chemical group from the ortho to the meta to the para position on a benzene ring. The antisera reliably distinguished these near-identical molecules, proving that antibody specificity could resolve differences at the level of a single atom's position. This was the first rigorous demonstration that the immune system's specificity is a chemical, not just biological, phenomenon, and it established the hapten-carrier system still used today to study exactly what a receptor can and cannot tell apart.

sections.heading: Epitopes and what sets immunogenicity
sections.body: The actual patch of an antigen that a receptor binds is called an epitope. B-cell receptors and antibodies can recognize linear epitopes (a contiguous stretch of sequence) or conformational epitopes (a shape formed by parts of the molecule that fold near each other, which is destroyed if the protein denatures). T-cell receptors, by contrast, only ever see linear peptide fragments, because antigen must first be processed and displayed on MHC. Beyond structure, four factors set how immunogenic a molecule is: foreignness (how different it is from self), molecular size (larger, more complex molecules are generally more immunogenic; this is why haptens need a carrier), chemical complexity (repetitive, simple polymers are weaker immunogens than structurally varied proteins), and valency (multiple copies of the same epitope on one molecule can cross-link B-cell receptors and trigger a response even without T-cell help).

lessons.workedExample: Penicillin is a small molecule and, by itself, is not immunogenic — it is far too small to cross-link receptors or provide enough surface for a sustained T-cell response. In some people, penicillin metabolites covalently bind host serum proteins, and the penicillin-protein conjugate now behaves exactly like Landsteiner's hapten-carrier system: the drug is the hapten, the host protein is the carrier, and the combined molecule is immunogenic enough to trigger an antibody response — which is the actual mechanism behind a penicillin allergy. The immune system was never reacting to penicillin as it exists in the pill; it was reacting to a hapten-carrier conjugate formed inside the body.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'is that actually an antigen, and would it provoke a response on its own?' to check whether a student can separate 'binds a receptor' from 'triggers immunity' rather than using the two ideas interchangeably. A weak answer calls any molecule involved in an immune reaction an antigen without distinction. A strong answer can state that a hapten is antigenic but not immunogenic alone, explain why (too small, insufficient valency and complexity), and name what changes when it is coupled to a carrier — showing they understand immunogenicity as a set of measurable molecular properties rather than a yes/no label.

questions.prompt: A small molecule can be bound tightly by an antibody but cannot trigger an immune response on its own unless attached to a larger protein. What is this molecule called?

options.text: An immunogen
A hapten
A carrier
An epitope

explanations.a: An immunogen is, by definition, capable of triggering a response on its own — the opposite of what is described here.
explanations.b: Correct — a hapten is antigenic (can be bound by antibody) but not immunogenic alone, becoming immunogenic only once linked to a carrier.
explanations.c: The carrier is the larger molecule the hapten must attach to, not the small molecule itself.
explanations.d: An epitope is the specific binding patch on any antigen, not a category defined by size or the need for a carrier.

questions.prompt: Landsteiner's experiments moved a chemical group between the ortho, meta, and para positions on a benzene ring attached to a carrier protein. What did the resulting antisera show?

options.text: Antibodies could not tell the three positions apart at all
Antibodies reliably distinguished the near-identical structural variants, showing atomic-level specificity
Only T cells, not antibodies, could distinguish the variants
The carrier protein alone determined specificity, regardless of hapten position

explanations.a: The opposite was found — this is precisely what made the experiments famous, since indistinguishability would not have demonstrated fine specificity.
explanations.b: Correct — the antisera resolved differences as small as a single substituent's position on the ring, establishing that immune specificity operates at extremely fine chemical resolution.
explanations.c: Landsteiner's classic hapten work used antibody (antisera) specificity as the readout, not T-cell recognition.
explanations.d: If the carrier alone determined specificity, varying the hapten position would have made no difference to the antisera's reactivity, which is not what was observed.

questions.prompt: Match each epitope-related term to its description.

right.text: A contiguous sequence stretch, recognizable even if the protein unfolds
A processed linear peptide displayed on MHC
A shape formed by folding, destroyed by denaturation

questions.explanation: Antibodies and B-cell receptors can recognize either linear or conformational epitopes on intact antigen, but T-cell receptors only ever see processed linear peptide fragments presented on MHC.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of a hapten becoming immunogenic, from the unconjugated hapten to a full antibody response.

items.text: Hapten alone: small, low complexity, cannot cross-link receptors effectively
Hapten-carrier conjugate: increased size and structural complexity
Immune system now able to mount a full antibody response against the hapten

questions.explanation: The hapten alone lacks the size and complexity to be immunogenic; conjugation to a carrier supplies both, which is what then permits a full response against the hapten's epitope.

lessons.label: Self versus Non-Self and Tolerance

sections.heading: Central tolerance: deleting the dangerous clones before they leave
sections.body: Because B-cell and T-cell receptors are generated by random gene rearrangement, a large fraction of newly made receptors will, by chance, bind the body's own proteins. Central tolerance is the first layer of defense against this: in the thymus, negative selection deletes any T cell whose receptor binds self-peptide-MHC too strongly, as covered in the lymphocyte-development lesson. In the bone marrow, B cells with receptors that bind self-antigen strongly get a second chance through receptor editing (re-activating RAG genes to rearrange a new light chain) before outright deletion if editing fails. The catch is that a typical protein in the thymus cortex would only ever encounter self-antigens made in the thymus itself — so how does the body delete T cells reactive against insulin, made only in the pancreas, or thyroid proteins, made only in the neck?

sections.heading: AIRE and the promiscuous expression trick
sections.body: The answer is the autoimmune regulator gene, AIRE, identified in 1997 (Nagamine et al.) as the gene mutated in the disease APECED. AIRE is a transcription factor expressed in medullary thymic epithelial cells that drives those cells to promiscuously express a huge range of tissue-restricted proteins — insulin, thyroid antigens, and thousands of others that normally belong only to peripheral organs — directly in the thymic medulla. This lets developing T cells reactive against peripheral-only self-proteins be caught and deleted before they ever leave, extending negative selection's reach far beyond what the thymus would otherwise display. People with AIRE mutations develop APECED, a syndrome combining true multi-organ autoimmune attack (commonly the adrenal glands and parathyroid, destroyed because that peripheral self-antigen display never happens) with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, a separate consequence caused by autoantibodies against the Th17 cytokines IL-17A/F and IL-22 that impair anti-fungal defense rather than by lymphocytes attacking skin tissue itself.

sections.heading: Peripheral tolerance and autoimmunity as its failure
sections.body: Central tolerance is not perfect — some self-reactive lymphocytes always escape into circulation. Peripheral tolerance is the backup layer: a self-reactive T cell that receives antigen signal without costimulation becomes anergic (functionally inactivated rather than deleted), and regulatory T cells actively suppress self-reactive cells that do escape. Sakaguchi and colleagues showed in 1995 that depleting CD25+ regulatory T cells from otherwise normal mice caused spontaneous autoimmune disease, directly demonstrating that ongoing suppression, not just earlier deletion, is required to keep self-reactive cells in check. Autoimmunity, seen this way, is not a mysterious attack from nowhere — it is tolerance failing at one or more of these specific, named checkpoints.

lessons.workedExample: A person with a loss-of-function mutation in AIRE cannot display insulin, thyroid, or adrenal proteins in their thymic medulla during T-cell development. T cells reactive against those peripheral organs are never caught by negative selection and exit into circulation as apparently normal naive T cells. Years later, those cells encounter their matching self-antigen in the actual pancreas, thyroid, or adrenal gland, get activated, and drive autoimmune destruction of multiple organs — the clinical picture of APECED. The mutation is in one gene expressed only in the thymus, but its consequence plays out as organ damage spread across the whole body, which is the signature of a central-tolerance failure rather than a peripheral one.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'why doesn't the immune system attack the body by default, given that receptors are made randomly' to see whether a student understands tolerance as an active, multi-layered process rather than an assumed given. A weak answer says the immune system 'knows' what is self. A strong answer names at least two concrete checkpoints — thymic negative selection and a peripheral backup like regulatory T cells or anergy — and can explain autoimmunity as a specific, nameable failure of one of those checkpoints rather than a vague malfunction.

questions.prompt: How does the AIRE gene extend central tolerance to organ-specific proteins like insulin that are not normally made in the thymus?

options.text: It drives medullary thymic epithelial cells to promiscuously express peripheral tissue-restricted antigens so reactive T cells can be deleted
It directly deletes insulin-producing cells in the pancreas
It suppresses T-cell receptor gene rearrangement entirely
It converts self-reactive T cells into regulatory T cells

explanations.a: Correct — AIRE causes thymic medullary epithelial cells to express a broad set of normally peripheral-only proteins, giving developing T cells a chance to be tested against them and deleted if overly self-reactive.
explanations.b: AIRE acts in the thymus on developing T cells, not on pancreatic cells directly.
explanations.c: AIRE does not block receptor gene rearrangement; rearrangement happens normally and AIRE instead affects what antigens the resulting cells are tested against.
explanations.d: AIRE's role is in negative selection (deletion), not in converting cells into the regulatory T-cell lineage.

questions.prompt: Sakaguchi and colleagues (1995) depleted CD25+ regulatory T cells from otherwise normal mice. What resulted, and what did it demonstrate?

options.text: The mice developed spontaneous autoimmune disease, showing ongoing peripheral suppression is required to keep self-reactive cells in check
Nothing changed, showing regulatory T cells are not important for tolerance
The mice became immunodeficient, showing regulatory T cells are required for all immune responses
The mice's thymic negative selection improved

explanations.a: Correct — spontaneous autoimmunity after depletion showed that regulatory T cells are actively needed on an ongoing basis, not just as a one-time developmental step.
explanations.b: The mice did develop disease, which is exactly why this experiment is a landmark demonstration of regulatory T-cell function.
explanations.c: The mice mounted an excessive self-directed response rather than losing immune function altogether.
explanations.d: The experiment depleted a peripheral cell population; it did not target or improve thymic selection, which happens earlier in development.

questions.prompt: Match each tolerance mechanism to where it acts.

right.text: Central tolerance, in the thymus or bone marrow
Peripheral tolerance, functional inactivation without costimulation
Peripheral tolerance, active ongoing suppression

questions.explanation: Deletion and receptor editing happen during development in the primary lymphoid organs, while anergy and regulatory T-cell suppression are backup mechanisms operating later, in the periphery, against cells that already escaped central tolerance.

questions.prompt: Order the events in an AIRE-deficient person developing APECED, starting from the genetic cause.

items.text: A loss-of-function mutation in AIRE prevents promiscuous self-antigen expression in the thymic medulla
T cells reactive against peripheral organ proteins are not deleted and exit the thymus
Those T cells later encounter matching self-antigen in organs like the adrenal gland or thyroid
Multi-organ autoimmune destruction results

questions.explanation: The mutation acts only in the thymus, but by failing to delete the right T cells there, it produces damage that later shows up spread across multiple peripheral organs.

lessons.label: The Clonal Selection Principle

sections.heading: The problem: how does one antibody fit one antigen?
sections.body: By the mid-20th century, immunologists agreed antibodies could bind an enormous range of shapes with high specificity, but they disagreed sharply about how. The dominant idea, an instructional or template theory championed by figures including Linus Pauling, held that a single kind of antibody protein existed and antigen itself acted as a mold, folding around the antigen to become complementary to it. Instructional theories could explain specificity for a single encounter, but they struggled badly with two other observations: immunological memory (why a second exposure is faster and stronger) and self/non-self discrimination (why the body does not fold antibodies around its own tissue), since in an instructional model any molecule present, self or foreign, should be able to act as a template.

sections.heading: Burnet's 1957 answer: selection, not instruction
sections.body: Frank Macfarlane Burnet, building on an idea from David Talmage, proposed the opposite logic in a short 1957 paper in the Australian Journal of Science, later formalized in his 1959 book The Clonal Selection Theory of Acquired Immunity. The core claim: each lymphocyte commits to a single receptor specificity before it ever meets antigen, generated by random gene rearrangement, so a vast repertoire of different specificities already exists in the body at any given time, most of them never used. Antigen does not instruct anything — it simply finds and binds whichever pre-existing clone happens to match, and that binding event triggers the matching clone to proliferate and differentiate into effector and memory cells. Specificity was already built in before the antigen ever arrived; antigen's only job is selection.

sections.heading: Why the selective model won
sections.body: Clonal selection immediately explained what instructional theories could not. Memory follows naturally: the expanded clone from a first exposure leaves behind memory cells at far higher frequency than the original naive population, so a second exposure finds many more matching cells already available. Self/non-self discrimination follows too, once paired with tolerance: clones reactive against self can be deleted during development (central tolerance, covered in the previous lesson) precisely because each clone's specificity is fixed and identifiable before antigen ever appears, something an instructional model has no mechanism to do. Later single-cell experiments confirmed Burnet's central prediction directly — that one lymphocyte makes receptors of only one specificity — which is why clonal selection, not the instructional model, became the organizing framework for the rest of adaptive immunology.

lessons.workedExample: A person is infected with a novel influenza strain for the first time. Under Burnet's model, a clone of B cells specific for that strain's hemagglutinin protein already existed in the body before infection, at extremely low frequency, purely by chance from random receptor generation. The virus's hemagglutinin does not create or reshape any antibody; it simply binds the one pre-existing clone whose receptor happens to fit, and that binding, together with T-cell help, drives that single clone to expand from a handful of cells into a large population of antibody-secreting plasma cells and memory cells. On a second exposure to the same strain, the memory cells left over from that expansion are far more numerous than the original naive frequency, so the response is faster and stronger — exactly the pattern an instructional, template-based model could never account for.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about clonal selection to see whether a student can state the actual logic of specificity — pre-existing and selected, not shaped on contact — rather than a vague 'the immune system learns' description. A weak answer cannot say what came first, the receptor or the antigen. A strong answer states that specificity is fixed in a lymphocyte before it ever meets antigen, that antigen's role is to find and expand a matching clone rather than to mold anything, and can explain why this selective logic — unlike an instructional model — naturally produces both memory and the possibility of deleting self-reactive clones.

questions.prompt: According to Burnet's clonal selection theory, what role does antigen play when it encounters a lymphocyte?

options.text: It molds the lymphocyte's receptor into a complementary shape on contact
It selects and binds a pre-existing clone whose receptor already matches, triggering that clone to expand
It randomly rearranges the receptor genes of the lymphocyte it binds
It has no effect on the lymphocyte unless costimulation is also present

explanations.a: This describes the instructional/template model Burnet's theory replaced, not clonal selection — receptor specificity is fixed before antigen ever appears.
explanations.b: Correct — in clonal selection, specificity pre-exists via random gene rearrangement, and antigen's role is purely to find and expand the clone that already fits.
explanations.c: Receptor gene rearrangement happens earlier, during lymphocyte development, before the cell ever encounters antigen — not as a result of the antigen encounter itself.
explanations.d: Antigen binding does have an effect (it is the trigger for clonal expansion); costimulation is a separate, additional requirement for full activation, not a precondition for antigen having any effect at all.

questions.prompt: Why did instructional (template) theories of antibody formation struggle to explain immunological memory?

options.text: They predicted memory would be too strong, not too weak
If antigen shapes antibody fresh at each encounter, there is no clear reason a second encounter should be any faster than the first
They could not explain antibody specificity at all
They predicted memory cells would only form in the bone marrow

explanations.a: Instructional theories did not make a strong quantitative memory prediction either way; the issue is that they lacked a mechanism for memory to exist at all.
explanations.b: Correct — without a pre-existing, expandable clone left over from the first exposure, an instructional model gives no reason a second exposure should start from a larger, faster-responding population.
explanations.c: Instructional theories were built specifically to explain specificity (via the mold/template mechanism); their weakness was memory and self/non-self discrimination, not specificity itself.
explanations.d: Instructional theories did not make specific claims about where memory cells would form, since they lacked a mechanism for memory in the first place.

questions.prompt: Order the events of clonal selection following a first-time infection.

items.text: A vast pre-existing repertoire of differently-specific lymphocyte clones already exists
Antigen binds the one rare clone whose receptor happens to match
The matching clone proliferates and differentiates into effector cells
A larger memory clone population persists after the effector response subsides

questions.explanation: Clonal selection requires the repertoire to exist before antigen arrives; antigen then selects and expands one clone, and memory is simply what remains of that expansion afterward.

questions.prompt: Match each theory to its core claim about antibody specificity.

right.text: Antigen physically molds antibody into a complementary shape at the time of encounter
Specificity is fixed in each lymphocyte before antigen ever arrives; antigen only selects and expands a matching clone

questions.explanation: The two theories disagree on timing: instructional theories put specificity-formation at the moment of antigen contact, while Burnet's clonal selection theory puts it earlier, during random receptor generation, with antigen acting only as a selector.

lessons.label: Antibody Architecture

sections.heading: A Y-shaped molecule built from four chains
sections.body: An antibody (immunoglobulin, Ig) is a Y-shaped protein built from two identical heavy chains (~50 kDa) and two identical light chains (~25 kDa), held together by disulfide bonds into a symmetric four-chain unit. This structure was worked out by Rodney Porter and Gerald Edelman, who shared the 1972 Nobel Prize for it. Porter used the enzyme papain to cleave IgG into three pieces: two identical fragments that still bound antigen, which he called Fab (fragment, antigen-binding), and one fragment that crystallized readily, Fc (fragment, crystallizable). Edelman used reducing agents like mercaptoethanol to break the interchain disulfide bonds and separate the heavy and light chains entirely, showing each chain is itself a distinct polypeptide with its own gene products.

sections.heading: Variable meets constant: each chain has two kinds of domains
sections.body: Each heavy and light chain folds into repeating ~110-amino-acid units called immunoglobulin domains. The domain nearest the chain's N-terminus is the variable (V) domain — VH on the heavy chain, VL on the light chain — whose sequence differs from antibody to antibody. The remaining domains are constant (C) domains: CL on the light chain, and CH1-CH3 on the heavy chain (IgG has three; IgM and IgE have four). Within each V domain, three short loops show the most sequence variability of all — the complementarity-determining regions (CDR1-3). A paired VH and VL bring their six CDR loops together at the tip of each arm to form the actual antigen-binding site, so specificity is concentrated in a small three-dimensional surface rather than spread across the whole molecule.

sections.heading: Structure maps directly onto function
sections.body: The two Fab arms, each built from VH+CH1 paired with VL+CL, are the business end: they bind antigen, and because there are two identical arms per antibody, a single IgG molecule is bivalent. The Fc stem, built from the paired CH2-CH3 domains, does not touch antigen at all — instead it is the handle that effector machinery grabs. Fc receptors on phagocytes bind Fc to trigger opsonization; the C1q complement component binds Fc to trigger the classical complement cascade; and the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) binds Fc to recycle IgG and extend its serum half-life to roughly three weeks. This division — a variable end that decides what to bind and a constant end that decides what happens next — is the organizing logic behind every antibody-based assay and every antibody-based therapy in use today.

lessons.workedExample: A student building an ELISA needs a detection antibody. She picks one raised against her target protein's variable region logic in reverse: the primary antibody's Fab arms bind the target antigen captured on the plate, while a secondary antibody's Fab arms bind the primary antibody's constant (Fc/CH1) region — recognizing it as 'mouse IgG' rather than any specific antigen. The secondary antibody's own Fc tail carries the enzyme (HRP) that produces the color signal. If she confused which end does the binding, she'd try to conjugate enzyme to the Fab region and lose antigen recognition, or try to raise a secondary antibody against the primary's CDR loops, which would only recognize that one primary and defeat the point of a universal secondary reagent.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'what part of the antibody actually binds your antigen, and how do you know?' to check whether a student understands their own assay reagents or is just following a kit protocol. A weak answer says 'the antibody binds the protein' with no structural detail. A strong answer names the Fab arms and CDR loops as the binding surface, explains that the Fc region is instead recognized by secondary antibodies or Fc receptors, and can say why a bivalent IgG binding two epitopes at once changes apparent binding strength compared to a single Fab fragment — showing they understand the reagent, not just the result.

questions.prompt: Papain digestion of an IgG antibody produces which fragments?

options.text: Two Fc fragments and one Fab fragment
Two Fab fragments and one Fc fragment
Four identical VH domains
One heavy chain and one light chain, fully separated

explanations.a: This reverses the actual ratio; papain yields two antigen-binding fragments and only one crystallizable fragment.
explanations.b: Correct — Porter's papain digestion cleaves IgG into two identical Fab arms (each still able to bind antigen) and one Fc stem.
explanations.c: Papain cleaves the whole antibody into fragments; it does not isolate single domains like VH.
explanations.d: Separating heavy from light chains entirely requires breaking interchain disulfide bonds (Edelman's method with reducing agents), not papain cleavage.

questions.prompt: Match each antibody region to its function.

right.text: Forms the antigen-binding surface
Holds the variable domain in position to reach antigen
Recruits complement and Fc receptors

questions.explanation: The CDR loops within the variable domains form the actual binding surface; the rest of the Fab arm scaffolds those loops into position; the Fc stem is bound by effector molecules like C1q and Fc receptors rather than by antigen.

questions.prompt: Order these structural levels of an antibody from smallest to largest.

items.text: A single CDR loop
A variable (V) domain
A full heavy or light chain
The complete four-chain antibody

questions.explanation: A CDR loop is one short stretch within a V domain; the V domain is one of several domains along a chain; a full chain (heavy or light) is one of four polypeptides; and the assembled antibody combines two heavy and two light chains.

questions.prompt: Why is an antibody typically described as bivalent?

options.text: It has two different antigen-binding specificities on the same molecule
It has two identical Fab arms, each capable of binding an antigen copy
It contains two Fc regions
It can switch between two different constant regions

explanations.a: A normal antibody's two Fab arms are identical, so both bind the same epitope, not two different ones.
explanations.b: Correct — two identical light-heavy chain pairs give two identical antigen-binding arms, letting one antibody engage two antigen copies at once.
explanations.c: A standard IgG monomer has a single Fc stem, not two.
explanations.d: Isotype switching changes which constant region a B cell uses, but that is a separate process from bivalency and happens once per cell, not per molecule.

lessons.label: The B-Cell Receptor and Soluble Antibody

sections.heading: One variable region, two destinies
sections.body: Every B cell displays a membrane-bound version of the antibody it is programmed to make — the B-cell receptor (BCR). The BCR uses the exact same heavy- and light-chain V(D)J-rearranged variable region that the cell's secreted antibody will eventually use; what differs is only the C-terminus of the heavy chain. The membrane form ends in a hydrophobic transmembrane sequence plus a short cytoplasmic tail that anchors it in the plasma membrane. The secreted form, produced by alternative RNA processing after a B cell differentiates into a plasma cell, swaps that transmembrane segment for a soluble tail, releasing the same antigen-binding molecule into the blood and tissue fluid as free antibody. Because the alternative splicing happens downstream of the V(D)J-recombined exons, a cell never needs to re-specify what it binds when it switches from receptor to secretion — it only changes how the protein is anchored.

sections.heading: A receptor with no signaling tail of its own
sections.body: The BCR's heavy and light chains have a cytoplasmic tail too short to signal on their own, so the complex is completed by a non-covalently associated heterodimer, Ig-alpha (CD79a) and Ig-beta (CD79b). Each carries an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif (ITAM) in its cytoplasmic tail. When antigen cross-links BCRs on the cell surface, Src-family kinases phosphorylate those ITAMs, recruiting the kinase Syk and triggering the downstream cascade (PLC-gamma2, calcium flux, NF-kB and NFAT activation) that drives B-cell activation, proliferation, and eventual antibody secretion or memory formation. This mirrors the CD3 module that signals for the T-cell receptor: in both lymphocyte lineages, the antigen-recognition chains and the signal-transduction chains are separate proteins bolted together into one functional receptor.

sections.heading: Monovalent versus multivalent binding: affinity meets avidity
sections.body: A single Fab-antigen interaction has an intrinsic strength, its affinity, set by the shape complementarity of one binding site to one epitope. But a BCR or antibody rarely engages antigen through just one site. The membrane-bound BCR is bivalent like secreted IgG, and secreted IgM — the first antibody a naive B cell makes — assembles into a pentamer with ten binding sites total. Multivalent engagement means several binding events must all break simultaneously for the molecule to release, so the combined strength (avidity) can be far higher than any single site's affinity alone. This is why low-affinity IgM, produced early in a response before affinity maturation has refined the antibody's fit, can still function effectively: it compensates for weak per-site affinity with high avidity from its ten-fold multivalency.

lessons.workedExample: A newly activated naive B cell has a BCR with modest affinity for a viral surface protein (Kd in the micromolar range). As a membrane receptor, its bivalent binding is enough to cross-link and trigger activation. Once that B cell differentiates into an early plasma cell, it secretes pentameric IgM built from the same V region. Even though each individual binding site is still only micromolar-affinity, the ten simultaneous contact points give the IgM pentamer nanomolar-or-better avidity for a repetitive viral surface — enough to agglutinate virus particles and fix complement, buying time for germinal-center affinity maturation to later produce higher-affinity IgG.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this concept asks 'is the antibody in your assay the same molecule as the receptor on the cell, or a different one?' A weak answer treats 'antibody' and 'B-cell receptor' as unrelated vocabulary. A strong answer explains they share an identical variable region and differ only in a C-terminal anchor versus secretion tail, and can distinguish affinity (one site) from avidity (all sites combined) — a distinction that matters directly if the student's project involves IgM versus IgG detection, since confusing the two leads to misinterpreting why an early-timepoint assay looks weaker or stronger than a later one.

questions.prompt: What structurally distinguishes the membrane-bound BCR from the secreted antibody made from the same V(D)J rearrangement?

options.text: The secreted form uses a different light chain gene
The heavy chain's C-terminus differs: a transmembrane anchor versus a soluble tail
The secreted form lacks CDR loops
The BCR has only one antigen-binding arm instead of two

explanations.a: Both forms use the identical rearranged light chain; the light chain is not what changes.
explanations.b: Correct — alternative RNA processing swaps a transmembrane/cytoplasmic segment for a secreted tail on the heavy chain, while the antigen-binding variable region stays identical.
explanations.c: CDR loops are part of the variable region, which is shared unchanged between both forms.
explanations.d: Both the BCR and secreted IgG are bivalent, built from two identical heavy-light chain pairs.

questions.prompt: Match each component to its role in B-cell receptor signaling.

right.text: Recognize and bind antigen
Carry ITAMs that get phosphorylated upon antigen cross-linking
Recruited to phosphorylated ITAMs to propagate the downstream signal

questions.explanation: The BCR chains only recognize antigen; they have short cytoplasmic tails that cannot signal alone, so Ig-alpha/Ig-beta supply the ITAMs, and Syk is recruited to those phosphorylated ITAMs to drive activation.

questions.prompt: Why can pentameric IgM be functionally effective despite having relatively low per-site affinity?

options.text: Each of its ten binding sites has unusually high affinity to compensate
Its ten simultaneous binding sites give it high avidity even with modest per-site affinity
IgM does not need to bind antigen to fix complement
IgM's Fc region binds antigen directly, bypassing the Fab arms

explanations.a: IgM produced early in a response is characteristically lower-affinity per site, not higher; the compensation comes from multivalency, not per-site strength.
explanations.b: Correct — multivalent engagement means many bonds must break at once, so combined avidity can be high even when individual-site affinity is modest.
explanations.c: IgM binding antigen (often multivalently, aiding complex formation) is what positions its Fc region to fix complement; it is not independent of antigen binding.
explanations.d: The Fc region does not bind antigen in any antibody; antigen binding is a Fab function.

questions.prompt: Order these events from initial antigen encounter to antibody secretion.

items.text: Antigen cross-links BCRs on the naive B-cell surface
Ig-alpha/Ig-beta ITAMs are phosphorylated, recruiting Syk
B cell differentiates into a plasma cell
Alternative splicing produces secreted-form heavy chain, releasing soluble antibody

questions.explanation: Antigen must first cross-link surface BCRs to trigger ITAM phosphorylation and downstream signaling, which drives the cell to differentiate into a plasma cell, at which point alternative splicing switches heavy-chain production to the secreted form.

lessons.label: The T-Cell Receptor

sections.heading: A receptor that cannot see free antigen
sections.body: The alpha-beta T-cell receptor (TCR) looks superficially like a single Fab arm: two chains, each with a variable and constant domain, each contributing CDR loops to a binding site. But the TCR binds a fundamentally different target. A BCR or antibody can grab an intact, free-floating antigen — a whole protein, a sugar, a small molecule. A TCR can only recognize a short peptide fragment that is already sitting in the peptide-binding groove of a major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecule on another cell's surface. It never binds free antigen at all. This principle, called MHC restriction, was demonstrated by Rolf Zinkernagel and Peter Doherty in 1974: cytotoxic T cells primed against virus-infected cells could only kill target cells that shared the animal's own MHC class I type, even when those other targets carried the identical virus. The finding earned them the 1996 Nobel Prize and reframed T-cell recognition as inherently dual — peptide plus MHC, read together as one composite ligand.

sections.heading: CD3 does the signaling; CD4 or CD8 stabilizes the contact
sections.body: Like the BCR, the TCR's alpha and beta chains have minimal signaling capacity on their own. They associate with the CD3 complex — gamma, delta, and epsilon chains plus a zeta-chain homodimer — whose cytoplasmic tails carry ten ITAMs total, phosphorylated by Lck upon receptor engagement to trigger the T cell's activation cascade. Alongside CD3, a co-receptor grips the MHC molecule itself, outside the peptide groove: CD8 binds MHC class I, restricting that T cell to recognizing peptide-MHC-I complexes, while CD4 binds MHC class II, restricting its T cell to peptide-MHC-II complexes. This co-receptor choice is what defines a T cell as cytotoxic (CD8+) versus helper (CD4+), and it is enforced early in thymic development through positive selection on cortical epithelial cells.

sections.heading: The exception: gamma-delta T cells
sections.body: A minority of T cells, typically under 5% of circulating T cells but enriched in epithelial tissues like gut and skin, carry a differently paired TCR built from gamma and delta chains instead of alpha and beta. Gamma-delta T cells generally do not require conventional peptide-MHC presentation at all; many recognize intact protein or lipid antigens directly, more like a BCR than an alpha-beta TCR, and some respond to stress-induced self-molecules such as MICA/MICB rather than to foreign peptide. They bridge innate and adaptive immunity, responding faster than conventional alpha-beta T cells and serving as an early sentinel population at barrier surfaces.

lessons.workedExample: A student modeling a T-cell response designs an experiment where cytotoxic T cells from Mouse Strain A are exposed to cells from Mouse Strain B infected with the same virus used to prime the T cells in Strain A. Naively, they expect killing, since both animals carry the virus. But by the Zinkernagel-Doherty logic, no killing occurs unless Strain A and Strain B share the relevant MHC class I allele — the T cells were never primed to recognize Strain B's MHC scaffold, only their own MHC class I displaying the viral peptide. The correct control is to also test Strain A T cells against Strain A cells infected with an unrelated virus (no killing, confirming peptide specificity) and against uninfected Strain B cells (no killing, confirming MHC mismatch alone isn't sufficient either).
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'what exactly does a T cell recognize?' to catch students who have absorbed 'T cells fight infected cells' without the mechanism. A weak answer says T cells recognize antigens, same as antibodies. A strong answer states that alpha-beta TCRs recognize a specific peptide only when displayed in a specific MHC molecule — never free antigen — and can explain why this means T-cell immunity is inherently restricted to genetically matched cells, which is exactly why organ and tissue transplants require MHC (HLA) matching in the first place.

questions.prompt: What did the Zinkernagel-Doherty 1974 experiments demonstrate?

options.text: Cytotoxic T cells recognize free viral protein directly, without MHC
Cytotoxic T cells kill infected targets only when the target shares the T cell's own MHC class I type
B cells require MHC presentation to secrete antibody
Gamma-delta T cells are the dominant T-cell population in blood

explanations.a: This is the opposite of their finding; T cells failed to kill infected cells that lacked the matching MHC, showing recognition is not of free viral protein alone.
explanations.b: Correct — killing required the target to present viral peptide on the same MHC class I allele as the primed T cells, establishing MHC restriction.
explanations.c: Their experiments concerned cytotoxic T cells and infected target cells, not B-cell antibody secretion.
explanations.d: Alpha-beta T cells, not gamma-delta T cells, dominate circulating blood; this was not their finding either.

questions.prompt: Match each receptor component to its role.

right.text: Bind the peptide-MHC composite via CDR loops
Transduce the activation signal via ITAMs
Bind MHC outside the peptide groove, restricting MHC class recognized

questions.explanation: The TCR chains themselves only recognize peptide-MHC; CD3's ITAM-bearing tails carry the signal; CD4/CD8 grip the MHC molecule itself and determine whether the T cell is restricted to class II or class I.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes most gamma-delta T cells from conventional alpha-beta T cells?

options.text: Gamma-delta T cells make up the majority of circulating T cells
Gamma-delta T cells generally do not require conventional peptide-MHC presentation and are enriched at epithelial barriers
Gamma-delta T cells use CD3 to signal while alpha-beta T cells do not
Gamma-delta T cells only develop after alpha-beta T cells are exhausted

explanations.a: Gamma-delta T cells are a minority (typically under 5%) of circulating T cells, not the majority.
explanations.b: Correct — many gamma-delta T cells recognize antigen more directly, without needing conventional peptide-MHC presentation, and are enriched in gut and skin epithelia.
explanations.c: Both alpha-beta and gamma-delta TCRs signal through the same CD3 complex.
explanations.d: Gamma-delta and alpha-beta T cells develop as separate lineages in the thymus; one is not a fallback for the other.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in a CD8+ T cell recognizing and killing an infected cell.

items.text: Infected cell displays viral peptide on MHC class I
TCR alpha/beta CDR loops engage the peptide-MHC-I complex
CD8 co-receptor binds MHC class I, stabilizing the contact
CD3 ITAMs are phosphorylated, triggering T-cell activation

questions.explanation: The infected cell must first display peptide on MHC-I; the TCR then engages that composite ligand; CD8 binding MHC-I stabilizes the interaction; and only then does CD3 transduce the activating signal.

lessons.label: MHC Class I and Class II

sections.heading: Two classes, two audiences
sections.body: Humans express MHC class I molecules (HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C) on essentially every nucleated cell in the body, from skin keratinocytes to neurons to hepatocytes. This near-universal expression makes sense given their job: MHC-I displays a sample of the cell's own internal protein production, so that any cell hijacked by a virus or turned cancerous can flag the abnormality to a patrolling CD8+ cytotoxic T cell. MHC class II molecules (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ), by contrast, are restricted mostly to professional antigen-presenting cells — dendritic cells, macrophages, and B cells — whose job is to sample the extracellular environment and report it to CD4+ helper T cells. This division means the two classes are not interchangeable readouts of the same information; MHC-I asks 'what is happening inside this cell right now' while MHC-II asks 'what has this cell recently engulfed from outside.'

sections.heading: A closed groove versus an open one
sections.body: The functional difference traces directly to the shape of each molecule's peptide-binding groove. The MHC-I groove is closed at both ends by conserved pockets that pin down the peptide's N- and C-termini, which constrains bound peptides to a narrow length window, typically 8-10 amino acids. The MHC-II groove is open at both ends, so the peptide backbone extends past the groove's edges and can be considerably longer and more variable in length, typically 13-25 residues or more. This structural distinction is not incidental trivia: it explains why MHC-I peptides come from precise proteasomal cleavage (which naturally yields short fragments) while MHC-II peptides come from broader lysosomal proteolysis, and it is the basis for peptide-length rules used in epitope-prediction software.

sections.heading: Why HLA polymorphism matters at the population level
sections.body: The HLA genes are the most polymorphic loci in the human genome — collectively thousands of documented alleles across the classical class I and class II genes, concentrated at codons that line the peptide-binding groove itself. Because groove-lining residues differ between alleles, different people's HLA molecules bind different subsets of peptides from the same pathogen, so no single mutation in a virus can evade every HLA type in a population at once. This diversity is thought to be maintained partly by balancing selection favoring heterozygotes, who can present a broader peptide repertoire than homozygotes. The same polymorphism is the practical reason organ and bone-marrow transplants require HLA typing and matching: a graft bearing unfamiliar HLA molecules looks, to the recipient's T cells, like it is universally covered in foreign 'peptide' at every cell surface, triggering rejection.

lessons.workedExample: A student studying a novel virus wants to predict which of its proteins will be presented to the immune system. They know the virus replicates inside host cells but is also endocytosed as free particles by macrophages before infection takes hold. Peptides from the intracellular replication cycle end up on MHC-I (8-10mers, proteasome-derived) and are surveilled by CD8+ T cells, which can kill any infected cell displaying them. Peptides from the endocytosed particle end up on MHC-II (13-25mers, lysosome-derived) in the macrophage and are shown to CD4+ helper T cells, which do not kill the macrophage but instead help coordinate the broader response. A design that only measures CD8 T-cell killing would miss the CD4-driven helper response entirely, since the two pathways sample different pools of viral protein.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why are there two separate MHC classes instead of one?' to test whether a student understands antigen presentation as a system, not a single fact to memorize. A weak answer says MHC-I is for CD8 and MHC-II is for CD4 with no explanation of why. A strong answer connects the closed groove of MHC-I to short, proteasome-derived peptides sampling the cell's own cytosol, and the open groove of MHC-II to longer, lysosome-derived peptides sampling engulfed extracellular material — and can explain why that split lets the immune system distinguish an infected cell from a merely-exposed one.

questions.prompt: Match each MHC class to its typical cellular expression pattern.

right.text: Nearly all nucleated cells
Professional antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells)

questions.explanation: MHC-I's near-universal expression lets any cell flag internal problems to CD8 T cells, while MHC-II is largely restricted to professional APCs that specialize in surveying the extracellular environment for CD4 T cells.

questions.prompt: What structural feature of the MHC-I peptide-binding groove constrains bound peptides to roughly 8-10 residues?

options.text: The groove is open at both ends, allowing peptides to extend indefinitely
The groove is closed at both ends, pinning the peptide's N- and C-termini
The groove only binds peptides containing a specific amino acid motif at every position
MHC-I molecules have no defined groove at all

explanations.a: An open-ended groove describes MHC-II, which accommodates longer, more variable peptides, not MHC-I.
explanations.b: Correct — conserved pockets at each end of the MHC-I groove anchor the peptide termini, physically limiting the accommodated peptide length.
explanations.c: While certain anchor residues do influence binding, the length constraint itself comes from the closed-groove geometry, not a rigid full-length motif.
explanations.d: Both MHC-I and MHC-II have well-defined peptide-binding grooves; the difference is open versus closed ends.

questions.prompt: Why does extensive HLA polymorphism across a population matter for infectious disease?

options.text: It has no immunological consequence; it only affects transplant matching
Different HLA alleles bind different peptide subsets, so a pathogen cannot evade presentation in every individual with one mutation
It ensures every person presents an identical set of peptides for any given pathogen
It prevents CD8 T cells from ever recognizing viral peptides

explanations.a: HLA polymorphism has direct infectious-disease consequences beyond transplant matching, including population-level resistance to immune-evading pathogen mutations.
explanations.b: Correct — because groove-lining residues differ between alleles, a pathogen escape mutation that evades one person's HLA presentation may still be presented by another person's different HLA allele.
explanations.c: The opposite is true: polymorphism means different people present different peptide subsets from the same pathogen.
explanations.d: HLA polymorphism is what allows diverse peptide presentation to CD8 T cells in the first place, not a barrier to it.

questions.prompt: Order these from narrowest to broadest cellular expression.

items.text: MHC class II on professional APCs
MHC class I on nearly all nucleated cells

questions.explanation: MHC class II expression is largely confined to a specialized subset of cells (professional APCs), while MHC class I is expressed far more broadly, across essentially all nucleated cells.

lessons.label: Antigen Processing and Presentation

sections.heading: The endogenous pathway: sampling the cytosol for MHC-I
sections.body: Any cell continuously degrades a fraction of its own cytosolic proteins through the proteasome, a barrel-shaped protease complex — a routine process of protein turnover that antigen presentation piggybacks on. Under inflammatory signaling (interferon-gamma), cells swap in an immunoproteasome variant tuned to generate peptides with C-termini favorable for MHC binding. The resulting short peptides are shuttled from the cytosol into the endoplasmic reticulum by a dedicated transporter, TAP (transporter associated with antigen processing), a heterodimer of TAP1 and TAP2. Inside the ER, a peptide-loading complex — including tapasin, calreticulin, and the oxidoreductase ERp57 — helps trim and load peptides onto newly folded MHC class I molecules before they traffic to the cell surface. Because this pathway samples whatever a cell is actively synthesizing, a cell infected by a virus will display viral peptides on MHC-I even before enough virus has been made to visibly harm the cell, giving CD8+ T cells an early warning system.

sections.heading: The exogenous pathway: sampling the outside world for MHC-II
sections.body: Material taken up from outside the cell — phagocytosed bacteria, endocytosed extracellular protein — is degraded in an acidified phagolysosome or endosome by cathepsin proteases, yielding longer peptide fragments than proteasomal digestion does. MHC class II molecules are synthesized in the ER with their groove pre-occupied by the invariant chain (Ii, CD74), which blocks premature peptide loading and helps direct trafficking to a specialized endosomal compartment (the MIIC). There, Ii is degraded down to a small residual fragment called CLIP still sitting in the groove, and the chaperone HLA-DM catalyzes the exchange of CLIP for whatever antigenic peptide is available in that compartment. The loaded MHC-II then moves to the surface for CD4+ T cell surveillance.

sections.heading: Cross-presentation: dendritic cells breaking the rule
sections.body: The pathway split is not absolute. Certain dendritic cells, especially the CD8alpha+ (cDC1) subset, can take up exogenous antigen and route it onto MHC class I instead of MHC class II — a process called cross-presentation, first functionally described by Michael Bevan in 1976 as 'cross-priming.' This lets a dendritic cell that has only engulfed extracellular material (a dying infected cell, a tumor fragment, or a vaccine antigen that never itself infects the DC) still activate CD8+ T cells against it, which would otherwise be impossible since CD8 T cells only patrol MHC-I. Cross-presentation is the mechanistic reason many vaccines and immunotherapies are designed to be taken up by dendritic cells at all — it is often the only route to a CD8 response against an antigen the immune system never directly synthesizes inside its own cells.

lessons.workedExample: A student is designing a vaccine concept and wants to elicit a CD8+ T-cell response against a tumor antigen that patients' own dendritic cells never naturally produce internally. If the vaccine simply delivers free antigen protein, it would default into the exogenous pathway — phagocytosed, degraded in the phagolysosome, loaded onto MHC-II via HLA-DM, and shown only to CD4+ helper T cells. To get a CD8 response, the design must exploit cross-presentation: formulate the antigen so dendritic cells (particularly cDC1s) route a fraction of it out of the endosome and into the cytosolic/proteasome/TAP pathway feeding MHC-I, or alternatively deliver the antigen gene itself (e.g., in an mRNA or viral vector) so the DC synthesizes it endogenously and the standard MHC-I pathway applies without needing cross-presentation at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why does it matter whether your antigen ends up on MHC-I versus MHC-II?' because it is the single fact that determines whether a project's intervention engages killer or helper T cells. A weak answer conflates the two pathways or says 'the antigen gets presented' without specifying which. A strong answer names the proteasome-TAP-MHC-I route for cytosolic antigen versus the phagolysosome-HLA-DM-MHC-II route for extracellular antigen, and can explain cross-presentation as the deliberate exception that lets dendritic cells prime CD8 responses to antigen they only engulfed rather than synthesized.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the endogenous (MHC-I) antigen processing pathway.

items.text: Cytosolic protein is degraded by the proteasome
Peptides are transported into the ER by TAP1/TAP2
Peptide-loading complex (tapasin, calreticulin, ERp57) loads peptide onto MHC-I
Loaded MHC-I traffics to the cell surface

questions.explanation: Cytosolic degradation by the proteasome comes first, then TAP shuttles the resulting peptides into the ER, where the peptide-loading complex loads them onto MHC-I before surface trafficking.

questions.prompt: Match each pathway component to its pathway.

right.text: Endogenous (MHC-I) pathway
Exogenous (MHC-II) pathway

questions.explanation: TAP feeds proteasome-derived peptides into the MHC-I pathway; invariant chain and HLA-DM govern MHC-II loading, and phagolysosomal degradation supplies the peptides for that MHC-II pathway.

questions.prompt: What is cross-presentation, as demonstrated in Bevan's 1976 work on cross-priming?

options.text: A CD4 T cell directly killing an infected cell without MHC-II
A dendritic cell loading exogenously acquired antigen onto MHC-I to activate CD8 T cells
An antibody binding two different antigens simultaneously
A B cell presenting antigen on MHC-I instead of MHC-II

explanations.a: This describes neither cross-presentation nor a normal CD4 T-cell function; CD4 T cells do not kill via MHC-II recognition in this way.
explanations.b: Correct — cross-presentation lets dendritic cells route exogenously acquired antigen onto MHC-I, enabling CD8 T-cell priming against material the DC never synthesized internally.
explanations.c: This describes antibody bivalency or cross-reactivity, an unrelated concept from a different lesson.
explanations.d: Cross-presentation is a dendritic cell function; the question is about which pathway (I vs II) an antigen enters, not which cell type does it generically.

questions.prompt: Why does the endogenous MHC-I pathway allow early detection of viral infection?

options.text: It only activates after a cell has already died from infection
It samples proteins the cell is actively synthesizing, so viral peptides appear on MHC-I as soon as viral protein is made
It requires the virus to be phagocytosed by a separate cell first
MHC-I is only expressed after interferon-gamma signaling begins

explanations.a: The pathway functions continuously during normal cell life and infection, not only after cell death.
explanations.b: Correct — because the pathway samples ongoing cytosolic protein synthesis, viral peptides reach MHC-I as soon as the infected cell starts making viral protein, well before visible cell damage.
explanations.c: The endogenous pathway processes a cell's own internally synthesized protein; phagocytosis by another cell describes the separate exogenous/cross-presentation route.
explanations.d: MHC-I is constitutively expressed on nearly all nucleated cells; interferon-gamma boosts expression and swaps in the immunoproteasome but is not required for baseline MHC-I presentation.

lessons.label: Building the Repertoire: V(D)J Recombination

sections.heading: Cutting and pasting a receptor gene from pieces
sections.body: No single gene in the human genome encodes a complete antibody or TCR variable region. Instead, each locus (immunoglobulin heavy chain, light chain, TCR alpha, TCR beta, and so on) contains separate arrays of Variable (V), Diversity (D, for heavy/beta chains only), and Joining (J) gene segments. During early lymphocyte development, one V, one D, and one J segment (or just one V and one J, for loci lacking D) are randomly selected and physically joined together, deleting the DNA in between, to build a single functional variable-region exon. Susumu Tonegawa demonstrated this somatic DNA rearrangement in immunoglobulin genes between 1976 and 1983, showing that B cells physically rearrange their own genome during development — work that earned him the 1987 Nobel Prize and overturned the assumption that every cell's DNA is identical and unchanging.

sections.heading: The recombinase and the diversity it adds beyond simple shuffling
sections.body: The enzymes that execute this cutting are RAG1 and RAG2, identified by David Schatz and Marjorie Oettinger working in David Baltimore's lab: RAG1 was isolated in 1989 and shown, together with the newly found RAG2 in 1990, to synergistically activate V(D)J recombination when introduced into fibroblasts that don't normally undergo it. The RAG complex recognizes conserved recombination signal sequences flanking each V, D, and J segment and introduces double-strand breaks precisely at those boundaries; the cut ends are then rejoined by the general non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) DNA repair machinery. Combinatorial joining alone (picking which V, D, and J) already generates substantial diversity, but junctional diversity adds far more: the enzyme terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) inserts random, template-independent 'N-nucleotides' at the V-D and D-J junctions during repair, and imprecise trimming of segment ends before rejoining adds further variability at exactly the junctional region that forms CDR3, the most variable of the antigen-contacting loops.

sections.heading: One receptor per cell, and a repertoire in the billions
sections.body: A developing lymphocyte has two alleles of each receptor locus but must end up expressing only one functional receptor, a phenomenon called allelic exclusion: once one allele rearranges productively, further rearrangement is suppressed, so a given B or T cell commits to a single specificity rather than expressing a confusing mixture. Combining combinatorial joining across V, D, and J segments with junctional N-nucleotide addition and imprecise trimming, the theoretical diversity of the antibody repertoire has been estimated at roughly 10^11 distinct possible specificities — far exceeding the number of genes in the genome, and achieved entirely by recombining a few hundred inherited gene segments rather than encoding each specificity directly.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to explain why identical twins, who share the same germline DNA, can still have measurably different antibody repertoires. Germline DNA determines only the inventory of V, D, and J segments available at each locus — it does not determine which segments get joined in any given lymphocyte, nor what N-nucleotides TdT inserts at the junction, nor how segment ends are trimmed before NHEJ seals them. Because RAG-mediated joining and TdT addition are stochastic processes happening independently in millions of developing lymphocytes in each twin, the two individuals end up with overlapping gene-segment inventories but largely non-identical actual receptor sequences — the repertoire is built by somatic recombination, not inherited wholesale.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'where does antibody diversity actually come from, mechanistically?' to separate students who can name RAG and V(D)J recombination from students who only know the vocabulary. A weak answer says 'the immune system generates lots of different antibodies.' A strong answer names RAG1/RAG2 cutting at defined V, D, and J segment boundaries, explains that TdT-added N-nucleotides at the junctions contribute disproportionate diversity concentrated exactly at CDR3, and can state that allelic exclusion is what keeps each individual lymphocyte monospecific despite having two gene copies to draw from.

questions.prompt: Order these events in building a functional antibody variable-region exon.

items.text: RAG1/RAG2 cut DNA at recombination signal sequences flanking V, D, and J segments
TdT adds random N-nucleotides at the cut junctions
NHEJ machinery rejoins the trimmed, nucleotide-added ends
A single rearranged V(D)J exon is transcribed and translated into the variable domain

questions.explanation: RAG1/RAG2 first cut at the segment boundaries, TdT then adds N-nucleotides at those cut ends, NHEJ rejoins the processed ends into one continuous exon, and only then is that exon expressed as the variable domain.

questions.prompt: Who identified RAG1 and RAG2, and roughly when?

options.text: Susumu Tonegawa in 1976, who found antibody genes rearrange
Zinkernagel and Doherty in 1974, studying MHC restriction
Schatz and Oettinger in Baltimore's lab, RAG1 in 1989 and RAG2 in 1990
Porter and Edelman in the 1960s, characterizing antibody structure

explanations.a: Tonegawa demonstrated that immunoglobulin genes physically rearrange, but he did not identify the RAG1/RAG2 recombinase genes themselves; that came later.
explanations.b: Zinkernagel and Doherty's 1974 work established MHC restriction of T-cell recognition, an unrelated discovery.
explanations.c: Correct — Schatz isolated RAG1 in 1989 and, with Oettinger, showed RAG2 synergistically activates recombination in 1990, both in David Baltimore's lab.
explanations.d: Porter and Edelman worked out antibody chain structure (Fab/Fc, heavy/light chains) in the 1960s, unrelated to the recombinase enzymes.

questions.prompt: What is allelic exclusion?

options.text: The process by which TdT adds N-nucleotides at V-D and D-J junctions
The mechanism ensuring only one allele at a receptor locus is productively rearranged and expressed per lymphocyte
The deletion of DNA between joined V, D, and J segments
The process by which RAG1 and RAG2 recognize recombination signal sequences

explanations.a: N-nucleotide addition is a source of junctional diversity, a separate concept from allelic exclusion.
explanations.b: Correct — allelic exclusion suppresses further rearrangement once one allele has productively rearranged, so each lymphocyte expresses a single receptor specificity.
explanations.c: This describes a mechanical byproduct of the joining process itself, not allelic exclusion.
explanations.d: Recognition of recombination signal sequences is how RAG1/RAG2 find their cut sites, unrelated to the one-allele-per-cell rule.

questions.prompt: Match each diversity-generating mechanism to what it contributes.

left.text: Combinatorial joining of V, D, J segments

right.text: Diversity from which segments are chosen and paired
Diversity from the exact sequence at the joint itself, concentrated in CDR3

questions.explanation: Combinatorial joining diversifies which V, D, and J segments end up paired together, while junctional diversity from TdT and end-trimming adds further sequence variability precisely at the joint, which forms the CDR3 loop.

lessons.label: Affinity, Avidity, and Cross-Reactivity

sections.heading: Affinity: quantifying one binding site's grip
sections.body: The strength of a single antibody binding site for a single epitope is measured as its affinity, expressed through the dissociation constant Kd — the antigen concentration at which half the binding sites are occupied at equilibrium. Kd is set by the ratio of the off-rate (koff, how fast the complex falls apart) to the on-rate (kon, how fast it forms): Kd = koff/kon. A lower Kd means tighter binding, since it takes a lower antigen concentration to half-saturate the site. Naive B cells entering a response typically produce antibodies with micromolar-range Kd values — comparatively weak. Over the course of a germinal-center response, somatic hypermutation and selection for higher-affinity variants (affinity maturation) can drive Kd down into the nanomolar or even picomolar range, meaning the antibody can bind up to a million times more tightly for the best picomolar responders by the time a response matures.

sections.heading: Avidity: what multivalency adds on top
sections.body: Affinity describes one binding site interacting with one epitope in isolation, but most real interactions are multivalent: a bivalent IgG has two arms, and a pentameric IgM has ten. Avidity is the combined strength of all simultaneous binding events, and it is not simply additive — because all bonds must break at once for the complex to fully dissociate, avidity can exceed the sum of individual affinities by orders of magnitude. This is why an antibody with only modest per-site affinity can still bind a repetitive surface (a virus capsid displaying many copies of the same epitope) essentially irreversibly in avidity terms, even though the same antibody as an isolated Fab fragment would dissociate readily. Avidity is also why decavalent IgM, produced early and with unrefined affinity, is still an effective first responder against particulate antigens like whole bacteria or virions.

sections.heading: Cross-reactivity: specificity is a matter of degree, not absolute
sections.body: No antibody binds a single, uniquely defined molecular shape and nothing else; specificity is really a probability distribution over how well a binding site accommodates related shapes. Cross-reactivity occurs when an antibody raised against one epitope also binds a structurally similar epitope on a different antigen, because CDR loops read surface shape and chemistry rather than molecular identity. This has real consequences on both sides: cross-reactive neutralizing antibodies can protect against related strains of a pathogen the immune system has never directly seen (part of why some vaccines confer partial cross-strain protection), while unwanted cross-reactivity is a recognized source of false-positive signal in immunoassays like ELISA, and molecular mimicry between a pathogen epitope and a self-protein is implicated in some autoimmune phenomena, such as cross-reactivity between streptococcal M protein and cardiac tissue proteins in rheumatic fever.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs an ELISA to detect antibodies against Protein X and gets a strong positive signal in a sample expected to be negative. Two explanations fit the affinity/avidity/cross-reactivity framework differently: (1) the antibody in the sample has genuinely low affinity for Protein X but the assay's coated antigen is presented at high density, so multivalent avidity effects amplify a weak true interaction into a strong signal; or (2) the antibody was raised against a different, structurally related protein Y and is cross-reacting with Protein X's similar epitope, giving a strong signal against the wrong target entirely. Distinguishing them requires a competition assay: pre-incubating the sample with free Protein Y before running the ELISA. If signal against Protein X drops sharply, cross-reactivity with Y is the likely explanation rather than genuine low-affinity avidity-amplified binding to X.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'is your antibody actually specific, or could it be cross-reacting?' because an uncontrolled positive signal in any antibody-based assay is uninterpretable without addressing this. A weak answer treats a positive signal as proof of specific binding. A strong answer distinguishes affinity (single-site Kd) from avidity (multivalent combined strength) and explains why high avidity can mask low affinity, then names a concrete control — such as a competition or blocking experiment — used to rule out cross-reactivity as the source of a signal.

questions.prompt: The dissociation constant Kd is defined as which ratio?

options.text: kon/koff
koff/kon
koff multiplied by kon
The number of binding sites divided by antigen concentration

explanations.a: This inverted ratio would give the association constant Ka, not Kd.
explanations.b: Correct — Kd = koff/kon; a lower Kd (favoring a slow off-rate relative to on-rate) indicates tighter, higher-affinity binding.
explanations.c: Multiplying the two rates does not yield a meaningful equilibrium constant in this context.
explanations.d: Kd is defined by binding kinetics (on- and off-rates), not by a simple site-count-to-concentration ratio.

questions.prompt: Why can pentameric IgM with only micromolar per-site affinity still bind a virus particle essentially irreversibly?

options.text: IgM's individual Fab arms have nanomolar affinity, unlike IgG
Its ten simultaneous binding sites give it high avidity, since all bonds would need to break at once to dissociate
IgM does not follow normal binding kinetics
The virus surface actively pulls IgM into place

explanations.a: Early IgM is typically not higher per-site affinity than later-matured IgG; the effect described comes from multivalency, not superior single-site affinity.
explanations.b: Correct — because dissociation requires all ten bonds to release simultaneously, combined avidity can far exceed what per-site affinity alone would predict.
explanations.c: IgM follows the same binding kinetics as any antibody; its ten valences change the effective combined strength, not the underlying kinetic rules.
explanations.d: There is no active pulling mechanism; the effect is purely a consequence of multivalent simultaneous binding.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct description.

right.text: Strength of one binding site for one epitope, measured by Kd
Combined strength of multiple simultaneous binding events
An antibody binding a structurally related but non-identical epitope

questions.explanation: Affinity is a single-site property quantified by Kd; avidity is the emergent combined strength of multivalent binding; cross-reactivity describes binding a related-but-different epitope due to shared shape or chemistry.

questions.prompt: Order these Kd values from tightest to weakest binding.

items.text: 1 picomolar (10^-12 M)
1 nanomolar (10^-9 M)
1 micromolar (10^-6 M)

questions.explanation: A lower Kd means tighter binding, since less antigen is needed to half-saturate the site, so picomolar is tightest, followed by nanomolar, then micromolar as the weakest of the three.

lessons.label: Activating a B Cell: T-Dependent and T-Independent

sections.heading: Two Signals, Not One
sections.body: A B cell's receptor (BCR) is a membrane-bound antibody that recognizes antigen directly, in its native three-dimensional shape, unlike a T cell receptor that only sees processed peptide on MHC. When antigen cross-links enough surface Ig molecules, the BCR delivers signal one: a cascade through Ig-alpha/Ig-beta that lowers the cell's activation threshold and drives it to endocytose the antigen. But for the vast majority of B cells responding to protein antigens, signal one alone produces anergy or no response at all rather than a full-blown antibody response. The requirement for a second, independent signal is a safety feature: most self antigens are abundant and would cross-link BCRs constantly, so making full activation depend on confirmation from a helper T cell -- itself already screened for reactivity against self peptides in the thymus -- adds a checkpoint against autoreactive B cells slipping through.

sections.heading: T-Dependent Activation: Linked Recognition and CD40
sections.body: For protein antigens, the B cell that has captured antigen via its BCR internalizes it, degrades it in endosomes, and displays peptide fragments on MHC class II. It then migrates to the border of the B cell follicle and T cell zone, hunting for a CD4+ helper T cell -- specifically a follicular helper (Tfh) cell -- that recognizes the same peptide-MHC-II complex. This is linked recognition: B and T cell must both be specific for epitopes on the same antigen, even if not the identical epitope. Contact triggers the B cell's second signal: CD40 ligand (CD40L, CD154) on the T cell engages CD40 on the B cell, alongside cytokines such as IL-21 and IL-4 delivered directly at the immune synapse. This combination drives proliferation, germinal-center entry, class-switch recombination, and somatic hypermutation. Loss-of-function mutations in CD40L cause hyper-IgM syndrome, in which patients make plenty of IgM but essentially no IgG, IgA, or IgE -- a direct clinical demonstration of what CD40 signaling is for.

sections.heading: T-Independent Activation: Fast, Shallow, No Memory
sections.body: Polysaccharide antigens -- bacterial capsules, LPS -- can activate B cells without T cell help. Their repetitive, densely spaced epitopes cross-link large numbers of BCRs at once (TI-2 antigens, like pneumococcal capsular polysaccharide), and some, like LPS, co-engage Toll-like receptors, supplying an intrinsic substitute for signal two. The response is quick and IgM-heavy but shallow: without CD40 signaling there is little class-switch recombination, essentially no somatic hypermutation, and no durable memory B cell pool. It is also weak in infants, whose marginal-zone B cells (the main responders to TI-2 antigens) are functionally immature until roughly age two -- the reason plain polysaccharide vaccines fail in young children and had to be re-engineered as protein-conjugate vaccines that force a T-dependent response instead.

lessons.workedExample: Compare two pneumococcal vaccines. PPSV23 is unconjugated capsular polysaccharide: it triggers a classic T-independent response, protects older children and adults, but essentially fails in infants under two and produces no boosted response on revaccination because no memory B cells form. PCV13 chemically conjugates the same polysaccharide to a carrier protein (a diphtheria toxin variant, CRM197). Now a B cell that binds the polysaccharide through its BCR endocytoses the whole conjugate, processes the attached protein, and presents protein peptide on MHC-II -- recruiting CD4 T cell help for what was originally a T-independent antigen. The result: strong IgG titers, affinity maturation, and immunologic memory in infants, which is why conjugate vaccines are now standard in the childhood immunization schedule.
