sections.body: When a bacterial population is not killed by an antibiotic, there are three mechanistically distinct explanations, and mixing them up is the single most common error in student write-ups. Resistance is a heritable change, usually a mutation or an acquired gene (a beta-lactamase, an efflux pump, a modified target), that raises the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) — the lowest drug concentration that stops visible growth. A resistant strain grows normally at a dose that would have stopped its ancestor. Tolerance is different: the MIC does not change, but the population is killed more slowly at doses well above the MIC. Tolerance is measured by the minimum duration for killing, most often MDK99 (the time to kill 99% of the population) — a tolerant strain might need many hours longer to hit the same kill fraction. Persistence is narrower still: it is not a property of the whole population but of a small subpopulation, typically 0.001-1%, of dormant cells that survive a lethal dose while genetically identical, drug-susceptible siblings die around them. Regrow that survivor fraction and it produces a population just as susceptible as the original — persistence is not inherited. This three-way framework was formalized by Brauner, Fridman, Gefen, and Balaban in a widely cited 2016 Nature Reviews Microbiology paper, 'Distinguishing between resistance, tolerance and persistence to antibiotic treatment,' which argued that conflating these phenomena has repeatedly confounded both laboratory measurements and the clinical interpretation of why an antibiotic course fails — the same Brauner-group MDK99 metric introduced in a later lesson traces back to this paper's push for a rigorous, measurable vocabulary.

sections.heading: Why a standard MIC test only ever catches resistance
sections.body: The MIC assay works by diluting drug across a plate or broth series and reading which wells show visible growth after roughly 16-20 hours of incubation. That endpoint measures whether growth was stopped, not how fast cells died — it is a snapshot of net proliferation, blind to killing kinetics. A tolerant strain has an unchanged MIC because the drug still eventually suppresses growth; the difference only shows up in a time-kill curve, where survivor counts are tracked over hours at a fixed lethal concentration. A persister subpopulation is invisible to MIC testing for the same reason: 99.9% of cells die on schedule and drop the count below the assay's detection floor, while the surviving fraction is too small to register as growth in the incubation window. Clinically, this matters because a lab report of 'susceptible' by MIC criteria says nothing about whether the standard antibiotic course will actually clear a tolerant or persister-forming strain from a patient — chronic and relapsing infections often involve organisms with unchanged MICs.

lessons.workedExample: Three E. coli cultures are each exposed to 10x the ampicillin MIC. Culture A carries a plasmid-borne beta-lactamase; its measured MIC is 500x higher than wild type, so 10x the original dose does nothing — that is resistance. Culture B has an unchanged MIC on the standard test, but a time-kill assay shows it takes 8 hours to reach a 99% kill instead of the wild type's 2 hours — that is tolerance, driven by slower growth and metabolism, not drug inactivation. Culture C also has an unchanged MIC and a normal initial kill rate, but after the first 2 hours, a residual 0.01% of cells stop dying and the curve flattens into a plateau — those are persisters, and if regrown from that plateau, the resulting culture is exactly as susceptible as the original.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this distinction because 'my bacteria became resistant' is the most common overclaim in an AMR project, and it is usually wrong — a slower kill curve or a survivor plateau is tolerance or persistence, not resistance, and conflating them misstates both the mechanism and the clinical stakes. A weak answer treats any surviving colony as proof of resistance. A strong answer names which metric was actually measured (MIC vs. a time-kill curve) and states what that metric can and cannot distinguish.

questions.prompt: A strain's MIC is unchanged from wild type, but a time-kill assay shows it takes 8 hours instead of 2 to kill 99% of the population at 10x MIC. This strain is best described as:

options.text: Resistant
Tolerant
Persistent
Susceptible with no notable phenotype

explanations.a: Resistance requires a raised MIC; this strain's MIC did not change.
explanations.b: Correct — an unchanged MIC with a slower population-wide kill rate, measured as an increased MDK99, is the definition of tolerance.
explanations.c: Persistence describes a small dormant subpopulation surviving while the bulk population dies at the normal rate; here the whole population's kill rate slowed.
explanations.d: An 8-hour vs. 2-hour difference in MDK99 is a real, measurable phenotype, not a null result.

questions.prompt: Why does a standard 16-20 hour MIC test fail to detect persister cells in a culture?

options.text: Persister cells actively grow faster than the MIC assay can track
The MIC assay only reads whether visible growth was stopped, not the killing kinetics or a rare surviving subpopulation
Persister cells are resistant to the dyes used in MIC assays
MIC assays are always run below the MIC, so no cells die

explanations.a: Persisters are dormant, not fast-growing; growth rate is not why they evade detection.
explanations.b: Correct — the MIC endpoint is a growth/no-growth snapshot after incubation, blind to the time course of killing and too coarse to register a tiny surviving fraction.
explanations.c: MIC assays typically read turbidity or visible growth, not a dye persisters would resist.
explanations.d: MIC testing deliberately spans concentrations above and below the MIC; that is not the reason persisters are missed.

questions.prompt: Match each survival phenotype to its defining feature.

right.text: Heritable increase in MIC
Unchanged MIC, but the whole population dies more slowly (higher MDK99)
A small dormant subpopulation survives while genetically identical siblings die

questions.explanation: Resistance changes the MIC itself; tolerance changes how fast the whole population is killed above an unchanged MIC; persistence is a subpopulation phenomenon where only a small fraction survives, without any change to the MIC or the bulk kill rate.

questions.prompt: Order these steps as they would occur when characterizing whether a strain is resistant, tolerant, or persistent.

items.text: Run a standard MIC assay to check whether the MIC itself is elevated
If the MIC is unchanged, run a time-kill assay at a dose well above the MIC
Check whether the whole population's kill rate is slowed (tolerance) or a small fraction plateaus and survives (persistence)
Regrow any surviving fraction and retest its MIC to confirm it is not heritable

questions.explanation: MIC testing comes first because it is the fastest way to rule resistance in or out; only if the MIC is unchanged does a time-kill curve become informative for distinguishing tolerance from persistence, and regrowth-and-retest is the final step that confirms survival was not due to a heritable change.

lessons.label: The Biofilm Lifestyle

sections.heading: From free-swimming to settled: the biofilm life cycle
sections.body: Most bacteria can switch between two lifestyles: planktonic, free-floating single cells, and sessile, attached to a surface inside a self-built community. The biofilm life cycle runs through four recognized stages. Attachment begins reversibly, when flagella- or pili-driven cells encounter a surface and stick loosely through weak physical forces; within hours this becomes irreversible as surface adhesins lock cells in place. Once attached, cells begin secreting the extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix, a self-produced scaffold built mainly from exopolysaccharides, extracellular DNA (eDNA) released by cell lysis, and structural proteins. In maturation, the community grows into a three-dimensional architecture — often mushroom- or tower-shaped, laced with water channels that ferry nutrients and remove waste, closely resembling a primitive circulatory system. Finally, dispersal releases cells (or fragments) back into the planktonic state, often triggered by nutrient depletion, oxygen limitation, or matrix-degrading enzymes the bacteria produce themselves, to seed new sites.

sections.heading: Quorum sensing: how a population decides together
sections.body: Building and dispersing a biofilm is a coordinated, density-dependent decision, not a cell-by-cell accident, and the coordination mechanism is quorum sensing. Bacteria continuously secrete small diffusible signal molecules called autoinducers; as the local population grows, autoinducer concentration rises in step. The founding system, discovered in the bioluminescent marine bacterium Vibrio fischeri, uses a LuxI synthase enzyme to produce an acyl-homoserine lactone (AHL) autoinducer and a LuxR receptor that binds it once concentration crosses a threshold, switching on a bank of genes in unison across the population — in V. fischeri, the light-producing luciferase operon; in biofilm-forming species, genes for EPS production, virulence factors, and dispersal enzymes. Because the LuxR-AHL complex only activates gene expression once enough cells are present to have driven autoinducer concentration high enough, a single bacterium 'senses' whether it has enough neighbors to make coordinated behavior worthwhile — hence quorum. Gram-positive species use an analogous logic with peptide autoinducers and two-component sensor systems instead of AHLs, but the density-threshold principle is the same. The term 'quorum sensing' itself was coined in 1994 by Fuqua, Winans, and Greenberg to name this density-dependent logic, replacing earlier, more mechanism-specific labels like 'autoinduction.' Because autoinducer diffuses away rapidly in an open, well-mixed liquid, the threshold concentration needed to activate LuxR is realistically only reached inside a diffusion-restricted space — a microcolony a few tens to a few hundred micrometers across, the same scale biofilm microcolonies actually grow to — which is why quorum sensing reliably switches on inside a crowded biofilm but rarely triggers in a dilute planktonic culture.

lessons.workedExample: A single Pseudomonas aeruginosa cell lands on the inner wall of a catheter tube. Within an hour it attaches irreversibly via surface adhesins, and over the next day it divides while secreting EPS, alginate polysaccharide, and eDNA from lysed neighbors, building a mushroom-shaped microcolony threaded with water channels. As the microcolony's cell density climbs, AHL autoinducer accumulates in the confined catheter lumen until it crosses the LuxR-homolog activation threshold, switching on genes for further matrix production and for the enzymes that will later degrade the matrix from within. Days later, nutrient depletion at the biofilm's core triggers dispersal: matrix-degrading enzymes free a subpopulation of cells, which re-enter the bloodstream planktonically and can seed a new infection site elsewhere in the body.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing biofilm biology wants to know whether a student understands that a biofilm is an actively built, regulated structure rather than passive sludge — because that distinction is exactly what makes biofilms a design target (disrupt the matrix, jam the signaling) rather than just a dose-more-drug problem. A weak answer describes a biofilm as 'bacteria sticking together.' A strong answer names the EPS components, at least one life-cycle stage besides attachment, and explains quorum sensing as a density threshold, not just 'bacteria communicating.'

questions.prompt: Order the four stages of the biofilm life cycle.

items.text: Reversible then irreversible attachment to a surface
Secretion of the EPS matrix
Maturation into a 3D architecture with water channels
Dispersal of cells back to the planktonic state

questions.explanation: A biofilm begins with surface attachment, is built up by matrix secretion, develops into a mature 3D structure with channels for nutrient and waste flow, and eventually disperses cells to seed new sites.

questions.prompt: In the LuxI/LuxR quorum-sensing system first described in Vibrio fischeri, what does the LuxR receptor do?

options.text: Synthesizes the autoinducer molecule
Pumps autoinducer out of the cell
Binds accumulated autoinducer and activates a set of genes once a density threshold is crossed
Degrades the EPS matrix during dispersal

explanations.a: Autoinducer synthesis is LuxI's job, not LuxR's.
explanations.b: Autoinducers diffuse rather than being actively pumped in this classic system; that is not LuxR's function.
explanations.c: Correct — LuxR binds the accumulated autoinducer and, once concentration (a proxy for cell density) crosses a threshold, activates transcription of the target gene set.
explanations.d: Matrix degradation during dispersal is carried out by separate enzymes, not by LuxR itself.

questions.prompt: Match each EPS matrix component to its origin or role.

right.text: Secreted polysaccharide forming the bulk scaffold
Released by lysed cells, contributes to matrix integrity
Provides structural cross-linking within the matrix

questions.explanation: The EPS matrix is a composite: exopolysaccharide forms the bulk scaffold, eDNA comes from lysed cells and reinforces matrix integrity, and structural proteins cross-link the whole assembly.

questions.prompt: Why is dispersal an important stage of the biofilm life cycle for infection spread?

options.text: It permanently destroys the biofilm so infection cannot recur
It releases cells back to the planktonic state, allowing them to seed new infection sites
It is when the EPS matrix is first produced
It only occurs in Vibrio fischeri, not in pathogenic biofilm formers

explanations.a: Dispersal releases a subset of cells; it does not eliminate the biofilm and a new one can regrow from remaining attached cells.
explanations.b: Correct — dispersal, often triggered by nutrient depletion or matrix-degrading enzymes, sends planktonic cells or fragments off to establish new colonization sites, which is central to how biofilm infections spread.
explanations.c: EPS secretion happens earlier, right after attachment, not during dispersal.
explanations.d: Dispersal is a general biofilm life-cycle stage seen across many biofilm-forming species, including pathogens like Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus.

lessons.label: Why Biofilms Defy Antibiotics

sections.heading: Recalcitrance without a single resistance gene
sections.body: A biofilm can survive drug concentrations hundreds of times its own planktonic MIC even when every cell inside it carries no resistance gene at all — a property called recalcitrance, and it is the reason biofilm infections are so hard to clear with standard dosing. The first layer of the explanation is physical: the EPS matrix of exopolysaccharide, eDNA, and protein restricts diffusion and can directly bind and sequester charged antibiotics like aminoglycosides before they ever reach a cell, so the effective dose deep inside a biofilm can be far lower than the dose applied outside it. This is a rate effect, not a wall — most drugs eventually penetrate given enough time — but that lag is often enough to let the second layer of defense engage. Tseng, Parsek, and colleagues demonstrated this rate effect directly in 2013, showing that Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilm matrix components measurably slow tobramycin penetration into a mature biofilm over a multi-hour timescale even though the drug eventually reaches interior cells, confirming that the matrix delays exposure rather than blocking it outright. Aminoglycosides like tobramycin are especially vulnerable to this effect because the drug's positively charged amine groups bind electrostatically to the anionic polysaccharides (such as alginate) and eDNA that dominate the matrix, sequestering a meaningful fraction of the applied dose near the biofilm surface before it ever reaches cells at depth.

sections.heading: Dormancy gradients and drugs with nothing to hit
sections.body: Nutrient and oxygen gradients form across a mature biofilm: cells near the surface and channels have full access and grow near-normally, while cells deep in the interior are starved and often near-dormant. This matters mechanistically because most antibiotics target active processes — beta-lactams block active cell-wall synthesis, aminoglycosides and other protein synthesis inhibitors require active ribosomes and, for aminoglycosides, an active proton-motive force to be taken up at all. A dormant cell that is not building wall or making protein simply presents no functional target, so the drug can be fully present at the cell and still do nothing — a mechanism entirely distinct from resistance or from matrix-limited penetration. On top of this metabolic gradient, biofilm cells mount generalized stress responses (including the same stringent response seen in free-living persisters) and the sessile environment itself enriches for the persister subpopulation, so a biofilm behaves like a tissue with a built-in tolerant core even before any single gene has changed. The result is that three separate mechanisms — matrix diffusion/binding, metabolic dormancy, and an enriched persister pool — stack on top of each other, so a treatment course calibrated to the planktonic MIC routinely fails against the same organism once it is living in a biofilm.

lessons.workedExample: A Staphylococcus aureus biofilm on an infected orthopedic implant is treated with vancomycin at 10x the strain's planktonic MIC. Surface-layer cells, well-supplied with oxygen and nutrients, die within hours as expected. But cells in the biofilm's anoxic interior are not actively synthesizing new cell wall, so vancomycin — which blocks wall cross-linking — has no active process to interrupt there; those cells survive the same drug exposure indefinitely, not because of any mutation, but because they are metabolically idle. When the implant is later removed and cultured, the recovered organisms test fully vancomycin-susceptible by standard MIC assay, confirming the biofilm survival was recalcitrance, not resistance.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on this because 'biofilms are resistant' is a common but sloppy claim — the correct and more interesting story is that biofilms survive through matrix limitation, metabolic dormancy, and persister enrichment, none of which show up as a changed MIC or a resistance gene. A strong answer names at least two of these three mechanisms and explains why a drug with no active target (a dormant cell) is a fundamentally different failure mode than a drug that is pumped out or degraded (true resistance).

questions.prompt: A cell deep in a biofilm's anoxic interior survives a beta-lactam treatment that easily kills genetically identical cells near the surface. The most likely explanation is:

options.text: The interior cell acquired a resistance mutation the surface cells lack
The interior cell is not actively synthesizing cell wall, so the drug's target process is not occurring
Beta-lactams cannot diffuse through any part of a biofilm matrix
The interior cell has a permanently higher MIC than the surface cells

explanations.a: Recalcitrance in this scenario requires no genetic change; interior and surface cells are genetically identical.
explanations.b: Correct — beta-lactams block active cell-wall synthesis, so a dormant cell not building wall presents no target for the drug to act on, regardless of drug concentration reaching it.
explanations.c: Matrix diffusion slows penetration but does not fully block it; the deeper issue for dormant cells is the lack of an active target, not zero drug exposure.
explanations.d: MIC is a population-level, heritable measure; a single non-growing cell does not have a separately elevated MIC.

questions.prompt: Match each biofilm survival mechanism to its description.

right.text: EPS components slow penetration or sequester charged drugs before they reach cells
Nutrient/oxygen limitation in the interior leaves cells with no active drug target
The sessile environment increases the fraction of dormant survivor cells beyond what a planktonic culture would have

questions.explanation: These are three distinct, stacking mechanisms: physical/chemical limitation of drug access, a metabolic gradient that removes the drug's active target, and enrichment of an already-existing dormant subpopulation.

questions.prompt: Why is 'recalcitrance' a more accurate term than 'resistance' for describing why an untreated biofilm survives high-dose antibiotics?

options.text: Because recalcitrance requires a heritable MIC increase, just measured differently
Because the surviving cells, once removed from the biofilm and retested, are typically still susceptible by standard MIC testing
Because recalcitrance only applies to Gram-positive bacteria
Because resistance genes are always silenced inside a biofilm

explanations.a: Recalcitrance specifically does not require any change to the MIC; that is what separates it from resistance.
explanations.b: Correct — biofilm cells recovered and tested outside the biofilm context are typically fully susceptible, showing the survival was due to the biofilm environment (matrix, dormancy, persisters) rather than any heritable genetic change.
explanations.c: Recalcitrance is documented across both Gram-negative (e.g., Pseudomonas aeruginosa) and Gram-positive (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus) biofilm formers.
explanations.d: There is no general silencing of resistance genes in biofilms; recalcitrance operates independently of whether resistance genes are present at all.

lessons.label: Persister Cells and Dormancy

sections.heading: Bigger's discovery and the biphasic kill curve
sections.body: Persister cells were first documented by Joseph Bigger in 1944, who found that penicillin, despite being highly effective against growing Staphylococcus cultures, always left behind a small surviving fraction — and that this fraction was not a resistant mutant, since regrowing it produced a population just as penicillin-susceptible as the original. Bigger coined the term 'persisters' for these survivors. The signature of persistence in a lab assay is a biphasic time-kill curve: plot surviving cell count (on a log scale) against time of drug exposure, and instead of a single straight decline, the curve shows a steep initial drop as the bulk, actively growing population dies quickly, followed by a shallow tail or plateau where a small subpopulation — often 0.001% to 1% of the original count — dies far more slowly or not at all over the assay window. That kink in the curve is the experimental fingerprint distinguishing a persister-forming strain from one that simply dies uniformly.

sections.heading: Seeing it in single cells, and what flips the switch
sections.body: For six decades after Bigger, persistence was inferred from population-level kill curves alone. In 2004, Nathalie Balaban and colleagues used time-lapse microscopy to track individual E. coli cells through antibiotic exposure and showed directly that persisters exist before drug is ever added — they are rare, pre-existing dormant cells within an otherwise growing population, not cells that are induced into dormancy by the drug itself. This confirmed persistence as a bet-hedging strategy: a lineage that stochastically produces a small number of slow- or non-growing cells at all times pays a fitness cost in normal conditions but gains a hedge against sudden, lethal stress. Two molecular switches are the leading proposed triggers for this dormant state. Toxin-antitoxin (TA) modules, such as the hipBA system, encode a stable toxin (HipA) that shuts down normal cell processes and a less stable antitoxin (HipB) that normally neutralizes it; when antitoxin degrades faster than it is replenished, free toxin accumulates and drives the cell into dormancy. Separately, the stringent response, triggered by nutrient starvation and mediated by the alarmone (p)ppGpp, redirects the cell's machinery away from growth and toward survival, and elevated (p)ppGpp is strongly associated with persister formation. Both mechanisms converge on the same outcome: a metabolically quiet cell with no active targets for most antibiotics to hit.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher exposes an exponential-phase E. coli culture to a high dose of ciprofloxacin and samples surviving CFU/mL every 30 minutes for 6 hours. The first 90 minutes show a steep log-linear drop of about 4 orders of magnitude as the bulk population dies. From 90 minutes onward, the curve flattens: surviving counts barely change for the remaining 4.5 hours, settling at roughly 0.01% of the starting population. That flat tail is the persister fraction. To confirm these are persisters rather than resistant mutants, the researcher isolates surviving cells, grows them into a fresh culture, and repeats the same ciprofloxacin exposure — the new culture shows the identical biphasic curve with the identical steep drop and 0.01% tail, rather than uniform resistance, exactly matching what Bigger found with penicillin in 1944 and what Balaban's 2004 single-cell imaging showed directly.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe persister biology because it is easy to state ('some cells survive') but the interesting content is mechanistic: a strong answer names Bigger's original 1944 penicillin finding or Balaban's 2004 single-cell confirmation, describes the biphasic kill curve as the diagnostic signature, and can name at least one proposed molecular trigger (a toxin-antitoxin module like hipBA, or the (p)ppGpp stringent response) rather than gesturing vaguely at 'dormancy.' A weak answer conflates persisters with resistant mutants or cannot explain what the plateau in a kill curve actually represents.

questions.prompt: Balaban and colleagues' 2004 single-cell microscopy study showed that persister cells:

options.text: Are induced into dormancy only after antibiotic exposure begins
Pre-exist as rare dormant cells within a growing population before any drug is added
Carry a mutation that raises their MIC
Make up roughly half of any bacterial population at all times

explanations.a: The study's key finding was the opposite — persisters were present before drug exposure, not created by it.
explanations.b: Correct — time-lapse imaging of individual cells showed rare dormant cells already existing within the population prior to antibiotic treatment, supporting a bet-hedging model.
explanations.c: Persisters are not defined by any MIC-raising mutation; regrown persister populations remain fully susceptible.
explanations.d: Persisters are typically a small minority, often well under 1% of a population, not roughly half.

questions.prompt: What does the shallow 'tail' in a biphasic antibiotic time-kill curve represent?

options.text: A pipetting artifact that should be discarded from the data
A slowly dying or non-dying subpopulation of dormant persister cells
The point at which all remaining cells have become resistant mutants
The moment the antibiotic has fully degraded in solution

explanations.a: The tail is a real, reproducible biological signal, first documented by Bigger in 1944, not an artifact.
explanations.b: Correct — the shallow tail is the persister subpopulation, dying much more slowly than the bulk population that produced the initial steep drop.
explanations.c: Regrowing cells from the tail typically reproduces the same susceptible, biphasic pattern, showing the survivors are not resistant mutants.
explanations.d: Drug degradation is not the standard explanation for a reproducible, regrowable persister tail.

questions.prompt: Match each proposed dormancy trigger to its mechanism.

right.text: A stable toxin accumulates when its antitoxin degrades faster than it is replenished, shutting down normal cell processes
An alarmone produced under starvation redirects cell machinery away from growth toward survival

questions.explanation: hipBA works through toxin-antitoxin imbalance (free HipA toxin driving dormancy), while the stringent response works through the (p)ppGpp alarmone produced under nutrient starvation; both converge on a dormant, low-target state.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the history of persister-cell discovery.

items.text: Bigger documents a small penicillin-surviving fraction in Staphylococcus and names it 'persisters' (1944)
Persistence is inferred from population-level biphasic kill curves for decades
Balaban and colleagues use time-lapse single-cell microscopy to show persisters pre-exist before drug exposure (2004)

questions.explanation: Bigger's 1944 work established the phenomenon at the population level; it was studied via kill curves for roughly six decades before Balaban's 2004 single-cell imaging directly confirmed persisters exist as a pre-existing dormant subpopulation.

lessons.label: Measuring Tolerance, Persistence, and Biofilm Susceptibility

sections.heading: Sizing the persister fraction with a time-kill curve
sections.body: Because MIC testing cannot see tolerance or persistence, quantifying either phenotype requires a time-kill assay: expose a culture to a fixed, lethal drug concentration (typically several multiples of MIC) and plate surviving CFU/mL at multiple timepoints. Plotted on a log scale against time, a biphasic curve separates into the steep initial slope, reflecting the bulk population's death rate, and the shallow late plateau, whose height directly estimates the persister fraction — the ratio of the plateau's surviving count to the starting count. This single assay format underlies most persister quantification in the literature, and comparing the slope of the initial phase across strains is also how tolerance is distinguished from a normal kill rate.

sections.heading: Standardized tolerance metrics: MDK99 and the TDtest
sections.body: To make tolerance comparable across strains and studies, Brauner and colleagues proposed the metric MDK99 (minimum duration for killing 99% of the population) and MDK99.99 (for a 99.99% kill), read directly off a time-kill curve as the time needed to reach that kill fraction at a defined drug concentration. A strain with an MDK99 several times longer than a reference strain, at an unchanged MIC, is operationally defined as tolerant. Running a full time-kill curve for every clinical isolate is slow, so a faster diagnostic, the TDtest, was developed to screen for tolerance from a modified disk-diffusion setup: a tolerant strain regrows within the normally-clear zone of inhibition after the disk is removed and fresh nutrient is supplied, producing a visually distinct 'haze' of regrowth that a standard zone-of-inhibition read would miss entirely.

sections.heading: Testing biofilms as biofilms: the MBEC device
sections.body: Because a biofilm's recalcitrance depends on its intact structure, biofilm susceptibility cannot be read from a broth MIC test at all — the biofilm has to be grown, then challenged, then assessed as an attached community. The Calgary Biofilm Device, commercialized as the MBEC (minimum biofilm eradication concentration) assay, grows biofilms on a set of plastic pegs fitted into a standard 96-well plate lid, exposes the peg-grown biofilms to a dilution series of antibiotic, then transfers the pegs to fresh drug-free medium and reads which concentrations prevented any regrowth. The resulting MBEC value — the lowest concentration that fully eradicates the attached biofilm — is routinely 10 to 1,000 times higher than the same strain's planktonic MIC, giving a concrete, quantitative measure of exactly how much recalcitrance the biofilm state adds.

lessons.workedExample: A lab wants to characterize a clinical Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate suspected of causing relapsing infections. First, a standard MIC assay returns 2 micrograms/mL of tobramycin, unremarkable and fully susceptible by breakpoint. A TDtest disk-diffusion assay is then run and shows regrowth haze inside the inhibition zone, flagging tolerance; a follow-up time-kill curve confirms an MDK99 of 9 hours versus 3 hours for a reference susceptible strain. Finally, the isolate is grown as a biofilm on Calgary Biofilm Device pegs and challenged with a tobramycin dilution series: the MBEC comes back at 512 micrograms/mL — 256 times the planktonic MIC — showing that the same organism that looks unremarkable by MIC testing is both tolerant in suspension and dramatically harder to eradicate once biofilm-attached.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks how a project actually measured tolerance, persistence, or biofilm susceptibility because 'we tested resistance' collapses three different assays into one word — a strong answer names the specific method (a time-kill curve and its MDK99 readout for tolerance, a TDtest for a faster tolerance screen, or an MBEC/Calgary device value for biofilm eradication) and explains why an ordinary MIC or disk-diffusion test would have missed the phenotype being claimed.

questions.prompt: What does MDK99 measure, and how is it obtained?

options.text: The MIC needed to kill 99% of cells, read from a broth dilution series
The time needed to kill 99% of a population at a fixed lethal drug concentration, read from a time-kill curve
The percentage of cells that survive a single antibiotic disk-diffusion test
The minimum biofilm eradication concentration for a peg-grown biofilm

explanations.a: MDK99 is a duration, not a concentration; it is not read from an MIC dilution series.
explanations.b: Correct — MDK99 is the minimum duration for killing 99% of the population at a defined lethal concentration, obtained directly from a time-kill curve.
explanations.c: That describes something closer to a TDtest readout, not MDK99, and disk diffusion alone does not report a percentage survival number.
explanations.d: That description matches the MBEC assay for biofilms, a separate metric from MDK99.

questions.prompt: In a TDtest, what visual sign indicates that a clinical isolate is tolerant rather than fully susceptible?

options.text: A larger-than-normal clear zone of inhibition around the disk
No growth anywhere on the plate, even far from the disk
Regrowth ('haze') appearing within the normally clear zone of inhibition after the disk is removed and fresh nutrient supplied
A change in colony color on the agar

explanations.a: A larger clear zone would suggest increased susceptibility, not tolerance.
explanations.b: No growth anywhere is not the tolerance signature and would be an unusual, uninterpretable result.
explanations.c: Correct — the TDtest's defining signal is regrowth haze inside the normally clear zone once the disk is removed and nutrients are refreshed, showing cells survived the drug exposure and resumed growth once it ended.
explanations.d: Colony color change is not part of the TDtest readout.

questions.prompt: Match each measurement method to what it quantifies.

right.text: Persister fraction, from the surviving plateau relative to starting count
Fast disk-diffusion screen for tolerance via regrowth haze
Lowest concentration that fully eradicates an attached, peg-grown biofilm

questions.explanation: Each method targets a different phenotype: the time-kill curve's plateau height estimates persister fraction, the TDtest is a rapid tolerance screen, and the MBEC/Calgary device measures biofilm eradication concentration directly on attached biofilms.

questions.prompt: Why can't a standard planktonic MIC test be used to measure biofilm susceptibility?

options.text: Because MIC tests are only valid for Gram-positive organisms
Because a biofilm's recalcitrance depends on its attached, matrix-embedded structure, which a free-floating broth culture does not reproduce
Because biofilms cannot be grown in a laboratory setting
Because MIC tests require live imaging equipment that most labs lack

explanations.a: MIC testing works for both Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms in their planktonic form; that is not the limitation here.
explanations.b: Correct — recalcitrance arises from the biofilm's matrix and dormancy gradients, structural features entirely absent in a planktonic broth culture, so a broth MIC cannot capture it; a dedicated attached-biofilm assay like the MBEC device is needed.
explanations.c: Biofilms are routinely grown in the lab, including on the Calgary Biofilm Device's pegs specifically for this kind of testing.
explanations.d: Standard MIC tests use ordinary broth dilution or disk diffusion and do not require live imaging.

lessons.label: Attacking Biofilms and Persisters

sections.heading: Taking the matrix apart
sections.body: Because the EPS matrix, not any resistance gene, is a major reason antibiotics fail against biofilms, one counter-strategy is to dismantle the matrix directly rather than raise the dose. Extracellular DNA is a load-bearing matrix component in many species, and Whitchurch and colleagues showed in 2002 that adding DNase I disrupts Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilm formation and can break down existing young biofilms, since digesting the eDNA scaffold destabilizes the whole structure. A second matrix-targeting enzyme, dispersin B, is a glycoside hydrolase (originally characterized from the oral pathogen Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans) that degrades poly-N-acetylglucosamine (PNAG), a polysaccharide many staphylococcal and other biofilms rely on for structural integrity and for attaching newly divided cells to the community. Neither enzyme kills bacteria on its own; both work by exposing cells that were previously matrix-shielded, making a co-administered antibiotic far more effective at reaching and killing them.

sections.heading: Jamming the signal and hitting the dormant
sections.body: A second strategy, quorum quenching, targets the signaling system that coordinates biofilm formation instead of the structure itself — enzymes that degrade AHL autoinducers, or small molecules that block LuxR-type receptors, can prevent a population from ever reaching the density threshold needed to switch on matrix genes and virulence factors, in principle blunting biofilm formation before it starts. The harder problem is the dormant, metabolically quiet persister cell, since most antibiotics need an active target and dormancy removes exactly that. Two experimental approaches attack persisters on their own terms. Acyldepsipeptides (ADEPs), shown by Brötz-Oesterhelt and colleagues in 2005, work by binding the ClpP protease and locking it into a permanently active, unregulated state that begins degrading proteins indiscriminately, giving them broad antibacterial efficacy against actively growing pathogens including MRSA. Because this mechanism does not depend on the cell actively growing, Conlon, Lewis, and colleagues showed in 2013 that activated ClpP can also kill dormant persisters that beta-lactams or aminoglycosides cannot touch, using an ADEP-rifampicin combination to eradicate a chronic biofilm infection. A second approach exploits the fact that aminoglycoside uptake itself requires active metabolism: Allison, Brynildsen, and Collins showed in 2011 that adding specific metabolites (such as certain sugars) to a persister population can restart enough central metabolism to drive proton-motive force and aminoglycoside uptake, re-sensitizing cells that were otherwise untouchable. Both approaches matter clinically because dormant, matrix-shielded cells are exactly what drive relapse in chronic wounds, cystic fibrosis lung infections, and implanted medical devices, where a course of antibiotics can clear the active majority yet leave behind the fraction that later regrows the infection.

lessons.workedExample: A chronic diabetic foot wound biofilm dominated by Staphylococcus aureus is treated with three parallel strategies in a research setting. Dispersin B is applied topically first, degrading the PNAG scaffold and loosening the biofilm's structure; a subsequent dose of a standard antibiotic then penetrates far more effectively than it would against the intact matrix. In a separate arm, ADEP is co-administered with rifampicin: the ADEP locks ClpP into constant activity, killing the dormant persister cells that rifampicin alone leaves behind, while rifampicin handles the actively growing majority. Neither strategy relies on a new resistance-defeating drug — both work by removing biofilm-specific and dormancy-specific protection so that existing antibiotics can finish the job.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe counter-strategies because a project claiming to 'fight biofilms' needs to say what it is actually disabling — the matrix (DNase, dispersin B), the coordination signal (quorum quenching), or the dormant persister state itself (ADEPs, metabolite-potentiated uptake) — since these are mechanistically distinct targets with different evidence bases. A strong answer names a specific enzyme or compound class and explains what vulnerability it exploits; a weak answer says 'a new antibiotic' without addressing why the old ones already failed against this exact population.

questions.prompt: How do acyldepsipeptides (ADEPs) kill dormant persister cells that beta-lactams cannot touch?

options.text: By blocking the cell's efflux pumps so more drug accumulates
By binding ClpP protease and locking it into an unregulated, constantly active state that degrades proteins regardless of growth state
By restoring active cell-wall synthesis in dormant cells
By digesting the eDNA component of the biofilm matrix

explanations.a: ADEPs act on the ClpP protease, not on efflux pump function.
explanations.b: Correct — Brötz-Oesterhelt and colleagues (2005) showed ADEPs bind ClpP and lock it into permanent, unregulated activity, causing indiscriminate protein degradation; because this does not require the cell to be actively growing, Conlon, Lewis, and colleagues (2013) showed activated ClpP kills dormant persisters that beta-lactams cannot touch.
explanations.c: ADEPs do not restore or depend on active cell-wall synthesis; that is precisely what makes them effective against dormant cells.
explanations.d: Digesting eDNA describes the DNase matrix-disruption strategy, a separate mechanism from ADEP action on ClpP.

questions.prompt: Match each counter-strategy to what it targets.

right.text: Degrades extracellular DNA in the matrix
Degrades PNAG polysaccharide holding cells together in the matrix
Blocks or degrades autoinducer signaling to prevent density-dependent gene activation
Restarts central metabolism in persisters so they take up an otherwise-ineffective drug

questions.explanation: Each strategy attacks a different layer: DNase and dispersin B dismantle two different matrix components, quorum quenching interrupts the signaling that coordinates biofilm gene expression, and metabolite potentiation re-enables drug uptake in dormant persisters.

questions.prompt: Why do dormant, matrix-shielded cells specifically drive relapse in chronic infections like cystic fibrosis lung infections or implanted-device infections?

options.text: Because they are the only cells targeted by the host immune system
Because a standard antibiotic course can clear the actively growing majority while leaving the dormant, shielded fraction intact to later regrow the infection
Because dormant cells acquire resistance mutations faster than active cells
Because implanted devices actively produce antibiotics that select for dormancy

explanations.a: Dormant cells are typically harder for the immune system to clear, not specifically targeted by it; this is not the mechanism of relapse.
explanations.b: Correct — a course calibrated to clear the actively growing population can leave the dormant, matrix-protected fraction behind, and that surviving fraction can later resume growth and cause relapse once treatment stops.
explanations.c: Dormant cells do not have an elevated mutation rate; relapse here does not require any new resistance mutation.
explanations.d: Implanted devices do not produce antibiotics; they provide a surface for biofilm attachment.

units.label: Drug Discovery: Screening for New Antibacterials

lessons.label: The Discovery Pipeline and the Void

sections.heading: Screen, hit, lead, optimize
sections.body: Antibacterial discovery moves through defined stages. A screen tests many candidates (soil isolates, extracts, synthetic libraries) against a pathogen for any sign of inhibition. Anything that clears that first bar is a hit — a raw, unconfirmed signal. A hit becomes a lead once it survives dose-response confirmation, shows a plausible mechanism, and looks chemically tractable. Optimization is the slow medicinal-chemistry grind after that: tweaking the lead's structure to improve potency, selectivity, and pharmacokinetics before it can even enter clinical trials. Most of antibacterial history's real chemistry happened in a burst: nearly every major class in clinical use today — beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, macrolides — was discovered between the 1940s and the early 1960s, largely by screening soil microbes. Since then, genuinely new classes have been vanishingly rare, a gap researchers call the discovery void.

sections.heading: The rediscovery problem
sections.body: A major cause of the void is rediscovery. Soil actinomycetes, especially Streptomyces, were screened so exhaustively during the golden age that an unguided modern soil screen overwhelmingly turns up compounds already known and shelved decades ago, rather than anything new. This pushes serious discovery programs toward untapped sources or techniques that dodge the well-picked, easily cultured organisms — the subject of later lessons in this unit.

sections.heading: The gram-negative wall
sections.body: Gram-negative bacteria carry an outer membrane studded with lipopolysaccharide that blocks large or hydrophobic molecules from entering, backed by efflux pumps like AcrAB-TolC that actively eject anything that does get through. Most natural products isolated from soil screens are active only against gram-positive bacteria, because they never evolved to cross that barrier. That is precisely why the WHO's 2017 global priority pathogens list put carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacteriaceae in its Critical tier — all gram-negative — alongside the broader ESKAPE group (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacter species) that dominates hospital-acquired resistant infections.

sections.heading: Economics that discourage the chase
sections.body: Even a genuine new antibacterial faces broken incentives. Antibiotics are taken for days, not years, and good stewardship deliberately shelves new drugs to slow resistance, so sales rarely recoup development costs. Achaogen won FDA approval for plazomicin in 2018 and still filed for bankruptcy in April 2019 after the drug generated under a million dollars in its first months on the market. Public and philanthropic funders (BARDA, CARB-X) now cover much of the early 'push' funding that private capital has largely abandoned.

lessons.workedExample: A team screens a backyard soil sample and gets a clean zone of inhibition against Staphylococcus aureus, but nothing against E. coli from the same extract. That split is itself informative, not a failure: it is the textbook signature of a compound that cannot cross the gram-negative outer membrane. Before celebrating a 'new antibiotic,' the team should also ask whether the active compound is simply a known Streptomyces product being rediscovered yet again — the single most common outcome of an unguided soil screen — which is exactly what dereplication (covered later in this unit) is for.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why hasn't someone already found this?' is testing whether a student understands the pipeline and the void, not just the biology of one pathogen. A strong answer names a specific bottleneck — the gram-negative permeability barrier, the rediscovery problem, or the economics that emptied pharma's antibacterial divisions — and connects it to their own project's target organism. A weak answer gestures vaguely at 'FDA regulations take a long time' without engaging why so few candidates even reach that stage.

questions.prompt: A soil extract shows a zone of inhibition in an initial screen. In pipeline terms, what is this result?

options.text: A lead
A hit
An optimized candidate
An approved drug

explanations.a: A lead is a hit that has already survived dose-response confirmation and looks chemically tractable — this extract hasn't been confirmed yet.
explanations.b: Correct — any raw, unconfirmed signal from an initial screen is a hit, the first and least certain stage of the pipeline.
explanations.c: Optimization is medicinal-chemistry refinement that happens well after a compound is established as a lead.
explanations.d: Approval requires clinical trials, which are far downstream of a single screening result.

questions.prompt: Why are natural-product hits from soil screens disproportionately active against gram-positive bacteria rather than gram-negative pathogens like Pseudomonas aeruginosa?

options.text: Gram-negative bacteria are naturally resistant to all chemicals
The gram-negative outer membrane and efflux pumps block or eject most compounds before they reach their target
Gram-positive bacteria are more common in soil, so screens are biased toward them
Gram-negative bacteria grow too slowly to be tested in a screen

explanations.a: Gram-negatives are not resistant to everything; they are especially good at physically excluding many compounds, which is a specific and different problem.
explanations.b: Correct — the LPS-containing outer membrane restricts entry and pumps like AcrAB-TolC actively remove what gets in, so compounds effective on gram-positives often fail entirely against gram-negatives.
explanations.c: The imbalance in hit spectrum is about the target's defenses, not the soil producer's abundance.
explanations.d: Growth rate is not the limiting factor in standard screening assays.

questions.prompt: Order these stages of the antibacterial discovery pipeline from earliest to latest.

items.text: Screen many candidates for any activity
Confirm a hit
Establish a lead
Optimize the compound

questions.explanation: Screening finds raw signals (hits); confirming a hit and establishing mechanism/tractability produces a lead; optimization then refines that lead's chemistry before clinical development.

questions.prompt: Match each ESKAPE letter to the pathogen it stands for.

right.text: Enterococcus faecium
Staphylococcus aureus
Klebsiella pneumoniae
Acinetobacter baumannii

questions.explanation: ESKAPE spells Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter species — the multidrug-resistant organisms that dominate hospital-acquired infection.

lessons.label: Classic Screening: Zone-of-Inhibition and Whole-Cell Assays

sections.heading: The Waksman method: cross-streak and overlay
sections.body: In the late 1930s, soil microbiologist Selman Waksman at Rutgers built a systematic program to screen soil actinomycetes for antimicrobial activity, rather than waiting for a lucky accident like Fleming's 1928 penicillin observation. His workhorse technique, the cross-streak assay, is simple and still used today: streak a candidate microbe down the center of an agar plate, let it grow for several days, then streak test pathogens perpendicular to it and incubate again. A gap where the pathogen fails to grow near the candidate is antagonism — a live signal that the candidate is secreting something inhibitory. An agar-overlay variant grows the candidate first, then floods a soft-agar layer containing the pathogen over the top, reading inhibition the same way. This program isolated streptomycin in 1943, when Waksman's graduate student Albert Schatz found that a strain of soil actinomycete inhibited even gram-negative bacteria — work published in 1944 with Schatz, Elizabeth Bugie, and Waksman as authors, and it was Waksman who coined the word 'antibiotic' for such compounds.

sections.heading: Disk and well diffusion: scoring extracts
sections.body: Once you have an isolate or a crude extract rather than a live antagonist, the standard test is diffusion: soak a paper disk (or fill a punched well) with the candidate and place it on an agar plate freshly spread with the test pathogen. After incubation, measure the clear zone's diameter in millimeters. This became a rigorous clinical tool as the Kirby-Bauer disk-diffusion method (1966), still used to classify patient isolates as susceptible or resistant to standard drugs. But a zone diameter is not a clean potency number — it depends on the compound's molecular size and polarity, how far it diffuses through the agar, and how deep the agar is poured, so two equally potent compounds can produce very different zones.

sections.heading: Broth microdilution: the real potency number
sections.body: Confirming a hit means moving to liquid culture. Broth microdilution serially dilutes the compound two-fold across a row of wells inoculated with a fixed number of pathogen cells, incubates, and reads which wells show visible growth. The lowest concentration that fully suppresses growth is the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) — a standardized, comparable number (CLSI protocols define the exact conditions), unlike a zone diameter that shifts with agar depth or disk placement.

sections.heading: Reading a zone as real, not an artifact
sections.body: A clear zone is not automatically a lead. Zones can appear from pH shifts caused by fermentation byproducts, local nutrient depletion, bacteriocins from a contaminating cell, or leftover extraction solvent like DMSO diffusing outward. Good practice runs a solvent-only disk as a negative control and confirms the effect survives into a purified or extracted fraction before trusting the result — the same discipline that later carries through to MIC confirmation.

lessons.workedExample: A team cross-streaks a soil isolate against Staphylococcus aureus and sees a 15 mm zone — promising. But their extraction used a methanol carrier, so they run a methanol-only disk on the same plate: it also shows a faint 4 mm zone from residual solvent toxicity, not a specific antibacterial. Subtracting that baseline, the real effect is still a solid 11 mm zone, so they move the extract to broth microdilution and confirm a reproducible MIC of 8 micrograms per milliliter — turning a possible artifact into a documented, quantitative hit.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge pressing on 'how do you know that zone is real?' is testing whether a student ran the actual antagonism screen or just eyeballed a plate. A strong answer names a solvent or growth-medium control, explains why zone diameter alone isn't potency, and reports a confirmed MIC value from broth microdilution. A weak answer treats 'we saw a clear zone' as the entire result, with no control and no quantitative follow-up.

questions.prompt: Order these steps of a classic antibacterial screening workflow from first to last.

items.text: Cross-streak candidate against test pathogens
Disk/well diffusion of the extract, measure zone
Broth microdilution to determine MIC

questions.explanation: Cross-streaking a live antagonist finds the initial signal; disk/well diffusion tests an extracted candidate and gives a rough zone reading; broth microdilution then confirms and quantifies potency as a standardized MIC.

questions.prompt: Why is the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) from broth microdilution considered a more reliable potency measure than a zone-of-inhibition diameter?

options.text: MIC testing does not require a live pathogen culture
Zone diameter depends on diffusion through agar (molecule size, polarity, agar depth), while MIC is a standardized concentration reading
MIC testing is faster to run than disk diffusion
Zone diameter cannot be measured accurately with a ruler

explanations.a: Broth microdilution still requires a live pathogen inoculum in each well; that isn't the distinguishing factor.
explanations.b: Correct — a zone's size is confounded by how well the compound diffuses through agar, not just how potent it is, while MIC directly reports the lowest concentration that stops growth under standardized (CLSI) conditions.
explanations.c: Speed isn't the reason MIC is preferred; the two assays are used for different purposes at different pipeline stages.
explanations.d: Zone diameters are routinely measured with a ruler or caliper; measurement precision isn't the issue.

questions.prompt: A soil isolate produces a zone of inhibition, but the same-sized zone also appears around a solvent-only control disk. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: The isolate is an unusually strong antibacterial producer
The zone is likely an artifact of the solvent, not a specific antibacterial effect from the isolate
The pathogen used in the test is resistant to all antibiotics
The agar plate was poured too deep

explanations.a: A zone that matches the solvent-only control undercuts, rather than supports, a claim of strong antibacterial activity from the isolate itself.
explanations.b: Correct — if the solvent control alone reproduces the zone, the effect is likely nonspecific solvent toxicity rather than a compound made by the candidate isolate.
explanations.c: Pan-resistance in the pathogen would not explain a zone appearing around the solvent control specifically.
explanations.d: Agar depth affects zone size generally, but it wouldn't explain why the solvent-only disk matches the sample disk.

questions.prompt: Match each screening method to what it primarily tells you.

right.text: Whether a live candidate organism antagonizes a test pathogen at all
A rough, diffusion-dependent zone size for an extract or isolate
A standardized minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC)

questions.explanation: Each method answers a different question: cross-streak/overlay finds the initial antagonism signal, disk/well diffusion scores an extract's zone, and broth microdilution gives the quantitative, standardized MIC used to confirm a hit.

lessons.label: Bioprospecting Natural Products

sections.heading: Why nature is the starting library
sections.body: Microbes in a single gram of soil compete fiercely for space and nutrients among roughly a billion cells, and many species evolved secreted chemical weapons to poison their neighbors. Actinomycetes — filamentous soil bacteria, above all the genus Streptomyces — are responsible for roughly two-thirds of all known natural-product antibiotics, including streptomycin, tetracycline, and erythromycin. Fungi contributed the other founding pillar: Alexander Fleming's 1928 observation of Penicillium mold killing Staphylococcus on a contaminated plate led to penicillin. Because soil actinomycetes were screened so heavily during the mid-20th century, marine environments — sediments, sponges, and marine-derived actinomycetes — are a comparatively underexplored frontier now drawing serious bioprospecting effort.

sections.heading: Sourcing beyond soil
sections.body: Plant extracts and propolis (the resin bees collect and use to seal and disinfect a hive) are older ethnobotanical sources now being screened more systematically; their flavonoids and phenolic compounds show antibacterial activity in disk-diffusion assays, though their overall hit rate for antibacterials is generally lower than for soil actinomycetes. Marine sediment-derived actinomycetes have yielded compounds like the salinosporamides, illustrating that the same producer genera that gave the golden age its antibiotics can still deliver novel chemistry from a less-picked-over habitat.

sections.heading: Bioassay-guided fractionation
sections.body: Turning a promising organism into a pure compound is an iterative narrowing process, not a single extraction. A crude solvent extract (methanol, ethanol, or hexane, depending on polarity) is first tested for activity with the disk-diffusion or MIC assays from the previous lesson. If active, the extract is split into a handful of fractions by column chromatography, and every fraction is retested — only the active fraction(s) move forward, and inactive ones are discarded. This split-and-retest cycle repeats through progressively finer chromatography, often HPLC, until a single active peak is isolated as a pure compound, which is then structurally characterized by mass spectrometry and NMR. Guiding each purification step by the bioassay, rather than blindly purifying the most abundant molecule, is what keeps the process pointed at the actual antibacterial.

sections.heading: Rediscovery pushes the search outward
sections.body: The trouble is that an unguided screen of easily cultured soil Streptomyces today overwhelmingly rediscovers compounds already catalogued decades ago — the golden-age low-hanging fruit was picked clean by the 1960s. That rediscovery rate is exactly why serious programs increasingly target underexplored niches (marine, extremophile, or symbiotic sources) or move past classical isolation altogether into the unculturable-organism and genome-mining techniques covered in the next lesson.

lessons.workedExample: A student extracts a soil Streptomyces isolate with methanol and gets a positive disk-diffusion result against Bacillus subtilis. They run the crude extract through a silica column, collecting four fractions, and retest all four: only fraction 3 retains activity, so fractions 1, 2, and 4 are discarded. Fraction 3 is then purified by HPLC, which resolves it into several peaks; retesting each isolated peak shows only one is active. That single active peak — now a pure compound — goes on to mass spectrometry for structural identification, completing a bioassay-guided fractionation from crude extract to isolated molecule.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe bioprospecting projects to see whether 'purification' was guided or just 'we filtered it and it looked cleaner.' A strong answer describes retesting each fraction at every chromatography step and explains why that discipline is necessary — otherwise you might purify an abundant but inactive molecule and lose the real antibacterial along the way. A weak answer describes only a single extraction with no fractionation or retesting logic at all.

questions.prompt: Roughly what fraction of known natural-product antibiotics come from the actinomycete genus Streptomyces?

options.text: About one-tenth
About one-third
About two-thirds
Essentially all of them

explanations.a: This understates Streptomyces's outsized historical contribution to antibiotic discovery.
explanations.b: This is closer but still understates the genus's share.
explanations.c: Correct — Streptomyces alone accounts for roughly two-thirds of known natural-product antibiotics, reflecting how heavily soil actinomycetes were screened during the golden age.
explanations.d: Fungi (penicillin) and other bacterial genera also contributed meaningfully, so it is not essentially all.

questions.prompt: Order these steps of bioassay-guided fractionation from first to last.

items.text: Make a crude solvent extract and test it for activity
Split into fractions by chromatography and retest each
Further purify the active fraction (e.g. by HPLC) and retest
Characterize the single pure active compound structurally

questions.explanation: Bioassay-guided fractionation always retests activity at each narrowing step: crude extract, then fractions, then finer purification of only the active fraction, ending in structural characterization of the isolated pure compound.

questions.prompt: In bioassay-guided fractionation, why is every fraction retested for activity rather than simply purifying the most abundant compound in the extract?

options.text: Retesting is required by journal publication standards, not by the chemistry
The most abundant molecule in an extract is not necessarily the active one, so skipping retesting risks losing the real antibacterial
Retesting makes the extraction process faster
Abundance and antibacterial activity are always the same thing in a natural extract

explanations.a: Retesting is a scientific necessity for tracking the active compound, not a publication formality.
explanations.b: Correct — the active antibacterial compound in a crude extract is often a minor component, so only tracking activity fraction-by-fraction keeps the purification pointed at the right molecule.
explanations.c: Retesting adds steps and time; it is done for accuracy, not speed.
explanations.d: This is precisely the false assumption bioassay-guided fractionation is designed to avoid.

questions.prompt: Match each bioprospecting source to a detail from this lesson.

right.text: Source of ~two-thirds of known natural antibiotics, esp. Streptomyces
Source of penicillin, via Fleming's 1928 observation
Comparatively underexplored frontier, yielded compounds like salinosporamides
Ethnobotanical source with flavonoids/phenolics but lower antibacterial hit rate

questions.explanation: Each source has a distinct track record: soil Streptomyces gave the bulk of golden-age antibiotics, fungi gave penicillin, marine sources are a newer and less-picked-over frontier, and plant/propolis extracts contribute antibacterial leads at a lower overall hit rate.

lessons.label: Mining the Unculturable and the Genome

sections.heading: The great plate count anomaly
sections.body: Roughly 99% of environmental bacteria fail to grow on a standard lab agar plate. This 'great plate count anomaly' happens because petri-dish media are a poor imitation of soil's real chemical world — the nutrient gradients, growth factors, and signaling molecules a cell needs are missing. Every classical screening and bioprospecting method from the earlier lessons in this unit can only ever see the culturable 1%, meaning the vast majority of potential antibiotic producers has simply never been tested.

sections.heading: The iChip: growing bacteria where they live
sections.body: The isolation chip (iChip), developed by Slava Epstein and Kim Lewis at Northeastern University and described around 2010, sidesteps the anomaly rather than fighting it. A soil sample is diluted until roughly one cell sits in each tiny well of a multi-channel plastic device; the device is sandwiched between semipermeable membranes and buried back in the original soil, so each cell grows in situ, bathed in the real nutrients and signals it evolved to need, before ever being transferred to a lab plate. Using this method, NovoBiotic Pharmaceuticals' team, led by Losee Ling, grew a previously unculturable soil bacterium, Eleftheria terrae, from a Maine field and isolated teixobactin, published in Nature in 2015. Teixobactin binds a conserved motif on lipid II and lipid III, precursors the cell wall needs for peptidoglycan and teichoic acid synthesis, and the original study reported no detectable resistance developing in testing.

sections.heading: Metagenomic mining: skipping culture entirely
sections.body: Metagenomics goes further and drops culturing altogether: researchers extract bulk environmental DNA directly from soil, clone large fragments into a lab-friendly host such as E. coli, and screen the resulting 'metagenomic library' for antibacterial activity, regardless of whether the original producing organism can ever be grown. Sean Brady's lab at Rockefeller University used this approach on DNA from roughly 2,000 soil samples to discover the malacidins, published in Nature Microbiology in 2018 — calcium-dependent lipopeptide antibiotics that also bind lipid II and proved active against multidrug-resistant gram-positive pathogens including MRSA and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium.

sections.heading: Genome mining and silent gene clusters
sections.body: Even bacteria that are easy to culture and fully sequenced often carry far more biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) — the co-located sets of genes encoding an enzyme pathway for one natural product — than the number of compounds they are ever observed making in the lab. Many clusters stay 'silent' because they only switch on under environmental cues the lab never provides. Bioinformatic tools such as antiSMASH, introduced in 2011, scan a genome's sequence and flag candidate BGCs by their conserved enzyme domains, letting researchers try to coax a silent cluster awake instead of waiting for the organism to volunteer it. This strategy, on symbiotic bacteria this time, led Kim Lewis's Northeastern lab to darobactin (Imai et al., Nature, 2019), discovered from Photorhabdus, a bacterium that lives inside insect-killing nematodes; resistant E. coli mutants all mapped to BamA, the essential outer-membrane protein-folding machine unique to gram-negative bacteria, making darobactin one of the very few genuinely new antibiotic classes active against gram-negative pathogens found in decades.

lessons.workedExample: A student weighing project designs compares two options against the 99%-unculturable problem. Option A: bury an iChip-style device in local forest soil for two weeks, then try to culture whatever grew. This still needs a live, recoverable organism and a return trip to the exact burial site. Option B: extract soil DNA directly and screen a cloned metagenomic library for activity, skipping live culture entirely but requiring cloning and expression steps the school lab may not have. Neither is strictly 'better' — iChip yields an actual organism you can regrow and study further, while metagenomics reaches genetic diversity no culture method ever will, at the cost of needing a functional expression host.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing these techniques wants to see the mechanism, not the buzzword. A strong answer explains why the plate-count anomaly makes 99% of bacteria invisible to classical screening, and can say concretely what iChip, metagenomics, or genome mining each does differently to reach that hidden majority. A weak answer says 'we used gene sequencing to find new antibiotics' without being able to say what a silent biosynthetic gene cluster is or why it stays silent.

questions.prompt: Approximately what fraction of environmental bacteria fail to grow under standard laboratory culture conditions?

options.text: About 10%
About 50%
About 99%
Essentially none — nearly all soil bacteria are culturable

explanations.a: This drastically understates the plate count anomaly.
explanations.b: Still a substantial understatement of the anomaly.
explanations.c: Correct — roughly 99% of environmental bacteria will not grow on standard lab media, which is exactly why techniques like the iChip and metagenomics were developed.
explanations.d: This is the reverse of the actual problem; the vast majority are not culturable by standard methods.

questions.prompt: Match each discovery technique to the compound it yielded in this lesson.

left.text: Genome mining of a silent gene cluster

right.text: Teixobactin, from Eleftheria terrae
Malacidins, from ~2,000 soil DNA extracts
Darobactin, from Photorhabdus

questions.explanation: iChip's in-situ culture grew the previously uncultured Eleftheria terrae for teixobactin; metagenomic DNA extraction across thousands of soil samples found the malacidins without culturing anything; genome mining of Photorhabdus's biosynthetic gene clusters uncovered darobactin.

questions.prompt: What does darobactin's target, BamA, do in a gram-negative bacterium?

options.text: It pumps antibiotics out of the cell via the efflux system
It is the essential machine that folds and inserts proteins into the outer membrane
It synthesizes peptidoglycan for the cell wall
It replicates the bacterial chromosome

explanations.a: Efflux pumps like AcrAB-TolC are a separate resistance mechanism, not BamA's function.
explanations.b: Correct — BamA is the essential chaperone of the beta-barrel assembly machinery that folds and inserts proteins into the gram-negative outer membrane; darobactin-resistant mutants all mapped to this gene.
explanations.c: Peptidoglycan synthesis is the target of teixobactin (via lipid II/III) and beta-lactams, not BamA.
explanations.d: BamA has no role in DNA replication.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the iChip method from first to last.

items.text: Dilute a soil sample to roughly one cell per device well
Sandwich the device between membranes and bury it back in the original soil
Let cells grow in situ using the soil's real nutrients and signals
Recover the device and transfer established colonies to lab culture

questions.explanation: iChip works by isolating single cells at very low dilution, returning them to their natural environment to grow using real soil chemistry, and only bringing the resulting colonies into the lab after they are established.

lessons.label: Beyond New Antibiotics: Adjuvants, Peptides, and Phage

sections.heading: Rescuing old drugs with adjuvants
sections.body: Instead of chasing a brand-new antibiotic, an adjuvant strategy disables the resistance mechanism itself so an existing drug works again. Clavulanic acid, isolated from Streptomyces clavuligerus, blocks the classic serine beta-lactamase enzymes that would otherwise chew up penicillin-class drugs; paired with amoxicillin, it launched in the UK in 1981 as Augmentin. Newer, non-beta-lactam inhibitors extended this further: avibactam, a diazabicyclooctane, was paired with ceftazidime and FDA-approved in 2015, covering class A, C, and some class D beta-lactamases; vaborbactam, a boronic-acid-based inhibitor, was paired with meropenem and FDA-approved in 2017, targeting KPC carbapenemases specifically. A related target is the efflux pump itself — since pumps like AcrAB-TolC are a major reason candidate drugs never reach their target in gram-negatives (see the barrier problem from Lesson 1), inhibiting the pump can restore an old drug's potency without touching the drug's own structure at all.

sections.heading: Antimicrobial peptides: a harder target to dodge
sections.body: Antimicrobial peptides are short, roughly 10-50 amino acid chains that are cationic and amphipathic — one face charged, one face oily — so they are electrostatically drawn to the negatively charged bacterial membrane and physically insert into and disrupt it. Human defensins and cathelicidin LL-37, and the frog-skin peptide magainin, all work this way; nisin, made by Lactococcus lactis, already sees wide use as a food preservative. Because the mechanism is blunt membrane disruption rather than binding one precise enzyme pocket, resistance is harder to evolve via a single mutation — but the same lack of selectivity risks toxicity to human cells if a candidate peptide isn't carefully screened for it.

sections.heading: Phage therapy's return
sections.body: Bacteriophages, viruses that infect and lyse specific bacteria, were discovered independently by Twort in 1915 and Félix d'Herelle in 1917; d'Herelle went on to co-found the Eliava Institute in Tbilisi, Georgia in 1923 with Georgian microbiologist George Eliava, and phage therapy remained in routine clinical use there through the Soviet era even as the West largely abandoned it once mass-produced antibiotics arrived in the 1940s. The AMR crisis has revived Western interest, most visibly through compassionate-use cases such as UCSD patient Tom Patterson in 2016, whose multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii infection was treated with an intravenous phage cocktail after antibiotics had failed, sourced with help from Texas A&M and U.S. Navy phage collections and championed by his wife, epidemiologist Steffanie Strathdee. Phages can be narrowly matched or even evolved against one specific resistant strain and largely spare the rest of the microbiome, but that same narrowness means slow, patient-by-patient matching and a regulatory pathway not built for a living, self-replicating drug.

lessons.workedExample: A hospital lab identifies a KPC-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae infection resistant to standard carbapenems. Two non-new-antibiotic options exist: give meropenem paired with vaborbactam, which blocks the KPC carbapenemase and restores meropenem's activity within hours using an already-approved combination; or source a phage cocktail matched to that exact Klebsiella strain, which could work even if the strain later evolves further resistance mechanisms, but takes days to identify, test, and obtain. The trade-off is speed and regulatory ease (adjuvant combination) versus strain-specific reach and microbiome sparing (phage).
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this territory to check that a student isn't conflating 'a new way to fight bacteria' with 'a new antibiotic' — they are mechanistically distinct. A strong answer names the specific resistance mechanism being bypassed (a beta-lactamase, an efflux pump, a membrane target, or a live predator virus) and explains why that bypass doesn't count as discovering a new antibiotic class. A weak answer describes phage therapy or an antimicrobial peptide as simply 'a type of antibiotic' without engaging its distinct mechanism.

questions.prompt: Match each beta-lactamase inhibitor to the antibiotic it is paired with in an approved combination.

right.text: Amoxicillin (Augmentin, 1981)
Ceftazidime (FDA-approved 2015)
Meropenem (FDA-approved 2017)

questions.explanation: Clavulanic acid pairs with amoxicillin as Augmentin; avibactam pairs with ceftazidime, approved 2015; vaborbactam pairs with meropenem, approved 2017 and targeted at KPC carbapenemases.

questions.prompt: Why is it harder for bacteria to evolve resistance to cationic antimicrobial peptides through a single mutation, compared to a drug that binds one specific enzyme?

options.text: Peptides work by physically disrupting the negatively charged bacterial membrane rather than binding one precise molecular target
Peptides are too large to enter bacterial cells at all
Bacteria cannot mutate their membranes under any circumstances
Peptides are chemically identical to human antibiotics already in clinical use

explanations.a: Correct — because the mechanism is broad electrostatic attraction and membrane insertion rather than a single lock-and-key binding site, there's no single mutation that easily blocks it, though it also raises the risk of nonspecific toxicity.
explanations.b: Peptides act at the membrane surface; they don't need to fully enter the cell to disrupt it.
explanations.c: Bacteria can and do alter membrane charge over time (e.g., via lipid modification); it's just harder to do with one mutation than defeating a single enzyme target.
explanations.d: Antimicrobial peptides and conventional antibiotics are structurally and mechanistically distinct classes.

questions.prompt: Order these phage therapy milestones chronologically.

items.text: Twort (1915) and d'Herelle (1917) discover bacteriophages
d'Herelle co-founds the Eliava Institute in Tbilisi (1923)
Western medicine largely abandons phage therapy after mass-produced antibiotics arrive (1940s)
AMR-driven compassionate-use revival, e.g. the Tom Patterson case (2016)

questions.explanation: Bacteriophages were discovered in the mid-1910s, institutionalized clinically at Eliava in 1923, sidelined in the West once antibiotics scaled up in the 1940s, and revived by AMR-driven compassionate-use cases like Tom Patterson's in 2016.
