questions.prompt: On the DRF's U-shaped curve of damage vs. host immune response strength, where does damage from an excessive, dysregulated response (e.g., cytokine storm) fall?

options.text: At the weak-response end of the curve
At the strong-response end of the curve
Exactly at the minimum, middle point of the curve
The DRF curve does not include host-response-driven damage at all

explanations.a: The weak-response end represents damage from unchecked microbial replication due to an inadequate response, the opposite case.
explanations.b: Correct — at the strong-response end, an excessive or dysregulated immune response itself becomes the dominant source of damage, as in septic shock or cytokine storm.
explanations.c: The middle of the curve represents a well-calibrated response and minimized damage, not the excessive-response case.
explanations.d: Host-response-driven damage at the strong-response end is one of the two poles the framework was specifically built to capture.

questions.prompt: Why does the DRF describe 'virulence' as relational rather than an intrinsic microbial property?

options.text: Because the same organism (e.g., Cryptococcus neoformans) can cause severe disease in one host's immune state and be handled with minimal damage in another's
Because virulence genes change spontaneously between hosts
Because all microbes are equally virulent under the DRF
Because the DRF only applies to viruses, not bacteria or fungi

explanations.a: Correct — since the same microbe's damage outcome depends on where the host's response falls on the DRF curve, virulence is a property of the interaction, not the microbe alone.
explanations.b: The framework does not require genetic change between hosts; the same fixed strain can produce different outcomes purely due to host-response differences.
explanations.c: The DRF does not flatten all microbes to equal virulence; it explains why the same microbe's apparent virulence varies by host.
explanations.d: The framework was proposed as a general model of microbial pathogenesis, applicable across bacteria, fungi, and viruses.

lessons.label: Colonization Resistance and the First Barriers

sections.heading: Exclusion before immunity: physical, chemical, and microbial barriers
sections.body: Before adaptive or even much of innate immunity engages a specific threat, the body's first line of defense is exclusion — a set of physical, chemical, and ecological barriers that prevent most microbes from ever establishing a foothold. Intact epithelium is the physical barrier: the stratified squamous cells of skin and the tight-junctioned epithelial sheets lining the gut and respiratory tract are largely impermeable to bacteria unless breached. Mucus is a chemical-and-physical hybrid, trapping organisms and, via ciliary action in the respiratory tract, sweeping them out before they reach deeper tissue. Antimicrobial peptides such as defensins and cathelicidins, secreted by epithelial and specialized cells (Paneth cells in the small intestine, for example), directly disrupt microbial membranes. Stomach acid, at pH 1.5-3.5, kills the vast majority of ingested organisms outright — a large part of why enteric pathogens need such high infectious doses in the first place, as seen with Vibrio cholerae. None of this requires recognizing a specific pathogen; it works against essentially anything that arrives.

sections.heading: Colonization resistance: the resident microbiota as a living barrier
sections.body: Layered on top of these physical and chemical defenses is colonization resistance — the phenomenon by which an intact resident microbiota actively excludes invading and opportunistic organisms, largely through competition. Resident microbes occupy adhesion sites and consume available nutrients, leaving little room or fuel for a newcomer; some also produce bacteriocins or alter local pH and metabolite levels (notably converting primary bile acids into secondary bile acids) in ways that are specifically inhibitory to competitors. The clearest demonstration of colonization resistance is what happens when it is removed. Clostridioides difficile is present at low levels in some healthy guts without causing disease, kept in check by a diverse resident microbiota. Broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment — clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, and cephalosporins are especially implicated — can devastate that resident community, including bile-acid-converting species such as Clostridium scindens. With competitors and inhibitory secondary bile acids depleted, C. difficile spores germinate and its vegetative cells proliferate largely unopposed, producing toxins A and B that damage the colonic epithelium and cause C. difficile-associated colitis, a leading cause of healthcare-associated diarrhea. The case is the standard teaching example precisely because it isolates the variable: the pathogen was often already present, and it is the loss of a competing microbial barrier, not new exposure, that converts silent colonization into overt disease.

lessons.workedExample: A patient is hospitalized and given a two-week course of a broad-spectrum antibiotic for an unrelated infection. Before treatment, C. difficile is present at low abundance in their gut but is suppressed by a diverse resident microbiota that occupies adhesion sites and maintains inhibitory secondary bile acid levels. The antibiotic course collapses much of that diversity, including bile-acid-converting species, without directly targeting C. difficile (which is often intrinsically resistant to the antibiotic used). With colonization resistance gone, C. difficile spores germinate, its population expands unopposed, and toxin production begins, producing watery diarrhea and colitis roughly days to weeks after the antibiotic course. Fecal microbiota transplantation, which directly restores a diverse resident community, is now a recognized treatment for recurrent cases precisely because it re-establishes the barrier that was lost, rather than only targeting the pathogen itself.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about colonization resistance to see whether a student recognizes exclusion as an active, mechanistic process rather than passive good luck. A weak answer says antibiotics 'kill the good bacteria' with no mechanism. A strong answer names at least one specific competitive mechanism (site/nutrient competition, secondary bile acid production, bacteriocins) and can walk through the C. difficile case as a controlled natural experiment showing what happens when that specific barrier, and only that barrier, is removed.

questions.prompt: What is 'colonization resistance'?

options.text: A host's acquired antibody response to a specific pathogen
The exclusion of invading/opportunistic organisms by an intact resident microbiota, largely through competition
The resistance of a pathogen's genome to antibiotic-induced mutation
A vaccine-induced barrier against gut pathogens

explanations.a: Colonization resistance is a pre-adaptive-immunity phenomenon driven by the resident microbial community, not by antibody responses.
explanations.b: Correct — the resident microbiota excludes competitors by occupying niches, consuming nutrients, and producing inhibitory metabolites like secondary bile acids.
explanations.c: This describes antibiotic resistance evolution, an unrelated concept.
explanations.d: Colonization resistance is provided by the microbiota itself, not by vaccination.

questions.prompt: Why does broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment specifically predispose patients to Clostridioides difficile overgrowth?

options.text: Antibiotics directly stimulate C. difficile toxin gene expression

Antibiotics deplete the resident microbiota, including bile-acid-converting species like Clostridium scindens, removing competition and inhibitory secondary bile acids that normally suppress C. difficile
C. difficile is only introduced to the gut through antibiotic pills themselves
Antibiotics lower stomach acid, allowing more C. difficile to survive ingestion

explanations.a: Antibiotics do not directly upregulate C. difficile's toxin genes; the mechanism is indirect, via ecosystem disruption.
explanations.b: Correct — collapsing the resident microbiota, including species that convert primary to inhibitory secondary bile acids, removes the competitive and chemical barriers that had kept C. difficile in check.
explanations.c: C. difficile is often already present at low levels before treatment; the antibiotic does not need to introduce it.
explanations.d: Antibiotics act on the microbiota, not on gastric acid secretion; stomach pH is not the relevant mechanism here.

questions.prompt: Order the events from a healthy gut microbiota to overt C. difficile disease.

items.text: Diverse resident microbiota maintains colonization resistance; C. difficile present at low levels, suppressed
Broad-spectrum antibiotic course disrupts resident microbiota, including bile-acid-converting species
Competition and inhibitory secondary bile acids are depleted
C. difficile spores germinate and vegetative cells proliferate, producing toxins A and B

questions.explanation: The sequence starts from a suppressed baseline, moves through antibiotic-driven ecosystem disruption, then loss of the specific competitive/chemical mechanisms, ending in unopposed C. difficile growth and toxin-mediated colitis.

questions.prompt: Match each first-line barrier to its primary mechanism.

right.text: Physical impermeability unless breached
Trapping and mechanically sweeping organisms out
Directly disrupting microbial membranes
Killing most ingested organisms via low pH

questions.explanation: Each barrier acts through a distinct mechanism: epithelium as a physical wall, mucus plus cilia as a trap-and-sweep system, antimicrobial peptides as direct membrane disruptors, and gastric acid as a chemical kill step for ingested organisms.

units.label: Virulence Factors: Adhesion, Invasion, and Secretion

lessons.label: Adhesins and the First Grip

sections.heading: Sticking before anything else can happen
sections.body: Before a bacterium can invade a cell, damage tissue, or evade immunity, it has to stay put against the constant flow of mucus, urine, or blood trying to wash it away. Adhesion is that first step, and it is carried out by adhesins: surface molecules that bind specific host receptors. The best-studied class is fimbrial (pilus-tipped) adhesins. Uropathogenic Escherichia coli assembles type 1 pili, hair-like fibers built by the chaperone-usher pathway, capped at the tip by the FimH adhesin. FimH binds terminal mannose residues on uroplakin proteins that coat the bladder epithelium. Duguid in the 1950s first characterized this mannose-sensitive hemagglutination, and later work from Sokurenko and Vogel's groups showed FimH is a catch bond: shear force from urine flow actually tightens its grip rather than tearing it loose, letting bacteria cling harder exactly when flushing pressure is highest. FimH has two domains, a mannose-binding lectin domain and a pilin domain, held in a compressed, low-affinity state at rest; tensile force from shear flow pulls the interface between them apart, and the resulting interdomain beta-sheet twist (a 'finger-trap' effect described by Le Trong and colleagues in 2010) snaps the lectin domain into its high-affinity, mannose-gripping conformation, so pulling harder makes the bond hold tighter rather than break.

sections.heading: P pili and a route to the kidney
sections.body: A second E. coli pilus, P pili (encoded by the pap operon), carries a different tip adhesin, PapG, which recognizes the Gal(alpha1-4)Gal digalactoside found in glycolipids on the upper urinary tract and kidney epithelium. Because that receptor is displayed there and not, at high density, lower in the tract, P pili are strongly associated with pyelonephritis (kidney infection) rather than simple cystitis; epidemiological surveys through the 1980s repeatedly found P pili enriched in pyelonephritis isolates compared with strains from asymptomatic bacteriuria. This is receptor specificity acting as a map: the sugar a pilus tip recognizes, and where that sugar is displayed in the body, determines which tissue the organism can colonize, i.e., its tropism.

sections.heading: Afimbrial adhesins and why adhesion is a drug target
sections.body: Not every adhesin sits on a pilus. Afimbrial adhesins are surface proteins expressed directly on the outer membrane or cell wall without a stalk, including the Afa/Dr family in E. coli, which bind the Dr blood-group antigen and decay-accelerating factor. Because adhesion is the mandatory first step, blocking it aborts infection before colonization, invasion, or toxin delivery ever begins, which makes adhesins an attractive anti-virulence target distinct from conventional antibiotics: mannoside compounds that competitively occupy the FimH binding pocket have shown efficacy against urinary tract infection in animal models without killing the bacteria outright, so they do not exert the same selective pressure for resistance.

lessons.workedExample: A team culturing E. coli from a patient with cystitis (bladder infection) versus one with pyelonephritis (kidney infection) runs a hemagglutination assay: mixing bacteria with red blood cells and, separately, with red blood cells plus free mannose. The cystitis isolate agglutinates red cells but stops when mannose is added (mannose-sensitive, type 1 pili/FimH). The pyelonephritis isolate agglutinates red cells regardless of mannose (mannose-resistant) but stops when a synthetic Gal-Gal digalactoside is added, identifying P pili/PapG and matching the strain's tropism to the kidney tissue it actually infected.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why does this bacterium infect the kidney and not just the bladder?' to test whether a student understands tropism as a molecular match, not a vague notion of 'more aggressive' bacteria. A weak answer says the bacteria 'traveled up' or 'got stronger.' A strong answer names the specific adhesin-receptor pair (PapG binding Gal-Gal glycolipid enriched in upper urinary tract tissue) and explains that tropism is set by where the matching receptor is displayed, not by bacterial willpower.

questions.prompt: Which receptor does the FimH tip adhesin of type 1 pili bind on bladder epithelial cells?

options.text: Terminal mannose residues on uroplakin
The Gal(alpha1-4)Gal digalactoside
Decay-accelerating factor
Sialic acid residues

explanations.a: Correct — FimH binds terminal mannose on uroplakin proteins coating the bladder epithelium, and this binding is blocked (mannose-sensitive) by free mannose.
explanations.b: That is the receptor for PapG on P pili, not FimH, and is enriched in the upper urinary tract, not the bladder.
explanations.c: Decay-accelerating factor is the receptor bound by Afa/Dr afimbrial adhesins, a different adhesin family entirely.
explanations.d: Sialic acid is not the FimH receptor in this system.

questions.prompt: Why are P pili specifically associated with pyelonephritis rather than simple cystitis?

options.text: P pili make bacteria swim faster
Their PapG tip binds a Gal-Gal glycolipid receptor enriched in kidney/upper urinary tract tissue
P pili are resistant to antibiotics
P pili are only expressed at body temperature

explanations.a: Pili are adhesion structures, not motility structures; flagella provide swimming.
explanations.b: Correct — receptor tropism, not motility or drug resistance, explains the tissue association: the Gal-Gal receptor is displayed at higher density in upper urinary tract and kidney epithelium.
explanations.c: Adhesins are unrelated to antibiotic resistance mechanisms.
explanations.d: Temperature-dependent expression is not what drives the tissue-specific association described here.

questions.prompt: Match each adhesin structure to its defining feature.

right.text: Binds terminal mannose; catch bond strengthens under shear
Binds Gal-Gal digalactoside; associated with pyelonephritis
Afimbrial (no pilus stalk); binds decay-accelerating factor

questions.explanation: FimH is the mannose-binding, shear-strengthened tip adhesin of type 1 pili; PapG is the P pilus tip adhesin linked to kidney infection; Afa/Dr adhesins act directly from the outer membrane without a pilus stalk.

questions.prompt: Why does blocking adhesion (e.g., with a FimH-targeting mannoside drug) make a promising anti-virulence strategy?

options.text: It kills bacteria directly, like an antibiotic
Adhesion is the mandatory first step, so blocking it aborts infection before invasion or toxin delivery can occur, without the same resistance pressure as killing the organism
It works only against Gram-positive bacteria
It permanently mutates the bacterial genome

explanations.a: Anti-adhesion compounds are not bactericidal; that is precisely why they avoid strong selection for resistance.
explanations.b: Correct — since adhesion must happen first, disrupting it prevents downstream pathogenesis while not killing the organism outright, reducing the selective pressure that drives resistance.
explanations.c: The strategy targets a specific Gram-negative adhesin (FimH) in this example; the logic is not restricted by Gram stain generally.
explanations.d: Anti-adhesion drugs act on protein binding, not on the genome.

lessons.label: Invasion I - The Zipper Mechanism

sections.heading: Letting the host do the work
sections.body: Some bacteria do not force their way into a cell that has no interest in taking them in; instead they present a surface protein that mimics a natural ligand, and the host's own receptor-triggered machinery pulls them inside. This is the zipper mechanism, named because sequential, close-range receptor-ligand contacts spread around the bacterium like a zipper closing, engaging membrane and cytoskeleton bit by bit rather than all at once. The bacterial protein does the targeting; the host cell does essentially all of the mechanical work.

sections.heading: Listeria: internalins meet cadherin and Met
sections.body: Listeria monocytogenes, a foodborne pathogen that crosses the intestinal, placental, and blood-brain barriers, expresses two surface internalins for this purpose. InlA binds E-cadherin, the adhesion protein that holds epithelial cells together at adherens junctions, and this interaction is famously species-restricted: human E-cadherin carries a proline at position 16 of the mature protein, right in the first extracellular domain that InlA docks against, a proline that mouse E-cadherin lacks, having a glutamic acid at the equivalent position instead, and InlA cannot engage that glutamate-bearing mouse residue well, which is why standard lab mice resist oral Listeria infection and why researchers such as Lecuit and colleagues built humanized E-cadherin mouse models around 2001 to study gut crossing properly. InlA-mediated entry in humans occurs preferentially where E-cadherin is transiently exposed at the apical surface, most notably at extrusion sites where dying enterocytes are squeezed out of the epithelium near villus tips, opening brief gaps in the adherens junctions that Listeria exploits to reach the receptor from the gut lumen. InlB engages a second receptor, Met, the hepatocyte growth factor receptor, on a broader range of cell types including hepatocytes. Both engagements trigger PI3-kinase signaling and localized actin polymerization through the Arp2/3 complex, curling the membrane around the bacterium into a phagosome-like vacuole that Listeria then ruptures using listeriolysin O to escape into the cytosol.

sections.heading: Yersinia: one adhesin, higher affinity than the real ligand
sections.body: Yersinia pseudotuberculosis and enterocolitica use a single outer-membrane protein, invasin, to trigger zipper entry into intestinal M cells and epithelial cells. Invasin binds beta-1 integrins, the receptors epithelial cells normally use to grip fibronectin in the extracellular matrix, and does so with markedly higher affinity than fibronectin itself, a property demonstrated by Isberg and colleagues in the late 1980s and early 1990s. Because integrins cluster and signal through focal-adhesion kinase and Src-family kinases when engaged, invasin binding recruits the same actin-polymerizing machinery a cell would normally use to grip matrix, and clustering multiple integrins around the bacterial surface is enough to drive its uptake, even though a single Yersinia expresses only this one invasion factor rather than an injection system.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher wants to know whether a Listeria strain uses InlA-mediated entry in a given cell line. She compares uptake into two epithelial lines: one expressing human E-cadherin, one expressing mouse E-cadherin (glutamate in place of the proline found at position 16 of human E-cadherin, the InlA-critical residue). Wild-type Listeria invades the human E-cadherin line efficiently but is largely blocked on the mouse E-cadherin line; an inlA-deletion mutant is blocked on both. This confirms InlA-E-cadherin engagement is necessary and explains why oral-infection Listeria studies moved to humanized-E-cadherin mice or guinea pigs rather than ordinary lab mice.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe zipper invasion to see whether a student understands that the bacterium is not physically pushing itself inside — it is hijacking a host receptor's normal signaling output. A weak answer says the bacterium 'forces its way in.' A strong answer names the specific receptor-ligand pair (InlA-E-cadherin or invasin-beta1 integrin), states that the host's actin machinery does the enveloping, and can explain a species-restriction detail like the mouse E-cadherin glutamate-for-proline swap at position 16 that made humanized mouse models necessary.

questions.prompt: Match each bacterial invasion protein to the host receptor it engages.

right.text: E-cadherin
Met (HGF receptor)
Beta-1 integrins

questions.explanation: InlA binds E-cadherin at adherens junctions, InlB binds the Met/HGF receptor, and Yersinia invasin binds beta-1 integrins with higher affinity than the natural ligand fibronectin.

questions.prompt: Why did standard laboratory mice prove poor models for oral Listeria infection via InlA?

options.text: Mice lack E-cadherin entirely
A glutamate in place of the proline at position 16 of mouse E-cadherin weakens InlA binding
Mice do not express the Met receptor
Listeria cannot survive at mouse body temperature

explanations.a: Mice express E-cadherin; the issue is a sequence difference at the binding interface, not absence of the protein.
explanations.b: Correct — mouse E-cadherin carries a glutamate in place of the proline found at position 16 of human E-cadherin, right where InlA docks, which disrupts efficient InlA binding and is why researchers built humanized E-cadherin mouse models to study gut invasion.
explanations.c: Met status is not the reason InlA-mediated entry fails in standard mice; the InlA-E-cadherin step is the specific bottleneck.
explanations.d: Temperature is not the mechanism described for this species restriction.

questions.prompt: What best describes the zipper mechanism of bacterial entry?

options.text: Injected bacterial effectors force membrane ruffling across a broad surface
Sequential, localized receptor-ligand engagement drives the host's own actin machinery to progressively envelop the bacterium
The bacterium secretes a pore-forming toxin to punch through the membrane
The bacterium is engulfed passively by fluid-phase pinocytosis with no receptor involvement

explanations.a: That describes the trigger mechanism (e.g., Salmonella/Shigella), which is the contrasting invasion strategy, not the zipper mechanism.
explanations.b: Correct — zipper entry is receptor-driven and localized, closing around the bacterium step by step as the host's own signaling and actin machinery respond to the engaged receptor.
explanations.c: Pore formation is unrelated to zipper entry; listeriolysin O acts later, to escape the vacuole, not to enter the cell.
explanations.d: Zipper entry is receptor-dependent, not a passive, receptor-independent process.

lessons.label: Invasion II - The Trigger Mechanism

sections.heading: An explosion instead of a zipper
sections.body: Where zipper entry is a slow, tight, receptor-by-receptor closure, trigger-mode invasion is fast and violent. The bacterium does not wait for a matching surface receptor to be present; it builds a molecular syringe, a type III secretion system (T3SS), that punches through the host plasma membrane and injects effector proteins directly into the cytosol. Those effectors artificially switch on the host's own Rho-family small GTPases, most importantly Cdc42 and Rac1, master regulators that normally control actin polymerization for processes like cell crawling. The result is membrane ruffling: large, transient sheets of actin-driven membrane that fold outward and back down over the bacterium, sweeping in a wide patch of extracellular fluid along with it. This uptake route is a form of macropinocytosis, and it can be seen by electron microscopy as dramatic, wavelike disturbances of the cell surface, first documented for Salmonella entry in studies by Francis, Ryan, and Falkow in the early 1990s.

sections.heading: Salmonella's SPI-1 effectors
sections.body: Salmonella enterica encodes its invasion T3SS on Salmonella Pathogenicity Island 1 (SPI-1). Among the effectors it injects, SopE and SopE2 act as guanine-nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) that directly activate Cdc42 and Rac1 by forcing them to swap GDP for GTP; SopB is an inositol phosphatase that alters membrane phosphoinositide composition to favor ruffling; and SipA and SipC bind actin directly, bundling and stabilizing filaments at the entry site. Together these effectors accomplish in minutes what a zipper-mode pathogen achieves through slow receptor engagement. The switch does not stay stuck on: Salmonella also injects SptP, a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) that drives Cdc42 and Rac1 back to their inactive, GDP-bound state within minutes of engulfment, so the ruffles collapse and the host cell's actin architecture is restored once the bacterium is safely inside.

sections.heading: Shigella's parallel toolkit and why the contrast matters
sections.body: Shigella flexneri, which invades colonic epithelium, uses an independently evolved but functionally convergent T3SS. Its effector IpaC also activates Cdc42 and Rac1-driven actin remodeling at the point of contact, while IpaA binds host vinculin to help remodel the actin network after entry. The contrast with zipper entry is not just mechanical detail: trigger-mode ruffles are large, transient, and metabolically expensive, disassembling again within minutes after the bacterium is engulfed, whereas zipper entry produces a tight vacuole matched closely to the bacterium's size. Because trigger entry does not depend on a specific host receptor being displayed on that cell type, it lets Salmonella and Shigella invade a broader range of non-phagocytic cells than a single lock-and-key adhesin would allow.

lessons.workedExample: A student treats cultured epithelial cells with a Rac1/Cdc42 inhibitor before exposing them to Salmonella. Uptake collapses even though the bacteria still contact and adhere to the cell surface normally, because the T3SS-injected SopE/SopE2 can no longer force the GTPases into their active, GTP-bound state and membrane ruffling never initiates. Repeating the same inhibitor treatment on Listeria has little effect on InlA-driven entry, since zipper entry depends on E-cadherin engagement recruiting a more localized, lower-magnitude actin response rather than a Rho-GTPase-driven ruffle — a clean way to distinguish the two invasion strategies experimentally.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about trigger-mode invasion to check whether a student can name the actual molecular switch being flipped, not just say 'the bacteria injects stuff and gets in.' A weak answer stays vague about what is injected or why membrane ruffling happens. A strong answer names specific effectors (SopE/SopE2 as GEFs for Cdc42/Rac1, or Shigella's IpaC) and explains that the T3SS bypasses the need for a matching host receptor altogether, which is precisely the mechanistic contrast with zipper entry.

questions.prompt: What is the core mechanism by which Salmonella SopE and SopE2 drive membrane ruffling?

options.text: They are GEFs that force Cdc42 and Rac1 into their active, GTP-bound state
They bind E-cadherin to trigger localized zipper-style entry
They form a pore that lyses the host membrane directly
They degrade host actin filaments to clear a path for entry

explanations.a: Correct — SopE and SopE2 act as guanine-nucleotide exchange factors, artificially activating the Rho-family GTPases Cdc42 and Rac1 that drive actin-based membrane ruffling.
explanations.b: E-cadherin engagement is the Listeria InlA zipper mechanism, a distinct invasion strategy from Salmonella's trigger mode.
explanations.c: SopE/SopE2 are GTPase-activating effectors, not pore-forming toxins.
explanations.d: SopE/SopE2 promote actin polymerization to build ruffles, not degrade actin.

questions.prompt: Order the events of Salmonella trigger-mode invasion from first to last.

items.text: T3SS needle contacts host membrane and injects effectors
SopE/SopE2 activate Cdc42 and Rac1
Actin-driven membrane ruffles form and sweep outward
Ruffles fold back over the bacterium, engulfing it into a macropinosome

questions.explanation: The T3SS first delivers effectors across the membrane, those effectors activate the Rho-GTPase switches, GTPase activation drives actin polymerization into ruffles, and the ruffles then close over the bacterium to complete macropinocytic uptake.

questions.prompt: Which feature distinguishes trigger-mode entry from zipper-mode entry?

options.text: Trigger mode requires a specific matching host surface receptor, zipper mode does not
Trigger mode produces large, transient membrane ruffles via injected effectors, while zipper mode is a tight, receptor-driven closure
Trigger mode is used only by Gram-positive bacteria
Zipper mode always kills the host cell immediately upon entry

explanations.a: This is reversed — zipper mode depends on a specific receptor (e.g., E-cadherin), while trigger mode bypasses the need for one by injecting effectors directly.
explanations.b: Correct — trigger mode drives broad, transient ruffling through injected effectors activating Rho GTPases, while zipper mode is a localized, tight engagement matched to receptor distribution.
explanations.c: Salmonella and Shigella, both Gram-negative, are the trigger-mode examples described here.
explanations.d: Zipper-mode entry (e.g., Listeria) does not inherently kill the host cell on entry.

lessons.label: Capsules and Antiphagocytic Surfaces

sections.heading: A physical shield against being eaten
sections.body: Many of the deadliest extracellular bacterial pathogens share a single trait: a thick outer polysaccharide capsule. Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Klebsiella pneumoniae all rely on capsules to survive in blood and mucosal surfaces where phagocytes are constantly patrolling. The capsule's job is mechanical and immunological at once: it physically masks complement fragments such as C3b that deposit on the underlying cell wall, keeping neutrophil and macrophage complement receptors from ever making productive contact with them. Without a capsule, C3b opsonization proceeds normally and the phagocyte engulfs the bacterium efficiently; encapsulated strains resist this opsophagocytosis and can persist and replicate in the bloodstream instead. Early work by Avery and colleagues in the 1920s-30s, studying pneumococcal capsular polysaccharide as a serotype-defining antigen, laid the groundwork for recognizing the capsule as both a virulence factor and a target for immunity.

sections.heading: Serotype diversity and the vaccine problem
sections.body: Capsules are chemically diverse: S. pneumoniae alone has more than 90 distinct capsular serotypes, each defined by a different polysaccharide structure, and antibodies raised against one serotype generally do not protect against another. This diversity is precisely why capsule serotype governs vaccine design. The original pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, PCV7, licensed in 2000, covered seven serotypes; it was replaced by PCV13 in 2010, and PCV20 broadened coverage further in 2021. Each expansion targeted the serotypes then causing the most invasive disease, but capsule switching and serotype replacement, where non-vaccine serotypes rise to fill the ecological niche once the covered serotypes are suppressed, has been observed after PCV7's introduction and remains a live surveillance concern. Conjugating the polysaccharide to a carrier protein (as in PCV vaccines) converts a T-independent antigen, which children under two respond to poorly, into a T-dependent one that generates strong memory responses even in infants.

sections.heading: When the capsule looks too much like self
sections.body: N. meningitidis serogroup B presents a special problem: its capsule is a polymer of polysialic acid that closely resembles polysialic acid found on human neural cell adhesion molecule (NCAM), particularly during fetal neurodevelopment. That molecular mimicry makes the group B capsule a poor vaccine antigen, since the immune system is tolerized against it to avoid autoimmunity, and it is why licensed MenB vaccines (such as Bexsero and Trumenba) are built from outer-membrane proteins rather than the capsular polysaccharide used for serogroups A, C, W, and Y.

lessons.workedExample: A lab compares an encapsulated wild-type S. pneumoniae strain with a capsule-deletion mutant in a whole-blood killing assay. After incubating both with fresh human blood (containing complement and phagocytes) for one hour, the capsule-deletion mutant is killed roughly 100-fold more efficiently than the wild type, and adding purified anti-capsular antibody specific to that serotype restores efficient killing of the wild type by promoting Fc-receptor-mediated phagocytosis on top of complement. The experiment demonstrates both that the capsule is protective on its own and that serotype-matched antibody, exactly the kind a conjugate vaccine elicits, is what overcomes it.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing capsule biology wants to know whether a student understands that vaccination against an encapsulated pathogen is a serotype-matching problem, not a single silver bullet. A weak answer says 'the vaccine protects against the bacteria.' A strong answer explains that immunity is largely serotype-specific, cites a concrete example like PCV13 versus PCV20 coverage or the reason MenB uses protein rather than polysaccharide antigens (molecular mimicry with NCAM), and can explain why capsule loss makes a strain more vulnerable to phagocytosis.

questions.prompt: Mechanistically, how does a polysaccharide capsule protect a bacterium from phagocytosis?

options.text: It physically masks deposited complement fragments like C3b from phagocyte receptors
It injects effectors that paralyze the phagocyte's actin cytoskeleton
It secretes a toxin that kills phagocytes on contact
It prevents complement from being produced by the host at all

explanations.a: Correct — the capsule sits over deposited C3b and other opsonins, sterically blocking phagocyte complement receptors from engaging them even though opsonization has occurred underneath.
explanations.b: That describes a T3SS-effector strategy, not a capsule's passive shielding mechanism.
explanations.c: Capsules are not toxins; this describes a different class of virulence factor.
explanations.d: Complement is still produced and deposited normally; the capsule blocks receptor access to it rather than blocking its production.

questions.prompt: Why are licensed vaccines against N. meningitidis serogroup B based on outer-membrane proteins rather than the capsular polysaccharide, unlike serogroups A, C, W, and Y?

options.text: Serogroup B does not have a capsule
The serogroup B capsule (polysialic acid) closely mimics human NCAM, making it a poor and potentially unsafe vaccine antigen
Serogroup B is not associated with invasive disease
Protein vaccines are always cheaper to manufacture than polysaccharide vaccines

explanations.a: Serogroup B does have a capsule; its chemical similarity to a human self-antigen is the specific problem.
explanations.b: Correct — molecular mimicry between the group B polysialic acid capsule and NCAM makes it a poor, tolerated antigen, so protein-based vaccines were developed instead.
explanations.c: Serogroup B causes significant invasive meningococcal disease, which is exactly why an alternative vaccine strategy was needed.
explanations.d: Cost is not the stated reason for the antigen choice here; the immunological mimicry problem is.

questions.prompt: Order the licensure of these pneumococcal conjugate vaccines from earliest to most recent.

items.text: PCV7 (7 serotypes)
PCV13 (13 serotypes)
PCV20 (20 serotypes)

questions.explanation: PCV7 was licensed in 2000, PCV13 replaced it in 2010 with broader coverage, and PCV20 further expanded coverage in 2021 as new serotypes rose in importance.

questions.prompt: Why does serotype-specific antibody matter so much for protection against S. pneumoniae, given it has more than 90 capsular serotypes?

options.text: Antibody raised against one capsular serotype generally does not protect against a different serotype's chemically distinct capsule
Pneumococcal capsules are identical across all serotypes, so any antibody works
Serotype only matters for diagnosis, not for immune protection
Antibodies against the capsule cannot activate complement

explanations.a: Correct — because each serotype's polysaccharide structure differs chemically, protective antibody responses are largely serotype-specific, which is exactly why vaccine coverage is described in terms of the number of serotypes included.
explanations.b: The serotypes are chemically distinct, not identical; that diversity is the whole reason vaccine coverage is a moving target.
explanations.c: Serotype governs protective immunity directly, not just diagnostic classification.
explanations.d: Anti-capsular antibodies can activate complement and promote opsonophagocytosis; that is part of how conjugate vaccines work.

lessons.label: Nutritional Immunity and Iron Piracy

sections.heading: Starving the invader of a nutrient it cannot do without
sections.body: Iron is essential for bacterial enzymes involved in respiration and DNA synthesis, and the host exploits that dependency as a defense. Microbiologist Eugene Weinberg coined the term 'nutritional immunity' in 1975 to describe host strategies that withhold trace nutrients, especially iron, from invading microbes. Free ferric iron in human serum is kept at an almost vanishingly low concentration, on the order of 10^-18 M, because transferrin in blood and lactoferrin in mucosal secretions and neutrophil granules bind iron with extremely high affinity and keep it locked away from anything that cannot pry it loose. During acute infection, the liver-produced hormone hepcidin adds a second layer: induced by IL-6 signaling, hepcidin binds and degrades ferroportin, the only known cellular iron exporter, trapping iron inside macrophages and intestinal cells and driving down circulating iron further, a response so central to infection physiology that it is also the mechanism behind the anemia of chronic inflammation.

sections.heading: Siderophores: molecular lockpicks
sections.body: Bacteria counter by secreting siderophores, small molecules with extraordinarily high affinity for ferric iron that scavenge it away from host iron-binding proteins and are then reimported through dedicated bacterial receptors. Enterobactin, produced by E. coli and Salmonella, has one of the highest known affinities for Fe3+ of any characterized siderophore, with a stability constant estimated near 10^49, high enough to strip iron directly from transferrin. But the host counterpunches again: neutrophils and epithelial cells secrete lipocalin-2 (also called siderocalin or NGAL), a protein that binds enterobactin directly and sequesters the iron-siderophore complex before the bacterium can reimport it, a mechanism demonstrated by Goetz and colleagues in 2002 and shown to matter for infection outcomes by Flo and colleagues in 2004.

sections.heading: Stealth siderophores and heme piracy
sections.body: Pathogens have answered lipocalin-2 in turn. Salmonella and some E. coli strains carry the iroA locus, which glucosylates enterobactin into salmochelin, a modified siderophore that lipocalin-2 can no longer bind effectively, letting the bacterium keep scavenging iron even in the presence of the host's countermeasure. Other pathogens sidestep siderophore competition altogether by pirating iron bound in host heme; Staphylococcus aureus, for instance, uses its Isd (iron-regulated surface determinant) system to strip iron directly from hemoglobin at the cell surface and relay it inward. The iron tug-of-war, host withholding met by bacterial scavenging met by host counter-sequestration, is a decisive determinant of whether an infection is cleared or established, and it continues at essentially every step of a systemic infection.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher compares wild-type Salmonella with an iroA-deletion mutant (unable to make salmochelin, limited to plain enterobactin) in mice with normal versus lipocalin-2-deficient backgrounds. In normal mice, the iroA mutant is significantly attenuated because its enterobactin is neutralized by host lipocalin-2. In lipocalin-2-knockout mice, the growth defect largely disappears, because there is no longer a host defense for the mutant's siderophore to fail against. The paired comparison isolates lipocalin-2 as the specific selective pressure that favors the stealth siderophore, salmochelin, during real infection.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about iron competition to see if a student can trace a specific molecular arms race step by step rather than gesture at 'the bacteria needs iron.' A weak answer stops at 'iron is important for bacteria.' A strong answer walks the exchange: host sequesters iron via transferrin/lactoferrin/hepcidin, bacterium counters with a high-affinity siderophore like enterobactin, host counters that with lipocalin-2, and some bacteria counter that with a modified stealth siderophore like salmochelin — naming each molecule and which side it belongs to.

questions.prompt: Order these moves in the host-pathogen iron tug-of-war from the host's initial defense to the pathogen's most advanced countermeasure described in this lesson.

items.text: Host sequesters iron with transferrin/lactoferrin
Pathogen secretes enterobactin to scavenge iron
Host neutralizes enterobactin with lipocalin-2
Pathogen deploys salmochelin (glucosylated enterobactin) to evade lipocalin-2

questions.explanation: The host first withholds iron via transferrin and lactoferrin; the pathogen counters with the high-affinity siderophore enterobactin; the host counters that with lipocalin-2, which binds enterobactin; and the pathogen counters again with the modified siderophore salmochelin, which lipocalin-2 cannot effectively bind.

questions.prompt: What is the functional role of hepcidin during infection?

options.text: It directly kills bacteria by lysing their membranes
Induced by IL-6, it degrades ferroportin, trapping iron inside macrophages and intestinal cells and lowering circulating iron
It is a bacterial siderophore that scavenges host iron
It binds enterobactin to sequester bacterial iron-siderophore complexes

explanations.a: Hepcidin does not lyse bacteria; it is a host hormone acting on iron transport.
explanations.b: Correct — hepcidin is induced by the inflammatory cytokine IL-6 and degrades the iron exporter ferroportin, restricting circulating iron as part of nutritional immunity.
explanations.c: Hepcidin is a host hormone, not a bacterial siderophore.
explanations.d: That role (binding enterobactin) describes lipocalin-2, not hepcidin.

questions.prompt: Why can salmochelin evade lipocalin-2 when plain enterobactin cannot?

options.text: Salmochelin has a much weaker affinity for iron, so lipocalin-2 ignores it
Salmochelin is glucosylated enterobactin, and the added glucose groups sterically block lipocalin-2's binding pocket
Salmochelin is produced only inside host cells, out of lipocalin-2's reach
Lipocalin-2 targets hepcidin instead of siderophores

explanations.a: Salmochelin retains high iron affinity as a modified enterobactin; affinity loss is not the mechanism of evasion.
explanations.b: Correct — the iroA locus adds glucose groups to enterobactin to make salmochelin, and this structural modification prevents effective binding by lipocalin-2's binding pocket, which is shaped for unmodified enterobactin.
explanations.c: Salmochelin acts extracellularly like other siderophores; location inside the cell is not the evasion mechanism.
explanations.d: Lipocalin-2's target is siderophores like enterobactin, not hepcidin.

lessons.label: The Type III Secretion System: The Molecular Syringe

sections.heading: Anatomy of the needle complex
sections.body: The type III secretion system (T3SS) is a nanomachine, roughly 3.5-4 megadaltons and built from more than twenty different proteins, that spans both bacterial membranes and the host plasma membrane to deliver effector proteins directly into the host cytosol without ever exposing them to extracellular space. Its structure was first directly visualized by electron microscopy in Salmonella by Kubori and colleagues in 1998, revealing a basal body of stacked rings anchored in the inner and outer bacterial membranes, an export apparatus at its base that unfolds and threads effector proteins through a hollow channel, and a needle filament, built from a single small protein (PrgI in Salmonella, YscF in Yersinia), extending roughly 40-80 nanometers outward. At the needle's tip, a translocon pore, assembled from two more secreted proteins (SipB/SipC in Salmonella, YopB/YopD in Yersinia), inserts directly into the host plasma membrane, completing a continuous conduit from bacterial cytoplasm to host cytoplasm.

sections.heading: A shared ancestry with the flagellum
sections.body: The T3SS injectisome is structurally and genetically homologous to the bacterial flagellar basal body and export apparatus; both use a strikingly similar set of proteins to build a ring-and-channel structure and to export unfolded proteins through a narrow central pore using a dedicated ATPase. Phylogenetic analyses, including work by Gophna, Ron, and Graur in 2003, place the flagellar apparatus as the evolutionarily older system, with virulence-associated injectisomes arising later through gene duplication and repurposing, though the exact direction and history remain an active area of comparative genomics. Either way, the relationship is a clean example of how a machine built for one purpose (self-propulsion) was co-opted evolutionarily for an entirely different one (interspecies protein injection).

sections.heading: Two case studies in injected function
sections.body: Yersinia pestis and related species use their T3SS to inject a defined set of Yop effectors directly into immune cells: YopH is a tyrosine phosphatase that dismantles focal adhesion signaling to block phagocytosis; YopE acts as a GTPase-activating protein that inactivates Rho-family GTPases, collapsing the actin cytoskeleton; and YopJ/YopP is an acetyltransferase that blocks MAPK and NF-kB signaling, both suppressing the inflammatory response and driving the target cell toward apoptosis. Salmonella, notably, carries two distinct T3SSs encoded on separate pathogenicity islands: SPI-1, which injects SopE, SopB, SipA, and SipC to drive invasion of non-phagocytic cells, and SPI-2, which is activated only after the bacterium is safely inside its vacuole and injects a different effector set (including SifA) to remodel that vacuole for long-term intracellular survival, showing that a single organism can deploy the same class of machine for two sequential, functionally opposite jobs.

lessons.workedExample: A lab wants to determine whether a Yersinia phenotype (phagocyte resistance) depends on the T3SS itself or on a specific injected effector. They compare three strains against neutrophils: wild-type Yersinia (resists phagocytosis), a T3SS-null mutant lacking the needle complex entirely (rapidly phagocytosed, since no effectors reach the neutrophil at all), and a yopH-deletion mutant that still assembles a functional needle but cannot inject YopH specifically (partially phagocytosed, intermediate resistance). The three-way comparison separates 'the machine is broken' from 'one specific cargo is missing,' pinning YopH's tyrosine phosphatase activity as necessary, though not solely sufficient, for full phagocytosis resistance.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about the T3SS to test whether a student can distinguish the delivery machine from its cargo, and can explain why that distinction matters experimentally. A weak answer conflates 'the needle' with 'the toxin' as if they were one thing. A strong answer describes the needle complex as a conduit and names specific injected effectors and their distinct enzymatic activities (a GEF versus a GAP versus a phosphatase versus an acetyltransferase), and can note the flagellar homology as evidence the system was evolutionarily repurposed.

questions.prompt: Match each Yersinia Yop effector to its molecular activity.

right.text: Tyrosine phosphatase that dismantles focal adhesion signaling
GTPase-activating protein that inactivates Rho-family GTPases
Acetyltransferase that blocks MAPK/NF-kB signaling

questions.explanation: YopH is a phosphatase disrupting adhesion/phagocytosis signaling, YopE is a GAP that collapses the actin cytoskeleton by inactivating Rho GTPases, and YopJ/YopP acetylates signaling kinases to suppress inflammatory pathways and drive apoptosis.

questions.prompt: What is the significance of the T3SS's structural homology to the bacterial flagellum?

options.text: It shows the T3SS and flagellum are unrelated but coincidentally similar-looking
It indicates the injectisome likely arose through evolutionary repurposing of the older flagellar export apparatus for protein injection
It proves all T3SS-carrying bacteria are also motile
It means the T3SS and flagellum are interchangeable and can substitute for each other's function

explanations.a: The similarity is genetic and structural, not coincidental; comparative genomic analyses support common ancestry.
explanations.b: Correct — phylogenetic analysis (e.g., Gophna, Ron, and Graur, 2003) supports the flagellar apparatus as ancestral, with virulence injectisomes representing a later evolutionary repurposing of the same core machinery.
explanations.c: Many T3SS-carrying pathogens (e.g., Shigella) are non-motile; the injectisome and flagellum are separate systems that can exist independently.
explanations.d: The two systems are homologous but functionally distinct and not interchangeable in a live bacterium.

questions.prompt: Why does Salmonella maintain two separate T3SSs, SPI-1 and SPI-2, rather than one?

options.text: SPI-1 drives invasion of non-phagocytic cells, while SPI-2 activates later to remodel the intracellular vacuole for long-term survival
SPI-1 and SPI-2 are redundant backups of the identical function
SPI-1 is used only in plants and SPI-2 only in animals
SPI-2 is a non-functional evolutionary remnant with no active role

explanations.a: Correct — SPI-1 effectors (SopE, SopB, SipA, SipC) drive initial invasion, while SPI-2 is induced after the bacterium is inside the vacuole and injects a different effector set, including SifA, to sustain intracellular survival, so the two systems serve sequential, distinct roles.
explanations.b: The two systems are functionally distinct and act at different infection stages, not redundant.
explanations.c: Both systems function within animal hosts; this option misrepresents their roles.
explanations.d: SPI-2 is an actively functioning system essential for intracellular Salmonella survival, not a vestigial one.

lessons.label: Type IV/VI Secretion and the Mobile Virulence Genome

sections.heading: Type IV secretion: a syringe descended from a mating machine
sections.body: Where the T3SS needle evolved from the flagellum, the type IV secretion system (T4SS) evolved from bacterial conjugation machinery, the apparatus bacteria use to transfer plasmid DNA between cells during mating. That ancestry shows in its range: Agrobacterium tumefaciens uses a VirB/VirD4 T4SS to inject actual T-DNA, a segment of its tumor-inducing plasmid, directly into plant cells, causing the crown gall tumors that made this system the basis of modern plant genetic engineering. Helicobacter pylori, which colonizes the human stomach and drives gastric cancer risk, uses its cag pathogenicity island-encoded T4SS to inject the CagA protein into gastric epithelial cells, a translocation event demonstrated directly by Odenbreit and colleagues in 2000; once inside, CagA is tyrosine-phosphorylated by host Src and Abl kinases and then dysregulates SHP-2 phosphatase signaling, disrupting cell junctions and proliferation control. Legionella pneumophila takes the T4SS concept furthest: its Dot/Icm system injects over 300 distinct effector proteins, identified across studies beginning with Segal and Shuman and Vogel and colleagues around 1998, remodeling a phagosome into the Legionella-containing vacuole where the bacterium replicates, hijacking host vesicular trafficking almost entirely.

sections.heading: Type VI secretion: a molecular harpoon aimed at neighbors, not just hosts
sections.body: The type VI secretion system (T6SS), identified independently in Vibrio cholerae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa by Pukatzki and colleagues and Mougous and colleagues in 2006, is structurally a contractile, phage-tail-like spike built from Hcp and VgrG proteins that fires like a harpoon, puncturing a target cell and injecting toxic effectors in one contraction-driven stroke. Uniquely among the secretion systems in this unit, the T6SS is used as often against other bacteria as against host cells: many T6SS effectors degrade peptidoglycan or membrane lipids of competing bacterial species, making it a weapon for interbacterial competition within a crowded microbial community, alongside T6SS-mediated attacks on host cells in some pathogens.

sections.heading: Virulence arrives in transferable blocks
sections.body: None of these systems exist as isolated genes; they arrive, and spread, as whole functional units. Pathogenicity islands, a term formalized by Hacker and Kaper around 2000 from earlier work on uropathogenic E. coli, are large chromosomal regions with a GC content that differs from the surrounding core genome, often flanked by tRNA genes and mobile-element remnants, that carry entire virulence gene sets (an adhesin operon, a whole T3SS, a toxin) as a single horizontally transferable block, rather than as genes accumulated one mutation at a time. Toxins, too, frequently arrive via phage: the tox gene encoding diphtheria toxin is carried by a lysogenic corynephage, a phenomenon of lysogenic conversion described by Freeman in 1951, and both cholera toxin (via the CTX phage, shown by Waldor and Mekalanos in 1996) and Shiga toxin in E. coli O157:H7 are similarly phage-encoded. This is why horizontal gene transfer, not slow point mutation, is the dominant force assembling a dangerous new pathogen from a harmless relative.

lessons.workedExample: A student sequencing an E. coli outbreak isolate finds it carries a large chromosomal block absent from a related non-pathogenic lab strain: it has different GC content from the rest of the genome, sits adjacent to a tRNA gene, and encodes an entire T3SS plus several effectors. This is a textbook pathogenicity island signature. Separately finding a phage-associated Shiga toxin gene elsewhere in the genome tells the student the strain acquired its two most dangerous traits, invasion machinery and a potent toxin, from two independent horizontal transfer events rather than by gradually evolving them from its harmless ancestor.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge raises T4SS/T6SS and pathogenicity islands to test whether a student sees virulence as modular and acquirable, not as a fixed species trait. A weak answer treats 'pathogenic E. coli' as a separate species from 'harmless E. coli.' A strong answer explains that a single horizontal transfer event, such as gaining a phage-encoded toxin gene or a whole pathogenicity island, can convert a commensal strain into an outbreak strain, and can name a specific system (CagA via H. pylori's T4SS, or T-DNA via Agrobacterium's T4SS) to ground the claim.

questions.prompt: Match each secretion system example to what it delivers into its target.

right.text: T-DNA from the tumor-inducing plasmid, into plant cells
CagA oncoprotein, into gastric epithelial cells
Over 300 effectors remodeling the host phagosome
Toxic effectors via a contractile harpoon spike, into host or competing bacterial cells

questions.explanation: Agrobacterium's T4SS delivers oncogenic T-DNA into plants; H. pylori's T4SS delivers CagA into gastric cells; Legionella's Dot/Icm T4SS delivers a huge effector repertoire to build its replicative vacuole; the T6SS fires a contractile spike carrying toxic effectors into host cells or rival bacteria.

questions.prompt: What structural feature distinguishes the T6SS from the T3SS and T4SS described in this lesson?

options.text: It is a contractile, phage-tail-like spike (built from Hcp/VgrG) that punctures targets in a single harpoon-like stroke
It is descended from the flagellar basal body, like the T3SS
It only functions when the target cell is a plant cell
It cannot target other bacteria, only host cells

explanations.a: Correct — the T6SS is structurally a contractile phage-tail-like apparatus built from Hcp and VgrG proteins, mechanically distinct from the flagellum-derived T3SS needle or the conjugation-derived T4SS.
explanations.b: The flagellar ancestry belongs to the T3SS, not the T6SS.
explanations.c: T6SS activity is documented against both host cells and, notably, competing bacteria, not plant cells specifically in the examples given.
explanations.d: A defining feature of the T6SS is that it is frequently used against competing bacterial cells, which sets it apart from T3SS/T4SS in this unit.

questions.prompt: What defines a pathogenicity island as a distinct genomic feature?

options.text: A large chromosomal region with atypical GC content, often flanked by tRNA genes, carrying a virulence gene set as one transferable block
A single point mutation that converts a harmless gene into a virulence gene
A gene found only on the bacterial chromosome, never on plasmids or via phage
A region of the genome with no relationship to horizontal gene transfer

explanations.a: Correct — pathogenicity islands are recognized by their atypical GC content relative to the core genome, association with tRNA genes/mobile elements, and their carriage of whole virulence gene sets as a horizontally transferable unit.
explanations.b: This describes gradual point mutation, the opposite of the block-transfer mechanism that defines pathogenicity islands.
explanations.c: Pathogenicity islands are specifically a chromosomal phenomenon distinguished by transfer history, but the broader concept of mobile virulence genes also includes phage- and plasmid-encoded elements described in this lesson.
explanations.d: Pathogenicity islands are, by definition, products of horizontal gene transfer.

questions.prompt: Diphtheria toxin, cholera toxin, and Shiga toxin share what common feature in how the bacterium acquired the ability to make them?

options.text: All three toxin genes are carried by bacteriophages that lysogenically convert their bacterial host
All three are encoded on the bacterial core chromosome and arose by point mutation
All three require a T6SS to be delivered
None of the three toxin genes can be horizontally transferred

explanations.a: Correct — the diphtheria tox gene (corynephage beta, Freeman 1951), cholera toxin (CTX phage, Waldor and Mekalanos 1996), and Shiga toxin (Stx-converting phages) are all phage-encoded, acquired through lysogenic conversion rather than originating in the core chromosome.
explanations.b: These toxin genes are phage-acquired, not products of core-genome point mutation.
explanations.c: These are secreted toxins delivered by their own mechanisms, not dependent on the T6SS described in this lesson.
explanations.d: Phage-mediated transfer is itself a form of horizontal gene transfer, so this option is the opposite of what is true.

lessons.label: Exotoxins vs Endotoxin: The Fundamental Divide

sections.heading: Two toxin classes, opposite logic
sections.body: Bacterial pathogens damage hosts with two fundamentally different kinds of poison. Exotoxins are proteins actively secreted (or released on lysis) by living bacteria, usually encoded by a specific gene that may sit on a plasmid or a lysogenic bacteriophage rather than the core chromosome. Most are heat-labile — boiling typically destroys their activity — and each one is exquisitely specific, binding and disabling one host molecule with enzymatic precision, though notable exceptions exist: staphylococcal superantigens like TSST-1 are unusually heat-stable and protease-resistant, and pore-forming toxins act physically rather than enzymatically. Endotoxin is a different animal entirely: it is not secreted but is the lipopolysaccharide (LPS) that forms the outer leaflet of every gram-negative bacterium's outer membrane, released mainly when the cell wall is damaged or the bacterium dies and lyses. Its toxic activity resides in a single conserved component, lipid A, which is heat-stable and survives autoclaving.

sections.heading: Potency and specificity compared
sections.body: The two classes differ by orders of magnitude in potency and mechanism. Exotoxins like botulinum toxin act at nanogram-per-kilogram doses because each molecule is a catalytic enzyme that can disable many copies of its target inside a cell. Endotoxin is far less potent gram-for-gram than a catalytic exotoxin — doses as low as a few nanograms per kilogram can trigger fever, though precipitating full septic shock takes a much larger cumulative burden — but it isn't an enzyme attacking one molecule; it is a single conserved structure, lipid A, recognized as a generic danger signal by the innate immune system's TLR4 receptor, so its damage comes from triggering the host's own inflammatory cascade rather than from direct enzymatic poisoning.

sections.heading: Why only exotoxins become toxoid vaccines
sections.body: Because an exotoxin is a folded protein whose toxic active site and its immunogenic surface epitopes are separable, treating it with formaldehyde or heat can destroy the toxic activity while leaving the antibody-recognizable shape intact — this inactivated but still-immunogenic protein is a toxoid, the basis of the diphtheria and tetanus vaccines in DTaP. Mechanistically, formaldehyde works by cross-linking lysine residues in the toxin's active site and on neighboring chains, locking the enzymatic pocket shut while leaving the outer, antibody-recognized surface largely undisturbed. The same trick extends beyond DTaP: anthrax vaccines use a similarly inactivated protective antigen protein to raise protective antibodies without exposing the recipient to active toxin. Endotoxin offers no equivalent trick: lipid A's toxicity and its recognition by TLR4 are the same molecular feature, so there is no way to strip toxicity while preserving a useful immunizing target, and no licensed endotoxin toxoid vaccine exists. Genetic encoding compounds the difference — because exotoxin genes are discrete and mobile, a strain can lose or gain toxigenicity (a nontoxigenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae lacking the tox-carrying phage causes no diphtheria), while LPS is a structural, non-optional part of every gram-negative envelope.

lessons.workedExample: Two organisms illustrate the divide. Corynebacterium diphtheriae only causes diphtheria if it is lysogenized by a bacteriophage carrying the tox gene; a phage-free strain is essentially harmless even though it is the identical species — because the toxin, not the bacterium, does the damage. Formalin-treated diphtheria toxin becomes the toxoid injected in DTaP. Contrast that with Escherichia coli: every strain, toxigenic or not, has LPS as an obligatory structural component of its outer membrane. Boiling an E. coli culture for an hour kills the bacteria but barely dents the pyrogenicity of the released LPS, because lipid A's heat-stable structure is untouched.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks this to see whether a student treats 'bacterial toxin' as one undifferentiated hazard or understands it as two distinct biological strategies with different consequences for vaccine design. A weak answer says toxins are 'proteins that make you sick.' A strong answer explains that exotoxins are gene-encoded, heat-labile, and separable into toxic and immunogenic components (hence toxoid vaccines), while endotoxin is a heat-stable structural molecule whose toxicity and immune recognition are inseparable — which is exactly why there is a tetanus vaccine but no vaccine against endotoxin itself.

questions.prompt: Why can exotoxins, but not endotoxin, be converted into toxoid vaccines?

options.text: Exotoxins are proteins whose toxic activity can be chemically destroyed while immunogenic epitopes survive; lipid A's toxicity and immune recognition are the same feature and can't be separated
Endotoxin is too large a molecule for the immune system to recognize at all
Exotoxins are heat-stable, so boiling preserves them for vaccine production
Endotoxin only affects gram-positive bacteria, so it is irrelevant to vaccine design

explanations.a: Correct — a toxoid works because formaldehyde or heat can wreck an exotoxin's enzymatic active site while leaving its antibody-recognizable shape intact; lipid A offers no such separation.
explanations.b: Wrong — LPS is very much recognized by the immune system (via TLR4); the problem is not detectability, it's inseparability of toxicity from that recognition.
explanations.c: Backwards — exotoxins are heat-labile, not heat-stable; it's endotoxin that survives boiling.
explanations.d: Wrong — endotoxin/LPS is specifically a gram-negative outer membrane component; gram-positive bacteria don't have it.

questions.prompt: Match each property to the toxin class it describes.

left.text: Often encoded on a plasmid or phage
Obligatory structural component of the outer membrane

right.text: Exotoxin
Endotoxin (LPS)

questions.explanation: Exotoxins are heat-labile secreted proteins, often on mobile genetic elements; endotoxin (LPS/lipid A) is a heat-stable structural molecule built into every gram-negative outer membrane.

questions.prompt: A Corynebacterium diphtheriae strain that lacks the tox-carrying bacteriophage causes no diphtheria disease even though it is the same species as toxigenic strains. What does this best illustrate?

options.text: Exotoxin production depends on a discrete, mobile genetic element, so toxigenicity can be gained or lost independent of the species' identity
Diphtheria is actually caused by endotoxin, not an exotoxin
All Corynebacterium species are nonpathogenic regardless of phage status
The bacteriophage itself is directly cytotoxic to host cells

explanations.a: Correct — the tox gene rides on a lysogenic phage, so a strain's disease-causing capacity tracks the phage, not the bacterial species itself.
explanations.b: Wrong — diphtheria pathology is caused by the secreted diphtheria exotoxin, not LPS.
explanations.c: Wrong — toxigenic strains carrying the phage do cause severe disease; the point is that phage status, not species, determines this.
explanations.d: Wrong — the phage's role is to carry the tox gene; it is the resulting protein toxin, not the phage particle, that damages host cells.

questions.prompt: In rough terms, how do exotoxin and endotoxin potency compare, and why?

options.text: Exotoxins act at nanogram-per-kilogram doses because they are catalytic enzymes hitting a specific target; endotoxin's fever threshold is also in the low nanogram-per-kilogram range but its effect works by triggering a generic host inflammatory response rather than enzymatic poisoning
Endotoxin is always more potent than any exotoxin because it is heat-stable
Potency is identical between the two classes since both are recognized by TLR4
Exotoxins require large doses because they must first be processed by the host immune system before acting

explanations.a: Correct — enzymatic exotoxins can be catalytically efficient at very low doses, and endotoxin's pyrogenic threshold is likewise low (nanogram-per-kilogram range), but its effect comes from triggering TLR4-driven inflammation across many immune cells rather than from direct enzymatic poisoning of one target.
explanations.b: Wrong — heat stability describes durability under heat, not potency per gram; several exotoxins are far more potent by mass.
explanations.c: Wrong — TLR4 recognizes LPS specifically, not exotoxins, and the two classes differ substantially in potency.
explanations.d: Wrong — exotoxins act directly and enzymatically on host targets without needing host immune processing first.

lessons.label: AB Toxins I - Blocking Protein Synthesis

sections.heading: The A-B logic and the 1888 proof of a soluble poison
sections.body: Many exotoxins share a modular architecture: a B (binding) component that recognizes a host cell surface receptor and gets the toxin inside, and an A (active) component, an enzyme that does the actual damage once delivered to the cytosol. The concept of a secreted toxin causing disease independent of the living bacterium was established by Roux and Yersin's 1888 experiment: they passed Corynebacterium diphtheriae broth culture through a fine filter that excluded the bacteria themselves, then injected the cell-free filtrate into animals, which developed the paralysis and tissue damage typical of diphtheria. This proved a soluble, secreted poison — not bacterial invasion — was doing the damage, founding the modern concept of the exotoxin.

sections.heading: Diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A: stopping elongation factor 2
sections.body: Diphtheria toxin is a single polypeptide organized into a receptor-binding domain, a translocation domain, and a catalytic domain — functionally an A-B toxin even though it isn't built from separate chains. It binds the proHB-EGF receptor, is endocytosed, and endosomal acidification drives the catalytic domain across the membrane into the cytosol, where it ADP-ribosylates a unique, post-translationally modified histidine residue called diphthamide on eukaryotic elongation factor 2 (EF-2). This blocks EF-2's translocation step in protein synthesis, so the ribosome stalls and the cell can no longer make protein, eventually dying. Pseudomonas exotoxin A, despite an unrelated domain arrangement, converges on the identical molecular target — ADP-ribosylating the same diphthamide residue on EF-2 — a functional identity established by Iglewski and Kabat in 1975.

sections.heading: Shiga toxin: attacking the ribosome directly
sections.body: Shiga toxin (from Shigella dysenteriae, first characterized by Kiyoshi Shiga in the 1890s) and the closely related Shiga-like toxins of enterohemorrhagic E. coli use a different chemistry to reach the same functional endpoint. They are AB5 toxins: a pentameric B ring binds the glycolipid receptor Gb3, which is enriched on renal endothelial cells — explaining why Shiga toxin-producing infections can progress to hemolytic uremic syndrome. The A subunit is not a transferase but an N-glycosidase: it depurinates a single specific adenine base, A4324, within the 28S ribosomal RNA of the large ribosomal subunit — the identical residue targeted by the plant toxin ricin, a striking case of two unrelated toxins converging on one nucleotide — which prevents elongation factor-dependent binding of aminoacyl-tRNA and halts translation just as effectively as diphtheria toxin, but by directly vandalizing the rRNA rather than modifying an elongation factor.

lessons.workedExample: Roux and Yersin's filtration design is the template for demonstrating any exotoxin: grow the organism, pass the culture through a filter fine enough to exclude intact bacteria, and test whether the filtrate alone reproduces disease. Applied conceptually to two different toxins: diphtheria toxin filtrate injected into an animal ADP-ribosylates EF-2's diphthamide residue in host cells, stalling the elongation step of translation; a Shiga toxin filtrate instead depurinates a single adenine in 28S rRNA, physically damaging the ribosome's RNA core. Both experiments end the same way — protein synthesis stops and the cell dies — but a lab distinguishing the two mechanisms would look for ADP-ribose covalently attached to EF-2 versus a depurinated, N-glycosidase-nicked rRNA.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this topic wants to know whether a student can name the actual molecular lesion, not just that 'the toxin stops the ribosome.' A weak answer conflates diphtheria and Shiga toxin as doing the same thing to the same molecule. A strong answer specifies that diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A ADP-ribosylate the diphthamide residue on EF-2, while Shiga toxin is an N-glycosidase that depurinates 28S rRNA — two different chemistries converging on the same outcome, protein synthesis arrest.

questions.prompt: What is the specific molecular target of diphtheria toxin's ADP-ribosylation activity?

options.text: The diphthamide residue on eukaryotic elongation factor 2 (EF-2)
A specific adenine base in 28S ribosomal RNA
The alpha subunit of the stimulatory G protein, Gs
SNAP-25 at the presynaptic membrane

explanations.a: Correct — diphtheria toxin's catalytic domain ADP-ribosylates diphthamide, a modified histidine unique to EF-2, blocking the translocation step of translation.
explanations.b: Wrong — depurinating 28S rRNA is Shiga toxin's mechanism, an N-glycosidase reaction, not ADP-ribosylation of a protein.
explanations.c: Wrong — Gs-alpha is the target of cholera toxin, a different AB toxin covered separately.
explanations.d: Wrong — SNAP-25 is cleaved by botulinum toxin's protease activity, unrelated to ADP-ribosylation.

questions.prompt: Match each toxin or historical experiment to what it does or demonstrated.

right.text: ADP-ribosylates EF-2's diphthamide residue, blocking translocation
Depurinates a specific adenine in 28S rRNA, blocking aminoacyl-tRNA binding
Proved a cell-free bacterial filtrate alone reproduces disease

questions.explanation: Diphtheria toxin modifies EF-2 by ADP-ribosylation; Shiga toxin is an N-glycosidase that damages 28S rRNA directly; Roux and Yersin's filtration established that a secreted, cell-free toxin — not the bacterium itself — causes diphtheria pathology.

questions.prompt: Order the steps by which diphtheria toxin travels from secretion to halting host protein synthesis.

items.text: Toxin is secreted and binds the proHB-EGF receptor via its receptor-binding domain
Toxin-receptor complex is endocytosed into the cell
Endosomal acidification drives the catalytic domain across the membrane into the cytosol
Catalytic domain ADP-ribosylates the diphthamide residue on EF-2
Translation elongation halts and the cell can no longer synthesize protein

questions.explanation: Binding precedes endocytosis, which precedes acid-triggered translocation of the catalytic domain, which precedes the ADP-ribosylation reaction itself, which finally produces the functional consequence of halted translation.

questions.prompt: Why did Roux and Yersin's 1888 filtration experiment matter for the concept of an exotoxin?

options.text: It proved that a secreted, soluble poison in cell-free filtrate alone was sufficient to cause diphtheria-like disease, independent of live bacteria
It proved that LPS in the bacterial cell wall triggers fever
It proved that direct bacterial contact with tissue is required for disease
It proved diphtheria toxin is heat-stable

explanations.a: Correct — filtering out the bacteria and still reproducing disease with the filtrate demonstrated a secreted toxin, not bacterial invasion, was the causative agent.
explanations.b: Wrong — that describes endotoxin/LPS biology, a separate topic from this bacterium-free protein exotoxin.
explanations.c: Wrong — the experiment showed the opposite: bacteria did not need to be present at all, only their secreted product.
explanations.d: Wrong — diphtheria toxin is heat-labile, and heat stability was not what this experiment tested.

lessons.label: AB Toxins II - Hijacking Signaling

sections.heading: Cholera toxin locks the 'on' switch of adenylate cyclase
sections.body: Vibrio cholerae's cholera toxin is a classic AB5 toxin: a pentameric B ring binds the GM1 ganglioside on intestinal epithelial cells, and the A1 fragment is delivered into the cytosol, where it ADP-ribosylates an arginine residue on the alpha subunit of the stimulatory G protein, Gs-alpha. Normally Gs-alpha's own GTPase activity turns adenylate cyclase back off after a brief burst of signaling; ADP-ribosylation disables that GTPase activity, locking Gs-alpha — and therefore adenylate cyclase — permanently in the 'on' position. Intracellular cAMP surges, activating protein kinase A, which phosphorylates and opens the CFTR chloride channel. The result is a massive, sustained efflux of chloride, sodium, and water into the gut lumen, producing the characteristic 'rice-water stool' and fluid losses that can reach liters per day. S.N. De's 1959 rabbit ileal loop experiments were pivotal in showing that a secreted, cell-free filtrate — not the live organism — was sufficient to cause this fluid secretion.

sections.heading: Why oral rehydration therapy works around, not against, the lesion
sections.body: Cholera toxin disables the CFTR-mediated chloride secretion pathway, but it leaves an entirely separate transporter untouched: the sodium-glucose cotransporter SGLT1 on the same epithelial cells. Because SGLT1 still functions normally, co-administering glucose with sodium and other electrolytes allows the gut to actively absorb sodium (with glucose riding along), and water follows osmotically back into the body — even while the toxin-driven secretory pathway remains fully active. This is the biochemical basis of oral rehydration solution (glucose plus electrolytes in a specific ratio, not water alone), a low-cost intervention credited with dramatically cutting global childhood diarrheal mortality.

sections.heading: Pertussis toxin: the opposite G protein, the same direction of effect
sections.body: Bordetella pertussis's pertussis toxin is also an AB5 toxin, but it ADP-ribosylates a cysteine residue near the C-terminus of the alpha subunit of the inhibitory G protein, Gi-alpha, instead of the arginine residue cholera toxin modifies on Gs-alpha. Gi-alpha's normal job is to restrain adenylate cyclase; ADP-ribosylation prevents Gi-alpha from doing that, so adenylate cyclase again runs unopposed and cAMP again rises — a different G protein disabled, but the same net direction of effect as cholera toxin.
