lessons.workedExample: A pharmaceutical microbiologist wants to find new antibiotics against MRSA. Screening the same handful of easily culturable soil actinomycetes that earlier antibiotic discovery programs already exhausted keeps turning up already-known compounds. Switching strategy, the team runs iChip in situ diffusion chambers on fresh soil, recovers dozens of previously unculturable strains, and screens each one's culture supernatant against MRSA in a simple zone-of-inhibition assay; one strain, a new betaproteobacterium, produces a clear inhibition zone. Following that hit through purification and structural work is exactly the pipeline that led from an iChip isolate, Eleftheria terrae, to teixobactin in Ling and colleagues' 2015 report.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why not just sequence the community and skip culturing?' to test whether a student sees the limits of sequence-only approaches. A weak answer cannot explain what an isolate provides that a metagenome does not. A strong answer states plainly that only a live isolate lets you measure growth, test compounds directly, or purify a molecule at scale, and backs it with a concrete case — teixobactin recovered from an iChip-cultured organism, or culturomics' hundreds-of-conditions strategy for the gut — showing cultivation and sequencing as complementary tools rather than sequencing having simply replaced cultivation.

questions.prompt: How was the antibiotic teixobactin discovered?

options.text: It was synthesized computationally from a metagenomic gene sequence with no live organism involved
It was produced by Eleftheria terrae, a soil betaproteobacterium recovered using iChip in situ diffusion chamber cultivation
It was isolated from a well-known, easily culturable Streptomyces species already in standard culture collections
It was discovered by screening human gut isolates obtained through culturomics

explanations.a: Teixobactin required an actual live producing organism, isolated via iChip cultivation, not a purely computational or cell-free synthesis route.
explanations.b: Correct — Ling and colleagues' 2015 Nature paper reported teixobactin from Eleftheria terrae, a previously unknown soil organism recovered using iChip in situ diffusion chamber cultivation, precisely because it had been unculturable by standard methods.
explanations.c: The producing organism was newly discovered and previously unculturable, not an already-known Streptomyces strain from existing collections.
explanations.d: Teixobactin came from soil cultivation via iChip, not from the gut-focused culturomics approach described later in this lesson.

questions.prompt: What is the central strategy behind culturomics as developed by Lagier and colleagues?

options.text: Running samples across hundreds of distinct culture conditions in parallel, then rapidly identifying growth with MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry
Using a single highly optimized medium designed to match the exact chemistry of the human gut
Sequencing every sample directly and never attempting to culture any organism
Burying diffusion chambers in situ in the gut to let native gut chemistry support growth

explanations.a: Correct — culturomics deliberately multiplies the number of distinct conditions (media, atmosphere, pH, temperature, additives) run in parallel, then uses fast MALDI-TOF identification, falling back to 16S sequencing only when needed, to process the resulting volume of colonies.
explanations.b: Culturomics is defined by breadth across many different conditions rather than a single optimized medium; that would be closer to a targeted enrichment strategy.
explanations.c: Culturomics is explicitly a culture-based method; sequencing is used only as a fallback identification tool for colonies MALDI-TOF cannot match, not as a replacement for culturing.
explanations.d: In situ diffusion chamber burial describes iChip-style methods from the previous lesson, not the culturomics approach, which uses standard lab-based parallel plating with varied conditions.

questions.prompt: Match each finding or method to its source in this lesson.

left.text: Discovery of teixobactin from Eleftheria terrae via iChip
Development of culturomics for the human gut microbiome

right.text: Ling and colleagues, 2015, Nature
Lagier and colleagues, 2012 and 2016

questions.explanation: The teixobactin discovery, led by Ling with Lewis's group, was published in Nature in 2015; culturomics was introduced by Lagier and colleagues in a 2012 paper with a larger 2016 follow-up expanding the cultured gut catalog.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the culturomics workflow as described in this lesson.

items.text: Split a single sample across hundreds of distinct culture conditions varying atmosphere, pH, temperature, and additives
Incubate and collect any colonies that grow under each condition
Identify colonies rapidly using MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry protein fingerprinting
Fall back to 16S rRNA gene sequencing only for colonies MALDI-TOF cannot match

questions.explanation: The sample is first spread across many conditions, colonies are then collected after incubation, MALDI-TOF provides the fast first-pass identification, and 16S sequencing is reserved as the slower fallback for whatever MALDI-TOF cannot resolve.

lessons.label: The 16S rRNA Gene as a Molecular Marker

sections.heading: Why one gene can stand in for a whole cell
sections.body: Most microbes in a soil sample, a gut, or a lake will not grow on any dish a lab offers them — estimates from environmental surveys have long put the culturable fraction at well under 1% in many habitats. Culture-independent microbiology gets around this by reading DNA directly, and the gene it reads most often is 16S rRNA, part of the small ribosomal subunit found in every bacterium and archaeon. Three properties make it work as a universal marker. First, it is present in every cell that has ever been checked, because ribosomes are essential machinery — no organism survives without one. Second, ribosome function is so tightly constrained by the physics of translation that the gene's sequence changes very slowly over evolutionary time — roughly 1% sequence divergence accumulates per 50 million years in many bacterial lineages — giving it a molecular clock steady enough to compare bacteria separated by billions of years, unlike faster-evolving genes that saturate with repeat substitutions at the same site over such timescales. Third, at roughly 1,500 base pairs, the gene alternates highly conserved stretches, nearly identical across all life, with nine hypervariable regions (V1-V9) that accumulate species-level differences. Conserved regions anchor universal PCR primers — such as the classic near-full-length 27F/1492R pair, which flanks almost the entire gene — while variable regions supply the taxonomic signal.

sections.heading: Woese, Fox, and a third form of life
sections.body: The tool's power was proven before sequencing was cheap. In 1977 Carl Woese and George Fox, comparing 16S rRNA oligonucleotide catalogs across dozens of organisms, found that a group of methane-producing microbes was as different from ordinary bacteria as bacteria are from eukaryotes — evidence for what they called archaebacteria, a lineage hiding in plain sight because it looked bacterial under a microscope. Woese, Otto Kandler, and Mark Wheelis formalized this into the three-domain tree of life — Bacteria, Archaea, Eucarya — in a 1990 paper, reorganizing all of biology around rRNA sequence rather than visible traits. Norman Pace pushed the same molecule further in the 1980s, cloning 16S genes directly out of environmental DNA without culturing anything first, and argued in a widely cited 1997 Science paper that this culture-independent rRNA approach revealed a microbial world far larger than the culturable slice biologists had been describing for a century.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to know whether a gut sample contains organisms from the phylum Bacteroidetes without culturing anything. They extract total community DNA, PCR-amplify the 16S gene with primers that bind the gene's conserved flanking regions (so every bacterium's copy gets amplified, not just one target species), and sequence the V4 hypervariable region. Aligning the resulting sequences against a reference database, they find several reads matching Bacteroides at over 97% identity. No dish, no colony, no incubator was involved — the identification rests entirely on the fact that the conserved regions guaranteed universal amplification while the variable region carried enough sequence divergence to distinguish genera.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why 16S and not some other gene?' to see whether the student understands marker choice rather than having memorized a protocol. A weak answer says 'it's the standard gene for bacteria.' A strong answer names the actual tradeoff: 16S is universal and slowly evolving because ribosome function constrains it, and its conserved/variable alternation lets one primer set amplify everything while still resolving taxonomy — properties a rapidly evolving or non-universal gene would lack. Naming Woese and Fox's 1977 discovery of Archaea signals the student sees 16S as a historically validated tool, not folklore.

questions.prompt: Why does the 16S rRNA gene make a good universal marker for identifying bacteria and archaea from environmental DNA?

options.text: It is the largest gene in the bacterial genome, giving the most sequence to work with
It is present in all bacteria and archaea and evolves slowly enough to compare distantly related organisms, while still containing variable regions
It is the only gene that can be amplified by PCR
It only appears in organisms that cannot be cultured

explanations.a: 16S rRNA is about 1,500 bp — modest in size; its usefulness comes from universality and evolutionary rate, not length.
explanations.b: Correct — universal presence plus a slow, steady rate of change (from ribosome function constraints) plus alternating conserved/variable regions is exactly what a phylogenetic marker needs.
explanations.c: Any gene with known flanking sequence can be PCR-amplified; 16S is not unique in this respect.
explanations.d: 16S rRNA is present in cultured and uncultured organisms alike — culturability is unrelated to whether a cell carries the gene.

questions.prompt: What did Woese and Fox's 1977 comparison of rRNA sequences reveal?

options.text: That all bacteria share an identical 16S sequence
That a group of methane-producing microbes formed a lineage as distinct from bacteria as bacteria are from eukaryotes
That mitochondria evolved from bacteria
That PCR could amplify DNA from single cells

explanations.a: The opposite is true — 16S sequences vary enough between organisms to reveal deep evolutionary splits, which is the paper's point.
explanations.b: Correct — this divergence is what led Woese and Fox to propose archaebacteria as a third form of life, later named Archaea.
explanations.c: The endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria is a related but separate line of evidence, not the finding of this paper.
explanations.d: PCR did not exist yet in 1977; Woese and Fox worked with oligonucleotide cataloging, not amplification.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the history of rRNA-based microbial classification.

items.text: Woese and Fox compare rRNA oligonucleotide catalogs and identify archaebacteria as distinct
Pace clones 16S genes directly from environmental DNA without culturing
Woese, Kandler, and Wheelis formalize the three-domain tree of life

questions.explanation: Woese and Fox's 1977 discovery came first; Pace's culture-independent cloning followed in the 1980s; the formal three-domain (Bacteria, Archaea, Eucarya) framework was published in 1990.

questions.prompt: Match each region type within the 16S rRNA gene to its role.

right.text: Anchor universal PCR primers across nearly all bacteria and archaea
Carry sequence differences used to distinguish taxa

questions.explanation: Conserved stretches are nearly identical across organisms, so primers binding there amplify broadly; the variable regions between them accumulate the taxonomic signal used to tell species and genera apart.

lessons.label: From Sample to Sequence: The Amplicon Workflow

sections.heading: Extraction: the bias hides in the lysis step
sections.body: The pipeline starts with breaking cells open to release DNA, and this step already distorts the community. Gram-positive bacteria and fungal spores have thick, tough walls that resist gentle lysis, while fragile Gram-negative cells pop easily; a kit tuned for speed can systematically under-recover the hardy taxa and over-represent the fragile ones. Bead-beating (physical shearing with silica or zirconia beads) recovers tough-walled cells better than chemical lysis alone but can shear DNA if overdone. Whichever method is chosen, it must be applied identically across every sample in a study, because extraction bias that differs between samples looks exactly like a real biological difference once the data are analyzed.

sections.heading: Choosing a window and reading it in bulk
sections.body: Because Illumina short-read sequencing tops out around 250-300 bases per read, the field cannot sequence the whole 1,500 bp 16S gene at once; it sequences one or two hypervariable regions instead. The Earth Microbiome Project standardized on the V4 region, amplified with the 515F/806R primer pair, because V4 balances taxonomic resolution against primer universality and lets studies from different labs be directly compared. PCR then amplifies that ~250-300 bp window using a thermal cycler, and a unique DNA barcode (index sequence) is attached to each sample's primers during amplification. Before pooling, each sample's PCR product is quantified — commonly via fluorometric methods like Qubit or PicoGreen, or by qPCR-based library quantification — and normalized so every sample contributes roughly equal molar amounts to the pool; skipping this step lets a sample with high PCR yield swamp the sequencing run at the expense of samples that amplified poorly, adding a further layer of coverage-depth bias with nothing biological behind it, and one that shows up as some samples ending with only a few hundred reads while others get hundreds of thousands from the same run. Only after normalization are the samples pooled and sequenced together in one Illumina run — a strategy called multiplexing — then computationally sorted back into per-sample files afterward by matching each read's barcode. Every step compounds the last: primers that bind V4 slightly unevenly across taxa (primer bias), templates with more starting copies out-amplifying rare ones during PCR's exponential phase, and sequencing depth that varies sample to sample all shape the final relative-abundance numbers before a single read has been classified.

lessons.workedExample: A lab compares gut microbiomes between two mouse cages using the standard pipeline: bead-beat extraction, V4 amplification with 515F/806R, barcoded PCR, and pooled Illumina sequencing. Cage A's samples were extracted on Monday with a fresh reagent lot; Cage B's were extracted the following week with a new lot showing weaker lysis efficiency. When Firmicutes (many Gram-positive, tough-walled) appear lower in Cage B, the honest first hypothesis is not 'a biological difference between cages' but 'a batch effect from extraction efficiency' — which is why careful studies randomize sample processing order across extraction batches rather than processing all of one group together.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the amplicon workflow because it is the single most common source of unacknowledged bias in student microbiome projects. A weak answer describes the steps as a checklist. A strong answer identifies where bias enters — lysis efficiency varying by cell wall type, primer binding varying by taxon, and PCR's exponential amplification favoring high-copy templates — and explains what was done to keep that bias constant across compared groups, such as processing samples from all conditions in the same extraction batch.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the amplicon workflow from raw sample to sequencer-ready pool.

items.text: Cell lysis / DNA extraction
PCR amplification of the target hypervariable region with barcoded primers
Pooling barcoded samples together
Illumina paired-end sequencing

questions.explanation: DNA must be extracted before it can be amplified; barcodes are attached during PCR so samples can be pooled for one sequencing run; sequencing happens last, after pooling.

questions.prompt: Why did the Earth Microbiome Project standardize on the V4 region with the 515F/806R primer pair rather than sequencing the full 16S gene?

options.text: Illumina short-read sequencing cannot read the full ~1,500 bp gene in one pass, and V4 balances resolution with primer universality
The V4 region is the only part of the gene that varies between species
515F/806R amplifies eukaryotic DNA more efficiently than bacterial DNA
Full-length 16S sequencing was scientifically impossible before 2020

explanations.a: Correct — short-read platforms cap out around 250-300 bases, well short of full-length 16S, so a single well-characterized hypervariable window is sequenced instead, and V4 became the comparable standard.
explanations.b: All nine hypervariable regions (V1-V9) vary between species to different degrees; V4 was chosen for its balance of properties, not because it is uniquely variable.
explanations.c: 515F/806R primers target the bacterial and archaeal 16S gene, not eukaryotic sequences.
explanations.d: Long-read technologies capable of full-length 16S existed earlier than 2020, but Illumina's cost and throughput advantages kept short-read amplicon sequencing the standard for large surveys.

questions.prompt: A study extracts all 'treatment' samples on Monday and all 'control' samples the following week with a new reagent lot. Why is this a design flaw?

options.text: It is not a flaw, since PCR corrects for any extraction differences
Batch effects from extraction efficiency become confounded with the treatment/control comparison, since they line up perfectly with group identity
Illumina sequencing cannot process samples extracted on different days
Barcoding removes the need to control extraction timing

explanations.a: PCR amplifies whatever DNA extraction happened to recover; it does not correct for differential lysis efficiency between batches.
explanations.b: Correct — because extraction batch and biological group are perfectly aligned, any difference in lysis efficiency between the Monday and following-week reagent lots is indistinguishable from a true biological effect.
explanations.c: Sequencing itself is agnostic to extraction date; the problem is upstream, in extraction bias correlating with group assignment.
explanations.d: Barcoding only tracks which sample a read came from after pooling — it has no bearing on lysis efficiency during extraction.

questions.prompt: Match each pipeline step to the type of bias it can introduce.

right.text: Under-recovery of tough-walled taxa (e.g., some Gram-positives) relative to fragile ones
Uneven amplification efficiency across taxa whose target sequence differs slightly from the primer
Templates starting with more copies out-competing rarer templates during exponential amplification

questions.explanation: Each step of the workflow distorts community composition in a distinct way: lysis by cell wall toughness, primers by sequence mismatch, and PCR by exponential competition between templates.

lessons.label: OTUs, ASVs, and Denoising

sections.heading: The old fix: cluster away the noise
sections.body: Illumina sequencing makes errors at a low but nonzero rate, and PCR can stitch together fragments from two different templates into a chimeric read that matches no real organism. Chimeras are typically caught with a two-parent reference check — the approach used by tools like UCHIME and DADA2's built-in chimera-removal step — which flags any read whose first half aligns cleanly to one abundant sequence and whose second half aligns cleanly to a different abundant sequence, a split-parentage pattern a genuine single-template amplicon essentially never produces. For decades the standard fix was to cluster reads into Operational Taxonomic Units, or OTUs, by lumping together any sequences at least 97% similar and treating each cluster as a stand-in for a 'species.' The 97% threshold was a deliberate compromise: loose enough to absorb sequencing errors and natural strain-level noise into one bin, but tight enough to roughly track species-level divergence in 16S. The cost was resolution — two organisms that differ by two bases in the 250 bp V4 window, a real and potentially ecologically meaningful difference, get merged into the same OTU, and clustering results shift depending on which algorithm and reference set are used, making OTUs hard to compare exactly across studies.

sections.heading: Denoising and the rise of ASVs
sections.body: Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs) replaced clustering with statistical error modeling. DADA2, introduced by Benjamin Callahan and colleagues in a 2016 Nature Methods paper, builds a per-run model of Illumina's error rates from the quality scores in the data itself, then asks for each unique sequence whether it is more likely to be a true biological variant or a sequencing error of a more abundant neighbor. Deblur, published around the same time, uses a related but distinct error-profile approach. Both output exact sequences down to the single nucleotide, so a one-base-pair difference is preserved as two distinct ASVs rather than erased by clustering, and — crucially — an ASV called 'ASV_x' by one study is directly comparable to the same exact sequence reported by an entirely different lab, something 97%-similarity OTUs could never guarantee. This portability, combined with finer taxonomic resolution and a principled statistical basis for separating signal from error, is why ASVs became the field's default resolution level after roughly 2016-2017, and why they are increasingly treated as the closest amplicon-based approximation to a strain-level unit.

lessons.workedExample: A dataset contains 10,000 raw V4 reads. Two singleton reads differ from a 500-copy sequence by exactly one base at a low-quality position near the read's end. Under DADA2's error model, that base position has a high modeled error rate, and a one-base difference from an abundant sequence at a low-quality position is far more consistent with a sequencing error than with a real rare organism — so DADA2 corrects (denoises) those two reads into the abundant sequence rather than reporting them as a new ASV. Contrast this with the old OTU approach, which would have clustered the same two reads into the 97%-similarity bin regardless of quality scores, discarding information about exactly why the reads differed.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe OTU-vs-ASV understanding because it tests whether a student can explain what their bioinformatics pipeline actually did rather than treating it as a black box. A weak answer says 'we used DADA2 because it's more accurate.' A strong answer explains the mechanism: DADA2 models per-run sequencing error from quality scores to separate true variants from errors, preserves single-base resolution, and — unlike 97%-OTU clustering — produces exact sequences that are directly comparable across independent studies without re-clustering.

questions.prompt: What made the traditional 97% similarity threshold for OTU clustering a deliberate compromise?

options.text: It was loose enough to absorb sequencing noise but tight enough to roughly track species-level divergence
97% was the exact similarity of all bacterial 16S genes to each other
It matched the error rate of Sanger sequencing exactly
It was required by the Illumina platform's software

explanations.a: Correct — the threshold traded resolution for noise tolerance, absorbing sequencing errors and minor strain variation while still roughly separating species.
explanations.b: 16S similarity between different bacterial species varies widely; 97% was a chosen threshold, not a universal property of the gene.
explanations.c: The 97% convention predates and is unrelated to any specific sequencing platform's error characteristics.
explanations.d: Clustering threshold is a choice made by the researcher's pipeline, not a platform requirement.

questions.prompt: How does DADA2 decide whether a rare sequence variant represents a true biological signal or a sequencing error?

options.text: It discards any sequence present in fewer than 100 reads
It clusters all reads within 3% similarity into one unit regardless of quality
It builds a per-run error model from quality scores and evaluates whether a rare sequence is more consistent with error from an abundant neighbor or a real variant
It relies entirely on comparison to a reference taxonomy database

explanations.a: DADA2 does not use a fixed abundance cutoff; a rare-but-error-inconsistent sequence can be retained as a real ASV.
explanations.b: That describes OTU clustering, the approach DADA2 replaced — DADA2 does not cluster by fixed percent similarity.
explanations.c: Correct — this per-run, quality-score-based error model is what lets DADA2 distinguish true rare variants from sequencing artifacts of abundant sequences.
explanations.d: Denoising happens before and independently of taxonomy assignment; DADA2 does not need a reference database to call ASVs.

questions.prompt: Why can an ASV reported by one lab be directly compared to the same ASV reported by an unrelated lab, while OTUs generally cannot?

options.text: ASVs are exact sequences, so an identical ASV in two studies is literally the same sequence; OTUs are cluster identities that depend on that study's own clustering run
ASVs are always shorter than OTUs
OTUs use a different gene than ASVs
ASV pipelines require a shared central database that all labs must use

explanations.a: Correct — because ASVs are exact nucleotide sequences rather than study-specific clusters, an identical ASV sequence means the same thing across any two independent analyses.
explanations.b: ASV and OTU sequence lengths are determined by the sequenced region (e.g., V4), not by the method used to define units.
explanations.c: Both approaches typically work from the same 16S amplicon data; the difference is in how reads are grouped into units, not what gene is targeted.
explanations.d: ASV comparability comes from using exact sequences, not from a mandated shared database.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the shift from OTU clustering to ASV denoising.

items.text: 97%-similarity OTU clustering becomes the field standard for handling sequencing noise
Callahan and colleagues publish DADA2 in Nature Methods
ASVs become the field's default resolution level for amplicon studies

questions.explanation: OTU clustering was the original standard approach; DADA2's 2016 publication introduced statistical denoising as an alternative; ASVs then became the default in the years that followed as the field adopted denoising methods.

lessons.label: Counting Copies: qPCR and Absolute Abundance

sections.heading: 16S sequencing tells you shares, not totals
sections.body: A standard 16S amplicon dataset reports relative abundance: what fraction of the sequenced reads belonged to each taxon, out of whatever total the sequencer happened to produce for that sample. This is compositional data, and compositional data has a mathematical trap — the fractions in a sample must sum to a fixed total (100%), so if one taxon truly blooms in absolute terms, every other taxon's reported share falls even if its real population did not change at all. A community that genuinely stayed flat except for a Proteobacteria bloom will show every other phylum apparently 'declining' in the 16S data, a purely arithmetic artifact with no biological cause. Sequencing depth also varies unpredictably sample to sample, so raw read counts cannot be compared as if they were counts of organisms.

sections.heading: Getting back to real numbers
sections.body: Quantitative PCR (qPCR) and droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) solve a different problem: they measure the absolute number of gene copies in a sample, typically reported per gram of soil or per milliliter of fluid. qPCR tracks fluorescence that rises each amplification cycle in proportion to DNA present, comparing the sample's rise against a standard curve built from serial dilutions of a template with known copy number: plotting each dilution's cycle threshold (Ct) against the log of its copy number gives a regression line whose slope determines the assay's amplification efficiency, ideally close to 100% (template roughly doubling each cycle); ddPCR partitions the sample into thousands of tiny droplets and counts the fraction that show amplification, avoiding the need for a standard curve entirely. Multiplying a taxon's 16S relative abundance by the sample's total 16S qPCR copy number converts a compositional fraction back into an estimate of absolute cells or gene copies. But that conversion runs into the 16S copy-number problem: bacterial genomes carry anywhere from 1 to 15 or more copies of the rRNA operon (the rrnDB database catalogs these counts genome by genome), so a taxon with many operons looks more abundant in raw 16S read counts than its true cell count would justify, independent of its real population size. Two other routes sidestep this distortion: spike-in controls, where a known quantity of a foreign DNA standard is added to each sample before extraction so the recovery efficiency and total yield can be back-calculated, and flow cytometry, which counts intact cells or stained particles directly and needs no genomic assumptions at all.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher tracks a gut community before and after antibiotic treatment using only 16S relative abundance and finds that Bacteroidetes' share falls from 60% to 20% while Proteobacteria's share rises from 10% to 55%. Read alone, this looks like Bacteroidetes was wiped out and Proteobacteria bloomed. But running qPCR for total 16S copies per gram of stool on the same samples shows total bacterial load collapsed roughly sixfold after treatment — meaning Bacteroidetes' absolute abundance actually collapsed even more sharply than antibiotic sensitivity alone would suggest, while Proteobacteria, largely resistant, held roughly steady in absolute terms and simply came to dominate a much smaller total pool. The relative-abundance data alone could not distinguish 'Bacteroidetes collapsed while Proteobacteria held steady' from 'Proteobacteria truly bloomed' — only the qPCR-derived absolute numbers could.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe relative-versus-absolute abundance because compositional artifacts are the most common statistical error in student microbiome presentations — claiming a taxon 'increased' when only its share of a shrinking or growing total changed. A weak answer treats 16S percentages as population counts. A strong answer names the compositional constraint directly, explains that qPCR or ddPCR (or spike-ins, or flow cytometry) is needed to recover absolute numbers, and can state the 16S copy-number caveat — that genomes with more rRNA operons will look more abundant in read counts than their true cell numbers warrant.

questions.prompt: Why can a 16S sequencing dataset show one taxon 'declining' even when its absolute population size did not change?

options.text: Because 16S data is compositional — the reported fractions must sum to a fixed total, so a real increase in one taxon mathematically shrinks every other taxon's reported share
Because Illumina sequencers systematically undercount rare taxa
Because PCR only amplifies the most abundant taxon in a sample
Because 16S primers cannot bind to declining taxa

explanations.a: Correct — because relative abundances are constrained to sum to 100%, any taxon's true absolute increase forces every other taxon's reported share down, regardless of whether their real populations changed.
explanations.b: This describes a separate potential bias (detection limits for rare taxa), not the compositional artifact described in the lesson.
explanations.c: PCR amplifies all template sequences that its primers bind, not just the most abundant one.
explanations.d: Primer binding does not depend on whether a taxon's population is rising or falling.

questions.prompt: What does the 16S rRNA operon copy-number problem cause, according to the rrnDB catalog of genome copy numbers (ranging roughly 1 to 15+ per genome)?

options.text: Organisms with more rRNA operon copies appear more abundant in 16S read counts than their true cell counts justify
Organisms with more rRNA operon copies cannot be amplified by PCR at all
qPCR cannot detect any organism with more than one rRNA operon
Copy number variation only affects archaea, not bacteria

explanations.a: Correct — since each genome copy of the rRNA operon produces its own amplicon, a taxon with 10 operons per genome contributes roughly 10x more reads per cell than a taxon with 1 operon, inflating its apparent abundance.
explanations.b: Copy number does not block amplification; every operon copy is amplified along with the rest.
explanations.c: qPCR measures total gene copies regardless of how many are present per genome; it does not fail on multi-copy organisms, though the same copy-number caveat applies to interpreting its results.
explanations.d: Copy number variation occurs across both bacteria and archaea; it is not domain-specific.

questions.prompt: Match each method to what it measures or provides.

right.text: Relative abundance (fraction of reads per taxon)
Absolute gene copy number per gram or mL
A known-quantity standard added before extraction, letting absolute abundance be back-calculated
Direct cell or particle counts with no genomic assumptions

questions.explanation: Amplicon sequencing gives compositional fractions; qPCR/ddPCR give absolute gene copy numbers; spike-ins let absolute abundance be recovered from relative data; flow cytometry counts cells directly without relying on any DNA-based assumption.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to convert a taxon's 16S relative abundance into an estimate of absolute abundance using qPCR.

items.text: Run 16S amplicon sequencing to get each taxon's relative abundance (fraction of reads)
Run qPCR on the same sample to measure total 16S gene copies per gram or mL
Multiply the taxon's relative abundance by the sample's total qPCR copy number

questions.explanation: Relative abundance alone cannot give absolute numbers; it must be paired with a total-copy-number measurement from qPCR, and the two are combined by multiplication to estimate a taxon's absolute abundance.

lessons.label: Shotgun Metagenomics: Who's There and What They Can Do

sections.heading: Sequencing everything instead of one gene
sections.body: Amplicon sequencing PCR-amplifies a single marker gene, which means it can only answer 'who is present' among organisms carrying that gene — it says nothing about what genes those organisms actually carry. Shotgun metagenomics skips the marker gene entirely and randomly fragments and sequences all the DNA in a sample: bacterial, archaeal, viral, fungal, and functional genes for metabolism, virulence, or antibiotic resistance all get captured together. This is also why shotgun sidesteps primer bias altogether — there is no taxon-specific primer to bind unevenly, since library amplification (when used) relies on universal adapter sequences rather than a gene-specific primer pair, so the taxon-selective bias that comes from primers mismatching some 16S variants more than others has no analog here (library preparation still introduces its own biases, but not that kind). The tradeoff is depth and cost: amplicon surveys commonly target on the order of tens of thousands of reads per sample, while shotgun work aiming to detect low-abundance genes or resolve strain-level differences commonly needs tens of millions of reads per sample — an order-of-magnitude-or-more jump in sequencing that drives shotgun's higher per-sample cost, often several times that of amplicon work.

sections.heading: From short fragments to genomes and functions
sections.body: Raw shotgun reads can be analyzed two ways. Read-based profiling compares short reads directly against reference gene and genome databases to estimate taxonomic composition and which functional pathways are present, without ever reconstructing a full genome — fast, but limited by how complete the reference databases are. The more ambitious route is assembly: overlapping reads are computationally stitched into longer contiguous sequences (contigs), and contigs are then sorted, or binned, by shared features like tetranucleotide frequency, GC content, and coverage depth across samples into groups that approximate individual organisms' genomes — metagenome-assembled genomes, or MAGs. A MAG is a genome reconstructed without ever culturing the organism it came from, and this approach has been central to describing thousands of bacterial and archaeal lineages known only from sequence, never grown in a lab. Because shotgun data reveals actual functional gene content, it can directly answer questions amplicon data cannot even in principle: whether a community carries genes for a specific metabolic pathway, an antibiotic resistance mechanism, or a virulence factor — questions where knowing only a 16S-based taxonomic label leaves the answer to guesswork, since closely related strains can differ sharply in gene content.

lessons.workedExample: A team wants to know whether a wastewater community carries genes conferring resistance to a specific antibiotic. Amplicon sequencing could tell them which bacterial genera are present, but resistance genes are often carried on mobile plasmids that jump between unrelated species, so taxonomy alone cannot confirm resistance-gene presence. They instead run shotgun metagenomics, assemble the reads into contigs, and search the assembly directly for resistance-gene sequences — finding a beta-lactamase gene on a contig binned into a MAG most closely related to a Pseudomonas species. This functional answer, tying a specific gene to a specific reconstructed genome, was unavailable from 16S data alone, which would only have told them 'Pseudomonas-like reads are present,' not what genes that population carries.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe amplicon-versus-shotgun choice because it reveals whether a student picked their method for the right reason or just because it was familiar. A weak answer says 'we used 16S because it's standard.' A strong answer states the actual tradeoff: amplicon is cheaper and sufficient when the question is compositional ('who is here, roughly'), while shotgun is justified specifically when the question needs functional gene content or strain-level resolution that a single marker gene cannot provide — and can name the added cost and depth shotgun requires.

questions.prompt: What is the key limitation of amplicon (16S) sequencing that shotgun metagenomics addresses?

options.text: Amplicon sequencing only reveals taxonomic composition from one marker gene, not the functional genes an organism actually carries
Amplicon sequencing cannot detect bacteria at all
Amplicon sequencing requires a culture step that shotgun does not
Amplicon sequencing is more expensive than shotgun metagenomics

explanations.a: Correct — because amplicon sequencing only ever reads one marker gene, it cannot say anything about the rest of an organism's genome, including functional or resistance genes.
explanations.b: Amplicon sequencing is specifically designed to detect and identify bacteria and archaea via 16S; this is its core strength.
explanations.c: Both approaches are culture-independent — neither requires growing organisms in a lab.
explanations.d: Shotgun metagenomics is generally the more expensive approach, since it needs far greater sequencing depth per sample.

questions.prompt: What is a metagenome-assembled genome (MAG)?

options.text: A genome reconstructed by assembling and binning shotgun reads, without ever culturing the source organism
A 16S amplicon sequence used to represent an entire genome
A genome sequenced from a single isolated colony grown in pure culture
A reference database of known bacterial genomes

explanations.a: Correct — MAGs are built by assembling overlapping shotgun reads into contigs and binning those contigs by shared features into genome-like groups, all without culturing the organism.
explanations.b: A single 16S amplicon sequence carries far too little information to represent a whole genome; MAGs come from whole-genome shotgun data.
explanations.c: A genome from pure culture is a conventional isolate genome, not a MAG — MAGs are defined by being reconstructed without culturing.
explanations.d: Reference databases like SILVA or GTDB are collections of genomes; a MAG is one reconstructed genome, not a database.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the assembly-based shotgun metagenomics workflow.

items.text: Randomly fragment and sequence all DNA in the sample
Computationally assemble overlapping reads into longer contigs
Bin contigs by shared features (e.g., tetranucleotide frequency, coverage) into MAGs

questions.explanation: Shotgun sequencing first generates fragmented reads from all DNA; assembly stitches overlapping reads into contigs; binning then groups those contigs into genome-approximating MAGs.

questions.prompt: Match each research question to the method better suited to answer it.

left.text: Roughly which bacterial genera are present in a sample, at low cost across many samples
Whether a community carries a specific antibiotic-resistance gene, regardless of which taxon carries it

right.text: Amplicon (16S) sequencing
Shotgun metagenomics

questions.explanation: Amplicon sequencing is cheap and sufficient for broad compositional questions; functional questions about specific genes, especially ones that move between taxa on plasmids, need shotgun data that captures actual gene content.

lessons.label: Beyond DNA: Activity, RNA, and Relic DNA

sections.heading: DNA shows who could act; it doesn't show who is acting
sections.body: DNA is stable and persists in cells whether they are actively dividing, dormant, or dead — a genome sitting in a spore or a recently killed cell reads identically to one in a thriving cell to a 16S or shotgun assay. This creates a present-versus-active gap: an organism detected in DNA-based sequencing might be a dominant, metabolically active player in the community, or it might be inert, dormant, or simply not yet decayed away. Messenger RNA is a better proxy for activity because cells only transcribe genes they are actively using, and mRNA degrades quickly once transcription stops, so metatranscriptomics — sequencing the community's total RNA rather than DNA — captures which genes are being expressed right now rather than which genes merely exist somewhere in the community's collective genome. Comparing a metagenome (DNA, potential) against a matched metatranscriptome (RNA, expression) from the same sample can reveal that an organism present at high DNA abundance contributes almost no transcripts, while a rarer organism drives a disproportionate share of active gene expression.

sections.heading: Dead cells leave a genetic trace, and isotopes can tag the living
sections.body: The gap between presence and activity has an even blunter cause: extracellular relic DNA, genetic material released by dead and lysed cells that persists in the environment, especially bound to soil particles that protect it from degradation. Paul Carini and colleagues, in a 2016 Nature Microbiology paper, treated soil samples with propidium monoazide (PMA), a dye that penetrates only cells with compromised membranes and blocks their DNA from being amplified, then compared PMA-treated to untreated 16S sequencing. Relic DNA accounted for roughly 40% of the prokaryotic DNA pool in the soils tested, and removing it substantially changed diversity estimates and community composition — meaning a meaningful share of any standard soil 16S survey may be sequencing organisms that are no longer alive. Two further methods tag metabolic activity directly rather than inferring it from RNA or subtracting it from DNA: stable-isotope probing (SIP) feeds a community an isotopically heavy-labeled substrate (such as ¹³C-glucose) and identifies which organisms' DNA or RNA becomes heavy-labeled, meaning they metabolized that specific substrate; BONCAT (bioorthogonal noncanonical amino acid tagging) feeds cells a modified amino acid that only actively translating (protein-synthesizing) cells will incorporate, then uses a click-chemistry tag to fluorescently label and sort those active cells for downstream sequencing.

lessons.workedExample: A soil ecologist sequences 16S DNA from a field plot and finds a fungal-resistant bacterial taxon at high relative abundance, and initially concludes it dominates the active community. Suspecting relic DNA inflation, they PMA-treat a parallel sample before extraction, following the Carini et al. approach: PMA binds the DNA of any cell with a compromised membrane and blocks it from PCR amplification, so only DNA from intact, likely-living cells gets sequenced afterward. The taxon's apparent abundance in the PMA-treated sample drops sharply, suggesting much of what the untreated sample detected was residual DNA from a past bloom that had since died off rather than a currently thriving population.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the DNA-versus-activity distinction because it is where 'we sequenced it, so it's there and doing something' claims fall apart under questioning. A weak answer treats detection in 16S or shotgun DNA as proof of an active, functioning population. A strong answer names the actual gap — DNA persists in dormant or dead cells, and Carini et al. (2016) found relic extracellular DNA made up roughly 40% of the DNA pool in the soils they tested — and can point to metatranscriptomics, SIP, or BONCAT as the tools that actually distinguish presence from activity.

questions.prompt: Why is detecting an organism's DNA in a sample not proof that the organism is metabolically active?

options.text: DNA is stable and persists in dormant, spore-form, or recently dead cells just as it does in active ones, so DNA presence alone cannot distinguish these states
DNA sequencing cannot detect dead cells at all
Active cells have less DNA than dormant cells
PCR only amplifies DNA from actively dividing cells

explanations.a: Correct — DNA's chemical stability means it reads the same whether a cell is thriving, dormant, or already dead, which is exactly the ambiguity that motivates activity-based methods.
explanations.b: DNA sequencing readily detects DNA from dead cells — that is precisely the relic DNA problem described in the lesson, not a detection failure.
explanations.c: DNA content is not systematically lower in dormant cells; the issue is that DNA does not encode information about the cell's current metabolic state.
explanations.d: PCR amplifies any DNA template present regardless of whether the source cell was dividing, dormant, or dead.

questions.prompt: According to Carini and colleagues' 2016 study, roughly what fraction of the prokaryotic DNA pool in the soils they tested was extracellular relic DNA?

options.text: About 40%
About 1%
About 95%
Essentially none — relic DNA degrades too fast to accumulate

explanations.a: Correct — roughly 40% of the prokaryotic DNA pool in the tested soils was found to be relic (extracellular, PMA-excluded) DNA, substantially altering diversity estimates once removed.
explanations.b: 1% would represent a negligible effect, which does not match the study's reported scale of impact on diversity estimates.
explanations.c: 95% is too high — the study found a substantial but not overwhelming majority-of-the-signal contribution from relic DNA.
explanations.d: Relic DNA can persist because it binds to soil particles that protect it from degradation, which is exactly why it accumulated enough to be detected at scale.

questions.prompt: Match each method to what it actually measures.

right.text: Genetic potential present in the community, regardless of whether cells are alive, dormant, or dead
Which genes are being actively transcribed right now
Which organisms metabolized a specific isotopically labeled substrate
Which cells are actively synthesizing new protein

questions.explanation: DNA-based sequencing captures genetic potential regardless of activity state; metatranscriptomics captures active gene expression; SIP tags organisms that metabolized a specific labeled substrate; BONCAT tags cells actively translating protein.

questions.prompt: In the Carini et al. method, what does propidium monoazide (PMA) treatment do before DNA extraction?

options.text: It penetrates cells with compromised membranes and blocks their DNA from being amplified, enriching the resulting signal for intact, likely-living cells
It amplifies all DNA in the sample equally, including relic DNA
It converts RNA into complementary DNA for sequencing
It attaches barcodes to each sample for multiplexed sequencing

explanations.a: Correct — PMA selectively enters compromised (dead or damaged) cells and blocks amplification of their DNA, so PMA-treated sequencing is enriched for DNA from cells with intact membranes.
explanations.b: PMA does the opposite — it suppresses amplification from compromised cells rather than treating all DNA equally.
explanations.c: Converting RNA to cDNA is a step in RNA-sequencing workflows (like metatranscriptomics), unrelated to PMA's membrane-based mechanism.
explanations.d: Barcoding is part of library preparation for multiplexed sequencing and is unrelated to PMA's role in distinguishing intact from compromised cells.

lessons.label: Bioinformatics and the Reference-Database Problem

sections.heading: Pipelines turn raw reads into a taxonomy table
sections.body: Raw sequencer output is just millions of short text strings; turning that into a table of 'which organism, how much' requires a bioinformatics pipeline. QIIME2 (built on top of DADA2 for denoising, described in a 2019 Nature Biotechnology paper by Evan Bolyen and colleagues) and mothur (introduced by Patrick Schloss and colleagues in 2009) are the two most widely used amplicon pipelines, handling quality filtering, denoising or OTU clustering, and taxonomy assignment inside one reproducible workflow. Taxonomy assignment itself works by comparing each ASV or OTU against a curated reference database using an automated classifier — commonly a naive Bayes classifier trained on the reference set (QIIME2's default) or a global-alignment best-hit method that reports the closest-matching reference sequence — commonly SILVA, the original Greengenes database (now succeeded by newer curated releases), or the more recently built Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB), which assigns taxonomy based on whole-genome phylogeny rather than 16S alone. No database is complete: environmental and understudied habitats routinely produce ASVs with no close match, which pipelines report as 'unclassified' or only assign to a coarse rank like phylum, silently leaving a chunk of the community formally unidentified even though it was successfully sequenced.

sections.heading: Contamination and parameter choices threaten reproducibility
sections.body: Low-biomass samples — skin, tumor tissue, ancient DNA, even samples with few true microbes — face a particular threat: laboratory reagents themselves are not sterile of DNA. Susan Salter and colleagues, in a 2014 BMC Biology paper, showed that DNA extraction kits and PCR reagents carry their own low-level bacterial contamination, dubbed the 'kitome,' which is negligible in a high-biomass gut sample swamped by real signal but can dominate the sequencing output of a low-biomass sample, producing 'community' profiles that are really profiles of what happened to be in that reagent lot. The fix is procedural: every extraction batch needs a no-template negative control carried through the entire pipeline, and any taxon appearing in the negative control gets flagged or subtracted from real samples. Reproducibility faces a second, quieter threat in ordinary parameter choices: two labs analyzing the identical raw reads can get different results depending on quality-filtering thresholds, denoising or clustering parameters, and which reference database version they used — none of which counts as an error, but all of which mean a single 'the microbiome analysis' summary hides real, defensible analytical choices that shift the final numbers.

lessons.workedExample: A student sequences skin swabs, a genuinely low-biomass sample type, and is excited to report a moderately abundant Ralstonia population. Before trusting it, they check their no-template negative control — a tube that went through DNA extraction and PCR alongside the real samples but received no swab material — and find Ralstonia present there too, at a similar relative abundance. Because Ralstonia is a known common reagent contaminant documented in the kitome literature following Salter et al. (2014), the student flags it as likely contamination rather than a genuine skin community member, and reports the finding as unresolved rather than presenting it as a real biological signal.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe database and contamination limitations because distinguishing 'we found nothing' from 'the database had nothing to match against' or 'that's contamination, not signal' is a mark of real methodological maturity. A weak answer treats every read that gets a taxonomy label as ground truth and ignores unclassified reads entirely. A strong answer names the reference database used, acknowledges that unclassified reads reflect database gaps rather than sequencing failure, and — especially for a low-biomass sample — describes running a no-template negative control to catch kitome contamination, citing the Salter et al. (2014) finding that reagents themselves carry detectable bacterial DNA.

questions.prompt: What does it mean when a pipeline reports a sequenced ASV as 'unclassified'?

options.text: The sequencing itself failed for that read
The ASV was successfully sequenced but had no close match in the reference database used for taxonomy assignment
The organism is definitely a laboratory contaminant
The read was a PCR chimera and should be discarded

explanations.a: Sequencing succeeded — the ASV exists as a real sequence; the failure is in matching it to a database entry, not in generating the read.
explanations.b: Correct — reference databases like SILVA, Greengenes, or GTDB are incomplete, especially for understudied habitats, so a real, successfully sequenced organism can still have no close database match.
explanations.c: Being unclassified says nothing about contamination status; a genuine, novel environmental organism is a common cause of unclassified reads.
explanations.d: Chimera detection and filtering happens as a separate step in denoising, distinct from taxonomy assignment against a reference database.

questions.prompt: According to Salter and colleagues' 2014 BMC Biology paper, what is the 'kitome'?

options.text: Bacterial DNA contamination present in DNA extraction kits and PCR reagents themselves, which can dominate results in low-biomass samples
A curated reference database of known bacterial genomes
The set of ASVs shared between two independent studies
A denoising algorithm used to correct sequencing errors

explanations.a: Correct — Salter et al. showed that extraction and PCR reagents carry their own trace bacterial DNA, negligible in high-biomass samples but potentially dominant in low-biomass ones.
explanations.b: Reference databases like SILVA or GTDB are unrelated to the kitome finding, which concerns reagent contamination, not taxonomy reference data.
explanations.c: Overlap between independent studies' ASVs is not what 'kitome' refers to; the term is specific to reagent-derived contaminant DNA.
explanations.d: The kitome is a contamination phenomenon, not a bioinformatics algorithm like DADA2 or Deblur.

questions.prompt: Why is a no-template negative control important when sequencing a low-biomass sample like a skin swab?

options.text: It carries reagents through the full pipeline with no real sample material, so any taxa it detects likely came from reagent contamination rather than the sample
It increases the sequencing depth available for the real samples
It replaces the need for a reference database
It is only useful for shotgun metagenomics, not amplicon sequencing

explanations.a: Correct — because it contains no real sample, any signal detected in the negative control must have come from the reagents or environment, flagging likely kitome contaminants in the real samples.
explanations.b: A negative control consumes sequencing capacity rather than adding usable depth to real samples; its purpose is contamination detection, not depth.
explanations.c: Negative controls address contamination, an entirely separate issue from taxonomy assignment against a reference database.
explanations.d: Kitome contamination and the need for negative controls apply to both amplicon and shotgun workflows, not just one.

questions.prompt: Match each tool or resource to its role in the amplicon bioinformatics workflow.

right.text: A reproducible pipeline (built on DADA2) covering filtering, denoising, and taxonomy assignment, described in Bolyen et al. 2019
An amplicon analysis pipeline introduced by Schloss and colleagues in 2009
A curated reference database used to assign taxonomy to ASVs or OTUs

questions.explanation: QIIME2 and mothur are both end-to-end amplicon analysis pipelines from different research groups; SILVA and GTDB are reference databases that pipelines query during the taxonomy-assignment step, not pipelines themselves.

lessons.label: Richness, Evenness, and What 'Diversity' Means

sections.heading: Richness: just a headcount
sections.body: Species richness is the simplest diversity measure: how many distinct taxa are present in a sample, full stop. In modern microbiome work the 'taxa' being counted are usually amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) resolved from 16S rRNA gene sequences at single-nucleotide precision by tools like DADA2 (Callahan et al., 2016), which replaced the older practice of clustering reads into operational taxonomic units (OTUs) at a fixed 97% similarity threshold. Richness answers one question only — how many kinds — and it treats a taxon represented by one read the same as a taxon representing 90% of the sample. That is exactly its blind spot.

sections.heading: Evenness: who's actually running the community
sections.body: Evenness describes how equally the relative abundances are distributed among the taxa a sample has. A community can be numerically rich and still be dominated by one or two organisms, with everything else present at trace levels. Pielou's evenness index, J = H'/ln(S) (Pielou, 1966), rescales the Shannon entropy H' by the maximum possible entropy for that many taxa (S), giving a value from 0 (total dominance) to 1 (perfectly even). Ecologically, evenness matters because a community running on one dominant taxon behaves very differently under stress than one where abundance is spread across many — dominance concentrates risk, the way a stock portfolio in one company concentrates risk regardless of how many tickers you technically own.

sections.heading: Why diversity needs both numbers at once
sections.body: 'Diversity' in the loose sense people use in conversation is really shorthand for a joint property of richness and evenness together, which is precisely why a single richness count can mislead: two communities can have identical richness and opposite biological stories. The next lesson's Shannon index, H' = -Σ p_i ln(p_i), makes the ceiling this imposes explicit: H' is mathematically bounded above by ln(S), reaching that maximum only when every one of the S taxa sits at equal abundance, and falling below it as soon as one taxon starts to dominate. So a richness count of S doesn't tell you how diverse a community actually is — it only tells you the most diverse that community could possibly be if it were perfectly even. A community with S = 20 but one taxon at 80% abundance might have H' sitting well under half of ln(20) ≈ 3.0, while a second S = 20 community that's close to even could have H' near that full 3.0 ceiling — same richness, roughly double the effective diversity. This is the entire reason diversity indices like Shannon's and Simpson's exist — they fold richness and evenness into one number that penalizes both a low taxon count and a lopsided abundance distribution, rather than reporting either alone, and the gap between a community's actual index value and the ln(S) ceiling its richness alone would allow is a direct, quantitative measure of how much evenness is costing it.

lessons.workedExample: Two gut microbiome samples each contain exactly 10 ASVs, so their richness is identical. Sample A is even: each of the 10 taxa sits at about 10% relative abundance. Sample B is dominated: one ASV (say an overgrown Escherichia) sits at 91%, and the other 9 taxa share the remaining 9% (1% each). A student who reports 'richness = 10 in both, so diversity is the same' has missed the story entirely — Sample B is functionally a near-monoculture with nine rare hangers-on, likely reflecting a disturbance like antibiotic exposure, while Sample A looks like a balanced, undisturbed community. Pielou's J makes the gap explicit: J is near 1.0 for Sample A and drops sharply toward 0 for Sample B, even though S = 10 for both.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'how diverse was your community?' is testing whether the student conflates richness with diversity — a common and revealing error. A weak answer reports only a taxon count ('we found 15 species'). A strong answer distinguishes richness from evenness, explains that a count alone can't tell you if the community is balanced or dominated by one organism, and names or computes an evenness or diversity index to back up the claim. Judges probe this because it's the fastest way to tell whether a student ran the numbers or just eyeballed a taxonomy table.

questions.prompt: Two soil samples both contain 12 distinct bacterial genera. Sample X has all 12 at roughly equal abundance; Sample Y has one genus at 85% abundance and the other 11 splitting the remaining 15%. What can you say about their richness and diversity?

options.text: Both richness and diversity are equal, since richness is the same.
Richness is equal, but Sample Y has lower evenness and would score lower on a diversity index than Sample X.
Sample Y has higher richness because one genus dominates.
Richness cannot be compared unless the samples are rarefied first.

explanations.a: Richness (the count of 12) is equal, but diversity indices weight abundance distribution too, so Y and X are not equally 'diverse.'
explanations.b: Correct — richness only counts taxa, so it ties at 12; evenness captures the abundance imbalance, and any index combining the two (Shannon, Simpson) will score Sample Y lower.
explanations.c: Richness is a taxon count, not a measure of dominance; both samples have richness 12.
explanations.d: Rarefaction addresses uneven sequencing depth between samples, not whether richness counts can be compared conceptually.

questions.prompt: What does Pielou's evenness index J = H'/ln(S) equal when a community is a near-total monoculture (one taxon dominates almost completely)?

options.text: J approaches 1
J approaches 0
J equals S
J becomes undefined

explanations.a: J near 1 describes a perfectly balanced community, the opposite of a monoculture.
explanations.b: Correct — H' (Shannon entropy) collapses toward 0 as one taxon dominates, so J = H'/ln(S) also approaches 0 regardless of how many rare taxa are technically present.
explanations.c: J is a ratio bounded between 0 and 1 by construction; it is never equal to the richness value S.
explanations.d: J is undefined only when S = 1 (ln(1) = 0), not in a dominated-but-multi-taxon community.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it actually measures.

right.text: How equally abundance is distributed across taxa
A single-nucleotide-resolution sequence unit from tools like DADA2
The count of distinct taxa present

questions.explanation: Richness is a headcount of taxa; evenness describes the balance of their relative abundances; an ASV is the modern, exact-sequence replacement for the older 97%-similarity OTU.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in reasoning about whether a community is truly diverse, from least to most informative.

items.text: Count the number of distinct taxa (richness)
Compute relative abundance of each taxon
Calculate an evenness or diversity index combining richness and abundance

questions.explanation: You start with a simple taxon count, then need relative abundances to see how balanced the community is, and only combining both into an index (like Shannon or Pielou's J) gives a defensible diversity claim.

lessons.label: Shannon and Simpson Indices

sections.heading: Shannon entropy: diversity as uncertainty
sections.body: The Shannon index, H' = -Σ p_i ln(p_i), was borrowed directly from Claude Shannon's 1948 paper on information theory, where it measured the uncertainty in a message source. Applied to a microbial community, p_i is the relative abundance of taxon i, and H' measures how uncertain you'd be about the identity of a randomly drawn individual. Because every taxon contributes -p_i ln(p_i) to the sum — and this quantity is nonzero even for small p_i — Shannon's index is comparatively sensitive to rare taxa: a long tail of low-abundance ASVs pulls H' upward even if one taxon still dominates numerically. The size of that pull is worth seeing in numbers, not just asserted: for a single rare ASV at p = 0.001, its Shannon contribution is -p·ln(p) = -0.001 × ln(0.001) ≈ -0.001 × (-6.908) ≈ 0.0069 — small, but not nothing, and it stacks additively with every other rare taxon in the tail. Its Simpson contribution, by contrast, is p² = 0.001² = 0.000001 — six orders of magnitude smaller and effectively invisible to the sum. That thousand-fold gap between 0.0069 and 0.000001 is exactly why a long tail of rare ASVs can move H' noticeably while leaving D almost untouched.

sections.heading: Simpson's index: diversity as dominance
sections.body: Simpson's index, D = Σ p_i², published by Simpson (1949) in a one-page Nature note, has a cleaner probabilistic meaning: it is the probability that two individuals drawn at random from the community, with replacement, belong to the same taxon. Because abundances are squared, D is driven almost entirely by whichever taxa are most common — rare taxa contribute almost nothing to the sum. Ecologists usually report either 1-D (the Gini-Simpson index, the probability the two individuals differ) or 1/D (inverse Simpson), both of which increase with diversity, unlike raw D which decreases.

sections.heading: Hill numbers: putting both on the same ruler
sections.body: The catch with both indices in their raw form is that they aren't directly comparable to richness or to each other — H' = 1.5 doesn't mean 'half as diverse' as H' = 3.0, because it's a logarithmic, not linear, scale. Jost's (2006) 'Entropy and Diversity' resolved this by reframing both as Hill numbers: qD = (Σ p_i^q)^(1/(1-q)), the 'effective number of equally abundant species' that would give the same index value. Setting q=0 recovers plain richness; taking the limit as q→1 recovers exp(H'); and q=2 recovers 1/D (inverse Simpson). Higher q weights common taxa more heavily, so plotting qD across q=0,1,2 for a sample shows at a glance how much of its apparent richness survives once dominance is taken into account.

lessons.workedExample: A gut sample has 4 ASVs with relative abundances 0.7, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1. Shannon: H' = -(0.7·ln0.7 + 3×0.1·ln0.1) = -(-0.2497 - 0.6908) = 0.940 nats; converting to an effective number of species gives exp(0.940) ≈ 2.56. Simpson: D = 0.7² + 3×0.1² = 0.49 + 0.03 = 0.52, so 1-D = 0.48 and inverse Simpson 1/D ≈ 1.92. Notice all three numbers — richness 4, Shannon-effective 2.56, Simpson-effective 1.92 — tell a consistent but progressively harsher story about the same community: raw richness ignores the dominant taxon entirely, Shannon discounts it partially, and Simpson (weighting by p²) discounts it the most, landing closest to the real answer of 'about 2 taxa are actually running this show.'
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why did you use Shannon instead of Simpson, or both?' is checking whether the student understands that these indices answer different questions, not that one is simply 'better.' A weak answer treats the two as interchangeable diversity scores. A strong answer says Simpson (or inverse Simpson) is the right call when the question is about dominance and evenness, Shannon when rare-taxon presence matters more, and — the marker of real fluency — converts to Hill numbers (effective species) before comparing across samples, since raw H' values aren't on a linear scale.

questions.prompt: A community has one very rare ASV (p = 0.001) added to it. Which index's value is more sensitive to this addition: Shannon's H' or Simpson's D?

options.text: Shannon's H', because it sums -p·ln(p), which stays non-negligible even for small p
Simpson's D, because it sums p², which stays non-negligible even for small p
Both are equally sensitive, since both are sums over all taxa
Neither changes, since a single rare taxon can't affect either index

explanations.a: Correct — -p·ln(p) shrinks slowly as p→0 (it actually peaks at p=1/e before falling), so rare taxa still contribute meaningfully to H'; Simpson's p² shrinks to nearly zero for small p, so rare taxa barely move D.
explanations.b: Simpson's D squares abundances, which crushes the contribution of rare taxa toward zero — the opposite of high sensitivity.
explanations.c: The two indices use different functions of p (p·ln p vs p²) that behave very differently as p shrinks, so their sensitivity to rare taxa is not equal.
explanations.d: Any change in richness or abundance shifts both indices at least slightly; the question is which shifts more, not whether either changes.

questions.prompt: For the 4-ASV community with abundances 0.7, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1 (Shannon H' ≈ 0.940, Simpson D ≈ 0.52), what is the correct effective number of species under the Shannon-based Hill number?

options.text: 0.940 itself, with no conversion needed
4, the raw richness

explanations.a: Correct — the q=1 Hill number is defined as exp(H'), converting the log-scale Shannon entropy into an effective number of equally-abundant species.
explanations.b: 1/D ≈ 1.92 is the Simpson-based (q=2) Hill number, not the Shannon-based one.
explanations.c: Raw H' is measured in nats (a log scale) and is not directly interpretable as a species count without exponentiating.
explanations.d: 4 is the plain richness (q=0 Hill number), which ignores how unevenly abundance is distributed.

questions.prompt: Match each Hill number order q to what it is equivalent to.

right.text: exp(Shannon's H')
Plain species richness
Inverse Simpson, 1/D

questions.explanation: Jost (2006) showed richness, exp(H'), and 1/D are all special cases of the same Hill-number family qD, differing only in how much weight q gives to common versus rare taxa.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to compare two samples' diversity on a fair, linear scale using Hill numbers.

items.text: Compute relative abundances p_i for each taxon in each sample
Compute the raw index (Shannon H' or Simpson D) for each sample
Convert each raw index to its effective number of species (exp(H') or 1/D)
Compare the effective-species numbers directly across samples

questions.explanation: You need abundances first, then the raw entropy/dominance index, then a Hill-number conversion to a linear effective-species scale before cross-sample comparisons are valid — comparing raw H' values directly is the classic mistake Jost's paper corrected.

lessons.label: Rarefaction and Sampling Depth

sections.heading: Rarefaction curves: diversity as a function of effort
sections.body: A rarefaction curve plots the number of distinct taxa observed against the number of reads (or individuals) sampled, built by repeatedly subsampling a dataset at increasing depths and averaging the taxon count found each time. Every curve rises steeply at first — the first few hundred reads turn up mostly new taxa — then bends over as sampling exhausts the common members of the community, and ideally flattens into a plateau once nearly all detectable taxa have been seen. A curve that is still climbing steeply at your sequencing depth is a warning sign: you haven't sampled deeply enough to characterize the community, and rare taxa almost certainly remain undetected.

sections.heading: Estimating the taxa you didn't see
sections.body: Because a plateau is rarely reached in practice, ecologists use nonparametric estimators to extrapolate 'true' richness from the shape of the abundance distribution. Chao's (1984) estimator, Chao1 = S_obs + f1²/(2f2), uses only the count of singletons (f1, taxa observed exactly once) and doubletons (f2, taxa observed exactly twice): a sample full of singletons is a sample that clearly hasn't exhausted the rare biosphere, so Chao1 inflates the estimate accordingly, while a sample with few singletons relative to doubletons is closer to complete. The related ACE estimator (abundance-based coverage estimator) generalizes this logic across the whole low-abundance tail rather than just the first two counts.

sections.heading: The depth confound, and the fight over how to fix it
sections.body: Sequencing depth is not the same across samples — one library might yield 5,000 reads and another 50,000 purely from run-to-run technical variation — and richness estimates scale with depth almost mechanically, since more reads simply give more chances to catch rare taxa. Left uncorrected, this makes deeper-sequenced samples look more diverse for reasons that have nothing to do with biology. The traditional fix is rarefying: randomly subsampling every sample down to the read count of the shallowest one before comparing. McMurdie and Holmes (2014), in a widely cited PLOS Computational Biology paper titled 'Waste Not, Want Not,' argued this practice is statistically inadmissible because it discards real data and introduces Monte Carlo noise from the random subsampling itself, and pushed instead for model-based normalization methods — though follow-up work, notably Weiss et al. (2017) in Microbiome, found rarefying still performs competitively for diversity estimation specifically, even if it's a poor choice for differential-abundance testing.

lessons.workedExample: A student sequences two soil samples: Sample A yields 5,000 reads and 120 ASVs; Sample B, run on a different flow cell lane, yields 50,000 reads and 300 ASVs. Reported naively, Sample B looks 2.5x more diverse. But when both are rarefied down to 5,000 reads, Sample B's subsampled ASV count drops to about 135 — barely above Sample A's 120. Almost the entire apparent gap was a sequencing-depth artifact, not a biological one. The student should report the rarefied comparison (or a Chao1 estimate paired with each sample's raw rarefaction curve) rather than the raw ASV counts, and should show both curves to demonstrate neither sample was undersampled to the point of an unreliable estimate.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'did you control for sequencing depth?' because uneven depth is the single most common way student microbiome projects fake a diversity difference. A weak answer reports raw ASV or OTU counts per sample with no mention of how many reads each sample got. A strong answer names the confound directly, describes rarefying to a common depth (or an estimator like Chao1) as the fix, and — for real credit — knows that rarefying trades away data and that McMurdie and Holmes's critique is why some studies prefer normalization methods instead, at least for testing which taxa differ in abundance.

questions.prompt: Sample A (5,000 reads) shows 120 ASVs; Sample B (50,000 reads) shows 300 ASVs. What is the most defensible immediate conclusion?

options.text: Sample B has 2.5x the biological diversity of Sample A
The comparison is confounded by sequencing depth and cannot be trusted until both are rarefied to equal depth or richness is estimated some other depth-independent way
Sample A must have failed quality control since it has fewer reads
ASV counts are always directly comparable regardless of read depth

explanations.a: Raw ASV counts scale with sequencing depth almost mechanically, so the 2.5x gap could be mostly or entirely a depth artifact rather than biology.
explanations.b: Correct — deeper sequencing finds more rare taxa by chance, so comparing raw richness across unequal depths conflates a technical variable with a biological one; equalizing depth (or using a depth-independent estimator) is required first.
explanations.c: A lower read count on its own doesn't indicate a failed sample; it's a normal outcome of sequencing run variability and needs to be handled statistically, not treated as a QC failure.
explanations.d: This is the exact misconception the lesson addresses — ASV counts are highly sensitive to depth and are not directly comparable without correction.

questions.prompt: In Chao1 = S_obs + f1²/(2f2), what does a sample with many singletons (f1) but very few doubletons (f2) suggest?

options.text: The sample has been sequenced to saturation and the estimate should barely exceed S_obs
The rare biosphere is likely undersampled, so Chao1 will estimate substantially more taxa than were actually observed
Singletons and doubletons are contaminants and should be removed before estimating richness
f1 and f2 do not affect the Chao1 estimate

explanations.a: A high proportion of singletons is a sign of undersampling, not saturation — saturation would show few or no singletons relative to more abundant taxa.
explanations.b: Correct — a small f2 in the denominator alongside a large f1 in the numerator inflates f1²/(2f2), which is exactly the intended behavior: many taxa seen only once and almost none seen twice signals many more rare taxa likely remain undetected.
explanations.c: Singletons and doubletons are the core data the estimator relies on; discarding them would make Chao1 impossible to compute, not more accurate.
explanations.d: f1 and f2 are literally the only two abundance-based inputs to the Chao1 formula beyond the observed richness S_obs.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its correct description.

right.text: A nonparametric richness estimator built from singleton and doubleton counts
Argued that subsampling to equal depth discards real data and is statistically inadmissible, especially for differential-abundance testing
A plot of taxa observed versus reads sampled, used to judge whether sequencing depth was sufficient

questions.explanation: Rarefaction curves visualize sampling completeness; Chao1 extrapolates unseen richness from rare-taxon counts; McMurdie and Holmes's 2014 paper challenged the standard practice of rarefying to equal depth.
