questions.prompt: Order the steps of a defensible richness comparison across samples with unequal sequencing depth.

items.text: Generate a rarefaction curve for each sample to check whether depth was sufficient
Identify that raw read depth differs substantially across samples
Rarefy to a common depth or apply a depth-independent estimator like Chao1
Compare richness/diversity values across samples using the corrected numbers

questions.explanation: You first notice the depth mismatch, check each sample's rarefaction curve to see how reliable its raw count is, correct for depth (rarefying or an estimator), and only then compare across samples.

lessons.label: Alpha vs Beta Diversity

sections.heading: Alpha diversity: what's happening inside one sample
sections.body: Alpha diversity is diversity measured within a single sample — everything from the previous lessons (richness, Shannon's H', Simpson's D, Chao1) is an alpha diversity metric. It answers 'how diverse is this one gut, this one soil core, this one swab?' and produces one number per sample, which you can then compare across groups with an ordinary statistical test like a t-test, Wilcoxon rank-sum, or ANOVA on the index values. That last step is worth pausing on, because it's the reason alpha diversity plugs so easily into standard statistics: reducing an entire sample's community to one index value produces a single independent observation per subject, exactly the data shape a t-test or ANOVA expects — one row per mouse, one column for the outcome. Beta diversity can't be tested the same way precisely because it doesn't produce that shape: its natural output is a pairwise distance between every two samples, so the observations aren't independent (each sample's distance to every other sample shares that sample in common), which is exactly why beta diversity needs its own distance-based machinery like PERMANOVA rather than a t-test on the distances themselves. Keeping that distinction straight early avoids a common analysis mistake — running an ordinary group-comparison test directly on a distance matrix — before beta diversity's own statistics are introduced later in this unit.

sections.heading: Beta diversity: how different are samples from each other
sections.body: Beta diversity is a different question entirely: not how diverse is any one sample, but how much does composition turn over between samples. Whittaker (1960, 1972) originally defined the three-way partition that gives this lesson its vocabulary — alpha (within-sample), beta (between-sample turnover), and gamma (total diversity across the whole region or study, pooling all samples together) — with the multiplicative relationship gamma = alpha x beta, or the additive version gamma = alpha + beta favored by later work such as Lande (1996). Beta diversity isn't a single index the way Shannon's is; it's built by computing a distance or dissimilarity between every pair of samples (Bray-Curtis, Jaccard, UniFrac — the subject of the next lesson) and then asking whether those distances differ systematically between groups.

sections.heading: Why a treatment can move beta without touching alpha
sections.body: Because alpha and beta measure different things, a manipulation can shift one while leaving the other flat — and missing this is a common source of a false negative in student projects. The clearest real example is Dethlefsen and Relman's (2011) PNAS study of ciprofloxacin's effect on the human gut microbiota: alpha diversity dropped during treatment but largely recovered afterward, yet each person's community took a distinct, individualized trajectory away from its pre-treatment state, so beta diversity — both between people and within a person over time — increased and stayed elevated even after alpha diversity looked normal again. A study measuring only alpha diversity after such a perturbation would conclude 'no lasting effect,' missing that the community had reorganized into a new, less predictable configuration. This is exactly why alpha and beta diversity require different statistical machinery: alpha is a single number per sample tested with standard group comparisons, while beta lives on a distance matrix and needs distance-based tests like PERMANOVA, covered in a later lesson.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher gives one group of mice a broad-spectrum antibiotic and compares their gut microbiota to untreated controls two weeks later. Alpha diversity (Shannon's H') in the treated group has returned to control-group levels — no significant difference, t-test p = 0.41. Concluding 'no effect' here would be premature: computing Bray-Curtis distances between all pairs of treated mice versus all pairs of control mice shows treated mice are far more dissimilar from each other than controls are from each other, i.e., beta diversity within the treated group has increased even though each individual mouse's alpha diversity looks normal. The antibiotic didn't reduce how diverse any one mouse's gut was in the end — it made the recovery path idiosyncratic, so each mouse landed in a different final community.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'did alpha diversity actually answer your research question?' because many students report only an alpha diversity comparison when their hypothesis is really about how a treatment reorganizes community composition — a beta diversity question. A weak answer treats 'no significant alpha diversity difference' as proof of no effect. A strong answer recognizes these are separate axes, reports both, and — ideally — cites something like the individualized post-antibiotic recovery seen by Dethlefsen and Relman (2011) as the reason a treatment can leave alpha diversity unchanged while beta diversity tells the real story.

questions.prompt: A study finds no significant difference in Shannon diversity between treated and control groups, but Bray-Curtis distances show treated samples are far more dissimilar from each other than controls are. What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: The treatment had no effect on the microbial community at all
The treatment altered beta diversity (community composition/turnover) without necessarily changing alpha diversity, and both should be reported
The Bray-Curtis result must be a statistical artifact since alpha diversity showed nothing
Alpha and beta diversity always move together, so this result is impossible

explanations.a: This ignores the beta diversity result entirely, which shows a real compositional effect the alpha diversity comparison missed.
explanations.b: Correct — alpha and beta diversity are separate axes; a treatment can leave within-sample diversity unchanged while still driving samples toward more individualized, divergent compositions, exactly as seen in Dethlefsen and Relman's (2011) antibiotic study.
explanations.c: There's no reason to distrust the beta diversity finding just because it disagrees with alpha diversity; they are legitimately independent measurements.
explanations.d: Alpha and beta diversity are conceptually and mathematically independent quantities; one can shift without the other, which is the entire point of measuring both.

questions.prompt: Under Whittaker's multiplicative partitioning, gamma = alpha x beta. If two habitats each have an average alpha diversity of 5 species, and the regional (gamma) diversity across both is 15 species, what is beta diversity?

explanations.a: Correct — solving gamma = alpha x beta for beta gives 15 / 5 = 3, meaning the two habitats' communities are, on this measure, about three times as different from each other as either is diverse internally.
explanations.b: 10 would come from gamma - alpha (the additive partition), not the multiplicative one specified in the question.
explanations.c: 20 is gamma + alpha, which isn't part of either Whittaker partitioning scheme.
explanations.d: 0.33 inverts the correct ratio (alpha/gamma instead of gamma/alpha).

questions.prompt: Match each diversity level to what it measures.

right.text: Diversity within a single sample
Turnover in composition between samples
Total diversity pooled across all samples in a study or region

questions.explanation: Whittaker's partition separates within-sample diversity (alpha), between-sample turnover (beta), and the total regional pool (gamma), which combine as gamma = alpha x beta (multiplicative) or gamma = alpha + beta (additive, per Lande 1996).

questions.prompt: Order these analysis steps for a study asking whether antibiotic treatment changes gut community composition.

items.text: Compute an alpha diversity index (e.g. Shannon's H') for each sample and compare groups with a standard test
Build a pairwise distance matrix (e.g. Bray-Curtis) between all samples
Compare within-group versus between-group distances to assess beta diversity differences
Interpret both alpha and beta results together before concluding the treatment had 'no effect'

questions.explanation: A complete analysis reports alpha diversity first (the simpler, per-sample metric), then constructs a distance matrix to evaluate beta diversity, compares those distances, and only then draws a conclusion — since either axis alone can miss a real effect.

lessons.label: Distance Metrics and Ordination

sections.heading: Bray-Curtis and Jaccard: abundance versus presence
sections.body: Beta diversity starts with a distance (dissimilarity) between every pair of samples, and the choice of distance changes what 'different' means. Bray-Curtis dissimilarity, BC = Σ|x_i - y_i| / Σ(x_i + y_i), uses relative abundances directly, so it is dominated by shifts in which taxa are common — two samples sharing all the same rare taxa but disagreeing on which one dominates will score as quite dissimilar. Jaccard distance instead only asks presence or absence: it is one minus the fraction of taxa shared out of the total taxa found across both samples, so it is blind to abundance shifts and sensitive instead to whether a taxon was detected at all, which makes it more affected by rare-taxon noise and sequencing depth than Bray-Curtis.

sections.heading: UniFrac: distance that knows evolutionary relatedness
sections.body: Both Bray-Curtis and Jaccard treat every taxon as equally unrelated to every other — losing an ASV and gaining an evolutionarily similar replacement counts the same as losing it and gaining something totally unrelated. Lozupone and Knight (2005) fixed this with UniFrac, which places all taxa from both samples onto a shared phylogenetic tree and measures the fraction of total branch length that leads to taxa found in only one of the two samples. Unweighted UniFrac uses presence/absence only, so it is driven by rare or unique lineages; weighted UniFrac (Lozupone et al., 2007) scales each branch's contribution by relative abundance, so it instead reflects shifts in which lineages dominate. The two can disagree sharply: a community that swaps a large fraction of its abundant taxa for close phylogenetic relatives looks similar under unweighted UniFrac (nothing evolutionarily novel appeared) but quite different under weighted UniFrac (the abundance profile changed a lot).

sections.heading: Ordination: projecting a distance matrix onto a plot you can read
sections.body: A distance matrix among dozens of samples can't be inspected by eye, so it gets projected into two or three dimensions via ordination. Principal coordinates analysis (PCoA, a form of classical multidimensional scaling going back to Gower, 1966) finds orthogonal axes that capture the most variance in the distance matrix, and every honest PCoA plot reports the percent variance explained by each axis — if axis 1 and axis 2 together explain only 25% of total variance, a tight visual cluster on the plot may not reflect a tight cluster in the real, high-dimensional data. Non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) instead preserves only the rank order of distances, not their magnitudes, and reports a stress value quantifying how well the 2D layout preserves that rank order; by the rule of thumb from Clarke (1993), stress under about 0.1 is a good fit and above 0.2 should not be trusted. Neither PCoA's variance percentages nor NMDS's stress value is optional to report — without them, a two-axis cluster plot is just a picture, not evidence.

lessons.workedExample: A diet-intervention study compares gut samples before and after switching mice to a high-fat diet. Unweighted UniFrac between pre- and post-diet samples is small — nearly the same set of bacterial lineages is detectable both before and after, just at different abundances. Weighted UniFrac between the same pairs is large, because the high-fat diet shifted the abundant Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes ratio dramatically even though few new lineages appeared or disappeared. Plotting both distance matrices via PCoA, the weighted UniFrac ordination shows clean pre/post separation on axis 1 (32% variance explained), while the unweighted UniFrac ordination shows no clear separation at all — the correct conclusion is 'diet shifted which lineages dominate, not which lineages are present,' a distinction only visible because both UniFrac variants were computed.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe 'why did you choose that distance metric, and can I trust that plot?' because the choice of distance encodes a hypothesis, and an unlabeled ordination plot is easy to fake confidence with. A weak answer picks Bray-Curtis by default without justifying it, or shows a PCoA/NMDS plot with no variance-explained percentages or stress value. A strong answer explains why abundance-based (Bray-Curtis, weighted UniFrac) versus presence-based (Jaccard, unweighted UniFrac) fits the biological question, and reports the axis variance or stress alongside the plot so the visual separation can be judged against how much of the real structure it actually captures.

questions.prompt: Two gut samples share the exact same set of bacterial taxa, but in Sample A one taxon makes up 80% of the community while in Sample B that same taxon makes up only 10%. Which distance will detect this difference more strongly: Bray-Curtis or Jaccard?

options.text: Bray-Curtis, because it is based on relative abundances rather than presence/absence
Jaccard, because it accounts for how dominant each taxon is
Both will detect it equally, since both are 'distance' measures
Neither will detect any difference, since the taxon lists are identical

explanations.a: Correct — Bray-Curtis sums absolute differences in relative abundance, so a taxon swinging from 80% to 10% drives a large dissimilarity even with an identical taxon list.
explanations.b: Jaccard only compares which taxa are present or absent; since both samples share the same taxon list, Jaccard distance would be near zero regardless of the abundance shift.
explanations.c: Jaccard is presence/absence-based and explicitly ignores abundance, so it would report near-zero distance here while Bray-Curtis would report a large one.
explanations.d: The taxon lists being identical only guarantees a small Jaccard distance; Bray-Curtis still detects the large abundance shift.

questions.prompt: A community loses several abundant taxa and gains close phylogenetic relatives of those same taxa at similar abundance. What pattern would you expect across the two UniFrac variants?

options.text: Both weighted and unweighted UniFrac would show a large distance
Unweighted UniFrac would show a small distance (little evolutionarily novel appeared); weighted UniFrac would also stay relatively small since abundances of comparable lineages are similar
Weighted UniFrac would show a large distance while unweighted stays small, since only weighted tracks abundance
UniFrac cannot be computed unless the exact same taxa are present in both samples

explanations.a: A large distance in both is what you'd expect if the replacement taxa were phylogenetically unrelated to the originals, not close relatives.
explanations.b: Correct — because the replacements are close phylogenetic relatives at similar abundance, little branch length is unique to either sample under either weighting, so both variants report a relatively small distance; the key UniFrac property is that swapping to a close relative barely moves the phylogenetic distance.
explanations.c: This describes what would happen if abundances shifted but taxonomic identity stayed the same, not the phylogenetic-replacement scenario described here.
explanations.d: UniFrac's entire purpose is comparing samples with different taxon lists by placing them on a shared tree; identical taxon lists are not required.

questions.prompt: Match each ordination concept to what it tells you.

right.text: How well a 2D layout preserves the rank order of the original distances (lower is better, per Clarke 1993)
A phylogeny-aware distance scaled by taxon relative abundance
How much of the total distance-matrix structure a given axis actually captures

questions.explanation: PCoA variance-explained tells you how much of the real structure an axis captures; NMDS stress tells you how faithfully a 2D plot preserves distance rankings; weighted UniFrac is UniFrac's abundance-scaled variant.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to build and honestly report a community ordination plot.

items.text: Choose a distance metric appropriate to the biological question (abundance- or presence-based, phylogeny-aware or not)
Compute the pairwise distance matrix across all samples
Run PCoA or NMDS to project the matrix into 2-3 dimensions
Report percent variance explained (PCoA) or stress (NMDS) alongside the plot

questions.explanation: The metric choice should be justified before computing distances; the matrix feeds the ordination; and the resulting plot is only interpretable once its variance-explained or stress value is reported alongside it.

lessons.label: Testing Community Differences

sections.heading: PERMANOVA: testing group separation on a distance matrix
sections.body: You can't run a t-test on an ordination plot, because the points aren't independent numeric measurements — they're derived from a distance matrix. Anderson (2001) solved this with PERMANOVA (permutational multivariate analysis of variance, implemented as adonis/adonis2 in R's vegan package): it partitions the total variance in a distance matrix into between-group and within-group components, computes an F-like statistic, then builds a null distribution by randomly reshuffling group labels thousands of times and recomputing the statistic each time. The p-value is simply the fraction of permuted statistics at least as extreme as the observed one — no assumption of multivariate normality required, which is exactly why it's the standard test for Bray-Curtis, Jaccard, or UniFrac distances.

sections.heading: The dispersion confound: significant for the wrong reason
sections.body: PERMANOVA can reject the null for two very different reasons: the groups' centroids sit in different locations (a real compositional shift), or the groups simply have different amounts of internal spread (dispersion) even if centered in the same place — and PERMANOVA's F-statistic conflates the two. Anderson (2006) built betadisper (a multivariate analogue of Levene's test) specifically to isolate this: it tests whether groups have homogeneous dispersion around their own centroid, independent of where that centroid sits. Running PERMANOVA without betadisper is the microbiome-stats equivalent of reporting a t-test without checking for unequal variances — a significant PERMANOVA paired with a significant betadisper result means you cannot cleanly attribute the difference to community composition shifting versus one group simply becoming more heterogeneous (a common, biologically real pattern after disturbance, but a different claim).

sections.heading: Compositional data and why diversity isn't differential abundance
sections.body: Relative abundance data are compositional — every sample's taxon proportions sum to 1 by construction — and Gloor et al. (2017), in a paper titled 'Microbiome Datasets Are Compositional: And This Is Not Optional,' argued that applying standard statistics (correlations, t-tests) directly to proportions is invalid because of this closure constraint: an increase in one taxon's proportion mechanically forces others down even with no real biological change, a problem traced to Aitchison's (1982) foundational work on compositional data analysis. Their recommended fix is the centered log-ratio (CLR) transform, clr(x_i) = ln(x_i / g(x)) where g(x) is the geometric mean of all taxa in that sample, which removes the sum-to-one constraint before testing. Crucially, this is a separate question from diversity entirely: diversity indices summarize the whole community's structure in one number, while asking which specific taxa differ between groups is differential abundance testing (tools like ALDEx2 or ANCOM, which are CLR- or compositional-aware) — a significant PERMANOVA tells you communities differ overall, not which taxa are driving it.

lessons.workedExample: A study compares gut communities of antibiotic-treated versus control mice using Bray-Curtis distances. PERMANOVA returns p = 0.01, seemingly confirming the treatment shifted community composition. But betadisper on the same distances also returns p = 0.02, showing the treated group has significantly more within-group spread than controls — consistent with the individualized recovery pattern from the earlier alpha/beta lesson. The honest conclusion isn't 'treatment changed composition' unqualified; it's 'treatment increased inter-individual variability, and centroid location may or may not also differ' — the two tests need to be reported together, and a PCoA plot showing treated points scattered widely around roughly the same centroid as controls would make the dispersion effect visible rather than mistaken for a location shift.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'did you check for dispersion effects?' or 'why CLR transform instead of raw proportions?' is testing whether the student understands what their significance test actually licenses them to claim. A weak answer reports a PERMANOVA p-value as proof the treatment changed the community, full stop. A strong answer pairs PERMANOVA with betadisper to rule out a pure-dispersion explanation, and — if testing individual taxa rather than overall community structure — explains why raw relative abundances are compositionally constrained and a CLR transform or a tool built for compositional data is needed instead of applying a standard test straight to percentages.

questions.prompt: A PERMANOVA on Bray-Curtis distances returns p = 0.01 for treatment vs. control. A follow-up betadisper test also returns p = 0.02, showing significantly different within-group dispersion. What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: The PERMANOVA result is fully explained by group composition differing in location; betadisper is irrelevant here
The significant PERMANOVA result cannot be cleanly attributed to a centroid (location) shift alone, since unequal dispersion between groups can itself produce a significant PERMANOVA
Betadisper being significant means the PERMANOVA result is invalid and should be discarded
Both tests being significant is impossible; one of them must be computed incorrectly

explanations.a: PERMANOVA's F-statistic conflates location and dispersion differences, so a significant result cannot be assumed to reflect location alone without checking dispersion.
explanations.b: Correct — this is precisely why Anderson (2006) built betadisper: a significant PERMANOVA paired with a significant betadisper result means dispersion differences are a plausible contributor, and the study should report both rather than claiming a clean compositional shift.
explanations.c: A significant betadisper result doesn't invalidate PERMANOVA; it means the PERMANOVA result needs a more careful interpretation, since it could reflect dispersion, location, or both.
explanations.d: Both being significant is a normal, well-documented scenario in beta diversity analysis, not evidence of a computational error.

questions.prompt: Why do Gloor et al. (2017) argue that applying a standard correlation or t-test directly to raw relative-abundance proportions is problematic?

options.text: Relative abundances are always normally distributed, which standard tests cannot handle

Because proportions in a sample must sum to 1, an increase in one taxon mechanically forces others down, creating a compositional constraint (the closure problem) that can produce spurious correlations unrelated to real biology
Sequencing machines cannot generate enough reads to satisfy the sample-size requirements of a t-test
Relative abundance values are always integers, which standard tests require to be continuous

explanations.a: Standard tests generally assume normality, but that's not the specific compositional problem Gloor et al. describe; their concern is the sum-to-one constraint itself.
explanations.b: Correct — the closure constraint (proportions summing to 1), rooted in Aitchison's (1982) compositional data framework, means taxon proportions are not independent of each other, which can manufacture correlations that have nothing to do with biology.
explanations.c: This is a read-depth/statistical-power issue, not the compositional closure problem the CLR transform is designed to address.
explanations.d: Relative abundances are continuous proportions between 0 and 1, not integers; this option misdescribes the data type.

questions.prompt: Match each method to what question it answers.

right.text: Do groups differ in within-group spread around their own centroid?
Do group centroids differ on a distance matrix overall?
Which specific taxa differ in abundance between groups?

questions.explanation: PERMANOVA tests overall group separation on a distance matrix; betadisper isolates whether that separation could instead (or also) reflect unequal dispersion; taxon-level differential abundance is a separate, compositionally-aware question about which taxa drive any difference.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a defensible test for whether two groups' microbial communities differ.

items.text: Build a distance matrix (e.g. Bray-Curtis or weighted UniFrac) across all samples
Run PERMANOVA to test whether group centroids differ overall
Run betadisper to check whether within-group dispersion is homogeneous
If asking which specific taxa differ, apply a compositional-aware differential abundance method rather than a standard test on raw proportions

questions.explanation: The distance matrix underlies the community-level test; PERMANOVA and betadisper together clarify whether any group difference is location, dispersion, or both; and a separate compositional-aware method is required only if the question shifts to which individual taxa differ.

lessons.label: Mapping the Human Microbiome: HMP and MetaHIT

sections.heading: Two consortia, one catalog problem
sections.body: In 2007 the NIH launched the Human Microbiome Project (HMP), a five-year effort to catalog the microbial communities living in and on healthy Americans at multiple body sites — skin, mouth, nose, gut, vagina. Across the Atlantic, the EU-funded MetaHIT consortium went narrower but deeper: the gut alone. Qin et al. (2010, Nature) sequenced fecal metagenomes from 124 Europeans and assembled a non-redundant catalog of 3.3 million microbial genes — roughly 165 times the ~20,000 genes in the human genome. Over 99% of those genes were bacterial, and the data implied the cohort collectively carried on the order of 1,000-1,150 prevalent bacterial species, with any one gut hosting around 160 of them. That gene-count ratio became the standard shorthand for 'we carry more microbial genetic capacity than human.'

sections.heading: What the flagship paper actually found
sections.body: HMP's headline 2012 Nature paper profiled 242 healthy adults across 5 major body habitats (18 specific sites total) and delivered a finding sharper than 'there are lots of microbes': composition and function decouple. Which species live in a given gut or mouth differs enormously person to person — no single core species is shared by everyone. But the metabolic pathways those species carry out (amino acid synthesis, vitamin production, carbohydrate breakdown) stay remarkably consistent across people, because many different taxa can perform the same job — functional redundancy. Health, by this logic, does not mean matching a fixed community; it means having the right pathways present, however they got assembled. Butyrate production is the textbook example: this short-chain fatty acid feeds colon cells and shapes local immune tone, and dozens of taxonomically unrelated gut species — from Faecalibacterium prausnitzii to various Roseburia and Eubacterium species — carry the enzymes to make it. Two people can share almost no butyrate-producing species by name and still both have a well-stocked butyrate-production pathway, because the function, not the organism, is what got selected for.

sections.heading: Reference range, not causal map
sections.body: Both consortia established something descriptive: a normal range of who's-there and gene content in disease-free volunteers, a baseline against which later disease-association studies could be measured. What they did not establish: which species or genes cause any particular health outcome, how a community assembles in the first place, or whether 'healthy' ranges drawn from largely Western, adult, urban cohorts generalize elsewhere. A catalog is a starting point for hypotheses, not a proof of any one of them.

lessons.workedExample: A student's science-fair poster on gut health cites the MetaHIT figure that gut bacteria carry '165 times more genes than we do' as proof the microbiome 'controls' digestion. A judge asks: controls compared to what baseline? The stronger move is citing HMP's decoupling finding instead — two healthy volunteers can share almost no gut species yet run the same core metabolic pathways, because dozens of unrelated taxa can encode the same enzyme. That reframes the poster's claim from 'more genes must mean more control' into a testable one: measure a specific pathway's presence across your own samples rather than just counting genes. The gene-count factoid is real and citable, but alone it is a size comparison, not a functional argument.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe HMP/MetaHIT because these are the numbers every microbiome-flavored project reaches for first, and the gene-ratio factoid gets repeated far more than it gets understood. A weak answer recites '165 times more genes' as if a bigger number equals more importance. A strong answer explains what the consortia actually measured — reference ranges of composition and gene content in healthy people — and is explicit that neither project assigned function or causation to any single organism. The tell of real understanding is naming the composition-vs-function decoupling: healthy people differ wildly in who's there while converging on what gets done.

questions.prompt: In the MetaHIT gene catalog (Qin et al., 2010), roughly how did the number of non-redundant microbial genes compare to the human gene count?

options.text: Roughly equal, about 20,000 each
About 165 times more microbial genes than human genes
About 10 times fewer microbial genes
Microbial genes could not be reliably counted

explanations.a: The catalog found 3.3 million microbial genes against ~20,000 human genes — nowhere near equal.
explanations.b: Correct — 3.3 million non-redundant genes versus ~20,000 human genes works out to roughly a 165-fold difference.
explanations.c: This reverses the actual relationship; microbial genes vastly outnumber human genes, not the other way around.
explanations.d: Metagenomic sequencing across 124 individuals is exactly what produced the 3.3-million-gene count; it was measurable.

questions.prompt: What was the key 'decoupling' finding of the 2012 HMP flagship paper across 242 healthy adults?

options.text: Species composition was nearly identical across healthy people
Composition varied widely between people, but the metabolic pathways present converged
Both composition and function varied unpredictably with no pattern
Function varied widely while composition stayed fixed

explanations.a: The paper found the opposite — no single core set of species was shared by everyone sampled.
explanations.b: Correct — who's there differed enormously between individuals, but the metabolic pathways those communities carried out stayed consistent, i.e., functional redundancy.
explanations.c: There was a clear pattern: variable composition paired with convergent function, not randomness on both axes.
explanations.d: This inverts the finding; function was the consistent axis and composition was the variable one.

questions.prompt: Put these Human Microbiome Project / MetaHIT milestones in chronological order.

items.text: NIH launches the Human Microbiome Project
Qin et al. publish the MetaHIT gut gene catalog
HMP Consortium publishes the flagship 'healthy microbiome' paper in Nature

questions.explanation: HMP began in 2007; MetaHIT's gene-catalog paper appeared in 2010; the HMP flagship paper describing the healthy human microbiome followed in 2012.

questions.prompt: Match each consortium to what it specifically produced.

right.text: Profiled 242 healthy adults across 5 body habitats, showing composition varies while function converges
Sequenced fecal metagenomes of 124 Europeans into a 3.3-million-gene catalog

questions.explanation: HMP was the broader, multi-site US project culminating in the 2012 flagship paper; MetaHIT was the European gut-focused consortium behind the 2010 gene catalog.

lessons.label: Enterotypes: A Debate in Real Time

sections.heading: A tidy claim: three gut 'types'
sections.body: In 2011, Arumugam et al. (Nature) proposed that human gut microbiomes fall into a small number of discrete configurations, not a continuum. Clustering fecal metagenomes by which genus dominated, they described three enterotypes named for their signature genus: Bacteroides, Prevotella, and Ruminococcus. The appeal was immediate — like ABO blood types, enterotypes promised a small, tractable classification for a bewilderingly variable ecosystem, and the paper reported the clusters held regardless of the donors' age, sex, body-mass index, or nationality. A clean typology like that is exactly what a field drowning in inter-individual variability wants: a handful of categories instead of thousands of unique compositions.

sections.heading: The pushback: gradient, not category
sections.body: Within a year, Jeffery et al. (2012) re-examined larger and more diverse cohorts and argued the data looked less like three separated islands and more like a continuous gradient, dominated in practice by how much Bacteroides versus Prevotella a sample carried, with the apparent 'Ruminococcus' cluster far weaker and less reproducible than the other two. Knights et al. (2014, Cell Host & Microbe), in 'Rethinking Enterotypes,' pushed further: reanalyzing a year of daily gut-microbiome samples from a single subject (Caporaso et al., 2011), they showed that individual's profile 'walking' from one putative enterotype to another over the course of days, which is not what a stable, discrete category should do, and demonstrated that the clustering algorithms used will report tidy clusters even when the underlying data is a smooth, unbroken gradient — the method can manufacture the pattern it was looking for. The mechanism is mundane: Arumugam's original pipeline used Jensen-Shannon divergence to measure how different two samples' genus profiles are, then forced that distance matrix into a fixed number of partitions-around-medoids clusters — a step that will carve out three tidy-looking groups even when fed synthetic data generated from a single smooth, continuous distribution, because the algorithm's job is to produce clusters, not to check whether real gaps exist between them.

sections.heading: Why this is a good case study, not a failure
sections.body: Enterotypes were never fully retracted — Bacteroides-dominant versus Prevotella-dominant guts really do correlate with long-term diet (protein/fat versus fiber-rich) and remain a useful rough descriptor. What changed is the claim's precision: from 'three discrete human types' to 'a continuous axis with two dominant poles, best treated as a gradient rather than hard categories.' The episode shows a field self-correcting in real time: an attractive, simplifying hypothesis, a methodologically sharp critique, and a settled, more modest consensus — exactly the trajectory good science is supposed to follow.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to sort their class's gut-microbiome survey data (donated stool samples, sequenced for genus abundance) into 'enterotypes' for a poster. Following Arumugam's original method, they force a clustering algorithm to output three groups and report clean percentages. A judge who knows the Knights (2014) critique asks: did you check whether the data actually separates into distinct clusters, or did the algorithm impose three groups on a continuum? The stronger analysis plots each sample's Bacteroides and Prevotella relative abundance on two axes first, visually inspects for real gaps between groups, and only then decides whether discrete categories or a gradient score is the honest way to describe the pattern.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe enterotypes because it is a rare case where the correction to a famous finding is itself well-documented and citable — so a student can be asked to argue both sides. A weak answer treats 'three enterotypes' as settled fact from a single 2011 paper. A strong answer knows the concept was contested within a year, names Jeffery (2012) and Knights (2014) specifically, and explains the actual statistical problem: clustering algorithms will report discrete groups even on continuous data, so 'the algorithm found clusters' is not by itself evidence the biology is discrete.

questions.prompt: What did Arumugam et al. (2011) originally propose about human gut microbiomes?

options.text: That gut composition is nearly identical across all healthy adults
That gut microbiomes cluster into three discrete enterotypes named for a dominant genus
That gut composition changes randomly day to day with no stable pattern
That diet has no measurable effect on gut microbial composition

explanations.a: The paper's whole point was that composition varies, just allegedly into a few types rather than being uniform.
explanations.b: Correct — the 2011 paper proposed three discrete enterotypes, dominated respectively by Bacteroides, Prevotella, and Ruminococcus.
explanations.c: The claim was the opposite of randomness — a small number of stable, reproducible categories.
explanations.d: Diet is central to the later debate (Bacteroides/Prevotella dominance tracks long-term diet), not something the original paper dismissed.

questions.prompt: What specific methodological problem did Knights et al. (2014) point to in 'Rethinking Enterotypes'?

options.text: The original DNA sequencing reads were contaminated with human DNA
Clustering algorithms can report discrete-looking clusters even when the underlying data is a continuous gradient
The original samples were not really from human guts
Ruminococcus does not actually exist in the human gut

explanations.a: This was not the critique; the issue was statistical interpretation, not sample contamination.
explanations.b: Correct — Knights et al. showed the clustering methods used will impose apparent groups on smooth, continuous variation, and that one subject's daily microbiome samples 'walked' between putative types over the course of days.
explanations.c: Sample identity was never in question in this debate.
explanations.d: Ruminococcus is a real gut genus; the critique concerned whether it defines a robust, separate cluster, not whether it exists.

questions.prompt: Order the enterotype debate from initial proposal to the settled, more modest consensus.

items.text: Arumugam et al. propose three discrete enterotypes (2011)
Jeffery et al. argue the data looks like a continuous gradient (2012)
Knights et al. show clustering-algorithm artifacts and temporal fluidity (2014)
Field converges on 'gradient with two dominant poles' rather than three hard types

questions.explanation: The discrete three-enterotype claim (2011) was challenged as a gradient the following year (2012), then given a sharper statistical critique in 2014, after which the field settled on a more modest gradient framing.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher/team to their specific contribution to the enterotype debate.

right.text: Proposed three discrete enterotypes
Argued the pattern is a continuous gradient in larger cohorts
Showed clustering artifacts and that individuals shift 'types' over time

questions.explanation: Each publication marks a distinct stage: the original discrete-cluster claim, the gradient re-analysis, and the methodological critique of the clustering approach itself.

lessons.label: The Obese Microbiome: A Cautionary Landmark

sections.heading: A ratio, and a transplant that made mice fat
sections.body: Ley et al. (2006, Nature) reported that obese mice and obese humans carried a higher ratio of Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes — the gut's two dominant bacterial phyla — than lean counterparts, and that the ratio shifted toward the lean pattern as obese subjects lost weight on a low-calorie diet. The same year, Turnbaugh et al. (2006, Nature) went further: they transplanted gut microbiota from obese versus lean mice into germ-free mice and found the obese-donor recipients gained significantly more body fat than lean-donor recipients — on the order of 1.5 to 2 times as much — despite eating the same amount of food. Metagenomic analysis suggested the obese microbiome carried more genes for extracting energy from food. Together the studies built a striking, causal-sounding story: a specific microbial signature drives excess energy harvest and, transplanted, drives obesity itself.

sections.heading: Ridaura (2013): causation gets more complicated
sections.body: Ridaura et al. (2013, Science) pushed the transplant logic further using human twin pairs discordant for obesity. Microbiota from the obese twin, transplanted into germ-free mice, again produced more fat gain than microbiota from the lean co-twin. But the twist came from cohousing: when obese-microbiota mice were caged with lean-microbiota mice, the obese mice were protected from weight gain — specific Bacteroidetes species (including Bacteroides cellulosilyticus, B. uniformis, B. vulgatus, B. thetaiotaomicron, and Parabacteroides merdae) invaded from the lean mouse's community — but only on a diet high in fruits and vegetables and low in saturated fat. Causation, in other words, was real in mice but conditional on diet, not a fixed microbial verdict.

sections.heading: The replication that didn't come
sections.body: As more human cohorts accumulated, the tidy Firmicutes:Bacteroidetes story stopped holding up. Finucane et al. (2014, PLOS ONE) reanalyzed existing 16S datasets and found no consistent F:B association with obesity across studies. Sze and Schloss (2016, mBio), pooling ten independent datasets in a formal meta-analysis, found neither the F:B ratio nor Firmicutes abundance alone was significantly associated with obesity in any single study, and that classifying a person as obese from microbiome data alone was barely better than a coin flip. The lesson for the field was not that the microbiome is irrelevant to metabolism — mouse transplant causality still holds under controlled conditions — but that a compelling small-study finding, repeated as a slogan ("gut bacteria cause obesity") before independent replication, outran the evidence and cost the field credibility it had to earn back.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to test whether their own Firmicutes:Bacteroidetes ratio predicts anything about metabolism, citing Ley (2006) as established fact. A judge who knows Sze and Schloss (2016) asks whether the ratio has held up across independent studies. The honest answer: no — a ten-study meta-analysis found no significant association between F:B ratio and obesity in any of them, and classification accuracy from microbiome data alone was only 33-65%, little better than chance. A stronger project either drops the F:B framing entirely and measures something with better-replicated support (like specific taxa tied to short-chain fatty acid production), or explicitly frames the F:B ratio as a historically important but now-unsupported hypothesis and explains why it failed to replicate.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges lean on this case because the Firmicutes:Bacteroidetes ratio is still floating around in popular science writing and supplement marketing years after the primary literature moved past it. A weak answer cites Ley (2006) or Turnbaugh (2006) as if the causal story were closed. A strong answer knows the arc has three acts — an exciting initial finding, a nuanced but still-positive follow-up (Ridaura, 2013), and a large-scale failure to replicate (Finucane 2014; Sze & Schloss 2016) — and can explain that a mouse-transplant result showing causation in a controlled system does not guarantee a biomarker generalizes across noisy human populations.

questions.prompt: In Turnbaugh et al. (2006), what happened when germ-free mice received gut microbiota transplants from obese versus lean donor mice?

options.text: Both groups gained identical amounts of fat
Obese-donor recipients gained significantly more body fat (on the order of 1.5 to 2 times as much) despite eating the same amount of food
Lean-donor recipients gained more fat than obese-donor recipients
Neither group of mice gained any measurable fat

explanations.a: The whole point of the experiment was a difference between groups, not an identical outcome.
explanations.b: Correct — obese-microbiota recipients gained substantially more fat than lean-microbiota recipients (on the order of 1.5 to 2 times as much), despite matched food intake, suggesting the microbiome itself affected energy harvest.
explanations.c: This reverses the actual, well-replicated result of this specific experiment.
explanations.d: Both groups gained fat; the finding was about the difference in degree between them.

questions.prompt: What did Sze and Schloss (2016) find when they pooled ten independent studies in a meta-analysis?

options.text: The Firmicutes:Bacteroidetes ratio was significantly associated with obesity in all ten studies
Neither the F:B ratio nor Firmicutes abundance was significantly associated with obesity in any of the studies
Obesity could be predicted from microbiome data with over 95% accuracy
Only Bacteroidetes abundance, not Firmicutes, predicted obesity

explanations.a: This is the opposite of what the meta-analysis found; the association did not hold up.
explanations.b: Correct — across the pooled studies, neither the F:B ratio nor Firmicutes abundance alone reached significance for an obesity association.
explanations.c: Classification accuracy from microbiome data alone was reported at only 33-65%, far below 95%.
explanations.d: The meta-analysis found neither phylum's abundance reliably predicted obesity, not a one-sided result favoring Bacteroidetes.

questions.prompt: Order these obese-microbiome landmark events chronologically.

items.text: Ley et al. report the F:B ratio difference in obese vs. lean mice and humans
Turnbaugh et al. show obese-microbiota transplants cause more fat gain in germ-free mice
Ridaura et al. show diet-dependent 'rescue' via cohousing in twin-derived microbiota
Sze and Schloss meta-analysis finds no consistent F:B-obesity association

questions.explanation: Ley and Turnbaugh both appeared in 2006, establishing the initial F:B and transplant-causality claims; Ridaura's twin-cohousing study followed in 2013; the large-scale failure to replicate came with Sze and Schloss in 2016.

questions.prompt: Match each study to its key finding.

right.text: Obese-microbiota transplant roughly doubled fat gain in germ-free mice
Lean microbiota could invade and protect obese-microbiota mice, but only on a produce-rich, low-saturated-fat diet
Reanalysis of existing datasets found no consistent Firmicutes:Bacteroidetes association with obesity

questions.explanation: Turnbaugh established transplant causality in mice, Ridaura showed it was diet-conditional using human twin donors, and Finucane's reanalysis was an early sign the F:B ratio itself did not generalize.

lessons.label: Correlation vs Causation and the Gut-Brain Case

sections.heading: Germ-free mice as the causal proving ground
sections.body: Most microbiome-disease literature is correlational: sequence a cohort, find a taxon enriched in the sick group, publish. Germ-free mice — raised with no microbiota at all in sterile isolators — are one of the few tools that can test causation directly, because a trait present in a germ-free mouse and absent (or reversed) once colonized implicates the microbiome specifically. Sudo et al. (2004) showed germ-free mice mount an exaggerated stress-hormone response to restraint stress compared to conventionally raised mice, and that colonizing them, especially early in life, dampened the response back toward normal. Diaz-Heijtz et al. (2011, PNAS) extended this to behavior and brain gene expression: germ-free mice showed altered motor activity and reduced anxiety-like behavior relative to colonized mice, along with changed expression of genes tied to synaptic plasticity in specific brain regions. In both studies, colonizing later in life produced weaker or no correction, pointing to an early developmental window in which gut microbes shape neural and endocrine development.

sections.heading: The confounder hiding inside the mouse cage
sections.body: Even germ-free experiments carry a trap: mice housed together share microbiota by coprophagy (eating each other's feces), so cage and litter become a hidden variable. If a 'treatment' group and a 'control' group are housed in separate cages rather than randomized across cages, any measured difference could be a cage effect — different microbiomes that arose from housing, not from the intervention — masquerading as the effect under study. This is why rigorous designs randomize littermates across cages and treatments, or use co-housing/cross-fostering controls. Pat Schloss has argued in print for exactly this kind of methodological discipline, pointing out how often microbiome papers under-report or under-control for cage, litter, and batch effects that inflate apparent significance.

sections.heading: Koch's postulates don't scale to a community
sections.body: Robert Koch's 19th-century postulates prove a single pathogen causes a single disease: isolate it, culture it alone, reintroduce it, reproduce the disease. A microbiome effect usually has no single causal agent — it is an emergent property of hundreds of interacting species, so there is nothing to isolate and reintroduce alone. The field's practical workaround is the gnotobiotic transplant: move a whole community into a germ-free host and see if the phenotype transfers, as in the gut-brain and obesity work. That recapitulates an effect, but it does not identify which member, interaction, or metabolite is doing the causal work — a weaker standard than Koch's original postulates, and one every gut-brain claim should be read against.

lessons.workedExample: A student reads that autism-spectrum traits correlate with a particular gut bacterial signature in several published cohorts and wants to claim the bacteria 'cause' the behavioral traits for their project. A judge asks how they would test causation, not just correlation. The rigorous answer models it on Diaz-Heijtz (2011): raise genetically matched mice germ-free versus colonized, randomize littermates across cages so housing itself isn't a hidden variable, and look for the behavioral difference to appear only with the microbiome present and to be sensitive to the timing of colonization. Absent that kind of gnotobiotic, cage-controlled design, the honest framing is 'associated with' — not 'causes' — and the project should say so explicitly rather than borrowing causal language its own data cannot support.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe correlation-versus-causation here because gut-brain and microbiome-disease claims are the most over-extended language in the whole field, routinely reported as causal in headlines when the underlying study was observational. A weak answer cannot name a method that actually tests causation. A strong answer names germ-free/gnotobiotic transplant as the real causal tool, can explain the cage/litter confound that undermines even some of those experiments, and recognizes that classical Koch's postulates do not translate cleanly to whole-community effects — so even a successful transplant experiment establishes 'this community is sufficient,' not 'this specific microbe is the cause.'

questions.prompt: What did Diaz-Heijtz et al. (2011) find when comparing germ-free mice to conventionally colonized mice?

options.text: No behavioral or gene-expression differences of any kind
Altered motor activity, reduced anxiety-like behavior, and changed brain gene expression, most correctable if colonization happened early in life
Germ-free mice were identical to colonized mice only if colonized as adults
Colonization at any age fully reversed all behavioral differences

explanations.a: The study specifically reported measurable behavioral and gene-expression differences between germ-free and colonized mice.
explanations.b: Correct — germ-free mice showed altered motor activity, reduced anxiety-like behavior, and changed synaptic-plasticity gene expression, with correction dependent on an early colonization window.
explanations.c: This reverses the actual finding; early colonization corrected the differences, not adult colonization.
explanations.d: The studies found colonization timing mattered — later colonization produced weaker or no correction, not full reversal at any age.

questions.prompt: Why is the cage/litter effect a serious confounder in germ-free mouse experiments?

options.text: Cages affect mouse body temperature, which changes gene expression
Mice housed together share microbiota through coprophagy, so unrandomized cage assignment can create a fake 'treatment effect' that is really just a housing effect
Cage material contains antibiotics that kill gut bacteria
Germ-free mice cannot be housed in cages at all

explanations.a: Temperature is not the mechanism described for this confound; microbiota-sharing via coprophagy is.
explanations.b: Correct — mice sharing a cage share microbiota by eating each other's feces, so if treatment and control groups aren't randomized across cages, a measured difference could just be a cage-of-origin effect rather than a real effect of the manipulation.
explanations.c: Cage material is not the confounding mechanism; shared coprophagy-driven microbiota transfer between cage-mates is.
explanations.d: Germ-free mice are housed in sterile isolators/cages; the confound arises specifically from cage-mates sharing microbiota, not from an inability to house them.

questions.prompt: Order the logic of testing a microbiome-behavior claim from weakest to strongest evidence for causation.

items.text: A correlational cohort study finds a taxon enriched in mice/people with a behavioral trait
Germ-free mice show the behavioral trait differs from colonized mice
The difference is shown to depend on the timing of colonization (early vs. late)
The experiment is repeated with littermates randomized across cages to rule out housing effects

questions.explanation: A raw correlation is the weakest evidence; showing the trait appears/disappears with microbiota presence (germ-free vs. colonized) is stronger; showing it is timing-dependent strengthens the developmental-window argument; and controlling for cage/litter effects is what makes the causal claim actually rigorous rather than confounded.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to what it describes in causal microbiome research.

left.text: Limit of Koch's postulates for microbiomes

right.text: Moving a whole microbial community into a germ-free host to see if a phenotype transfers
A hidden confound where housing, not the intervention, explains a measured difference
There is usually no single causal agent to isolate and reintroduce alone, unlike a classic single pathogen

questions.explanation: Gnotobiotic transplant is the practical causal tool for whole communities; the cage effect is the confound that can undermine it if not controlled; and the Koch's-postulates limit explains why even a successful transplant experiment falls short of pinpointing a single causal microbe.

lessons.label: How Sterile Is the Womb? The In-Utero Debate

sections.heading: A doctrine, then a challenge
sections.body: For decades, the working assumption in medicine was the 'sterile womb' doctrine: a healthy fetus develops in a microbe-free environment, and the first real colonization happens during birth, seeding differently depending on vaginal delivery versus C-section. Aagaard et al. (2014, Science Translational Medicine) challenged this directly, reporting 16S rRNA sequencing evidence of a distinct, low-abundance bacterial community in placental tissue from healthy pregnancies — a 'placental microbiome' whose composition resembled the oral microbiome more than the vaginal one, which the authors interpreted as bacteria arriving via the bloodstream from the mother's mouth. If true, it meant fetal microbial exposure, and by extension immune priming, began well before birth.

sections.heading: The low-biomass reckoning
sections.body: The placenta is a low-biomass sample: if it carries any bacteria at all, the true signal is extremely faint. That is exactly the condition under which sequencing is most vulnerable to what the field now calls the 'kitome' — contaminating bacterial DNA present in the DNA-extraction kits, reagents, and lab surfaces themselves, first characterized systematically by Salter et al. (2014, BMC Biology). When true biomass is near zero, contaminant DNA in the reagents can dominate the sequencing output and produce a plausible-looking, reproducible 'community' that never actually lived in the sample. Placental tissue, along with amniotic fluid and other rarely-microbial sites, became a central test case for whether a reported microbiome was real biology or a reagent artifact.

sections.heading: de Goffau (2019): contamination, mostly, with one exception
sections.body: de Goffau et al. (2019, Nature) ran the largest and most methodologically careful test of the placental-microbiome claim: over 500 placentas, extensive negative controls (paired negative extraction-kit and reagent-only controls, processed and sequenced through the identical pipeline alongside each real sample), and statistical methods that subtracted, sample by sample, any signal also present in that sample's matched blank before calling anything a genuine bacterial read. Their conclusion was blunt: the human placenta has no microbiome. Nearly every earlier signal was traceable to reagent contamination or to bacteria picked up during labor and delivery itself, not before. The one notable exception was Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Strep), detected as a genuine, non-contaminant signal in roughly 5% of samples collected before labor began — a real pathogen occasionally present, not evidence of a normal resident microbiome. The debate resolved largely back toward the sterile-womb view, with low-biomass contamination control now treated as a mandatory step in any such study.

lessons.workedExample: A student designs a project sampling placental tissue for bacterial DNA and, using a single extraction kit with no negative controls, finds a clear 16S signal and concludes the placenta has its own resident microbiome, citing Aagaard (2014). A judge who knows de Goffau (2019) asks: what did you sequence alongside your real samples to check for contamination? Without a blank extraction-kit control processed and sequenced the same way, the student cannot rule out that their entire signal is kitome. The stronger design runs extraction blanks and empty-reagent controls through the identical pipeline, subtracts anything found in both, and only reports what remains — the exact discipline that let de Goffau's team distinguish a true 5% Group B Strep signal from what turned out to be a field-wide contamination artifact.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the placental-microbiome debate because it is one of the cleanest examples in the whole field of a plausible, published, headline-making claim being overturned not by new biology but by better negative controls. A weak answer treats Aagaard (2014) as the final word or, at the other extreme, dismisses low-biomass microbiome work entirely. A strong answer explains the specific mechanism of failure — kitome contamination dominating a near-zero true signal — names de Goffau (2019) and its scale (500+ placentas, contamination-aware statistics), and can state the one finding that survived (Group B Strep in a small pre-labor minority), showing they understand the debate resolved on evidence, not by assumption.

questions.prompt: What did Aagaard et al. (2014) originally claim about the placenta?

options.text: That the placenta is completely sterile with no detectable DNA of any kind
That the placenta harbors a distinct, low-abundance bacterial community resembling the oral microbiome
That placental bacteria are identical in composition to skin microbiota
That placental bacteria only appear after labor begins

explanations.a: Aagaard's claim was the opposite of sterility — a detectable bacterial community, not an absence of DNA.
explanations.b: Correct — the 2014 paper reported a distinct low-abundance placental bacterial community whose profile resembled the oral microbiome, suggested to arrive via the bloodstream.
explanations.c: The claimed resemblance was to the oral microbiome, not skin microbiota.
explanations.d: The claim specifically concerned bacteria present in placental tissue from ongoing, not necessarily post-labor, pregnancies.

questions.prompt: What is the 'kitome,' and why does it especially threaten low-biomass samples like placental tissue?

options.text: A specific bacterial species that lives exclusively in DNA extraction kits
Contaminating DNA present in extraction kits and reagents, which can dominate sequencing results when the true bacterial signal is very faint or absent
A technique for sterilizing samples before sequencing
The natural, healthy microbiome of a newborn's gut

explanations.a: The kitome is not a single species but contaminating DNA present broadly across kits and reagents.
explanations.b: Correct — reagents and extraction kits carry trace contaminating bacterial DNA that can swamp the true signal in a low-biomass sample, producing a plausible but false 'community.'
explanations.c: It describes a contamination problem, not a sterilization method.
explanations.d: This describes an unrelated concept; the kitome specifically concerns reagent contamination in sequencing workflows.

questions.prompt: Order the events of the placental-microbiome debate chronologically.

items.text: Salter et al. characterize reagent/kitome contamination as a general problem in low-biomass sequencing
Aagaard et al. report a distinct placental bacterial community
de Goffau et al. conclude the placenta has no microbiome, using large-scale contamination controls

questions.explanation: Salter's 2014 characterization of kitome contamination appeared the same year as Aagaard's placental-microbiome paper, and both preceded de Goffau's 2019 large-scale study that applied contamination-aware methods to overturn the placental-microbiome claim.

questions.prompt: Match each finding to the study that produced it.

right.text: Reported an oral-like bacterial community in placental tissue
Found no true placental microbiome in over 500 samples, except a genuine Group B Strep signal in ~5% of pre-labor samples

questions.explanation: Aagaard's 2014 paper made the original placental-microbiome claim; de Goffau's 2019 large-scale, contamination-controlled study overturned it, with Group B Strep as the one confirmed exception.

lessons.label: The Hologenome and Host-Microbe Evolution

sections.heading: A bigger unit of selection
sections.body: Zilber-Rosenberg and Rosenberg (2008, FEMS Microbiology Reviews) proposed the hologenome theory of evolution: treat the holobiont — a host plus every microorganism living in and on it — as a single unit that natural selection can act on, and the hologenome as the combined genetic information of host plus microbiota. Their argument rested on four claims: virtually all animals and plants host symbiotic microbes; those microbes are transmitted between generations, whether vertically (parent to offspring directly) or via the shared environment; the host-symbiont partnership shapes the holobiont's fitness; and — the theory's most provocative piece — the hologenome can evolve faster than the host genome alone, because a microbial community can shift its composition or acquire new genes (via rapid reproduction, mutation, or horizontal gene transfer) on timescales a multicellular host's own mutation rate could never match.

sections.heading: The coral test case
sections.body: Rosenberg's group extended the idea into the coral probiotic hypothesis: reef corals live in tight partnership with photosynthetic algae and a resident bacterial community, and when ocean warming stresses that partnership — triggering coral bleaching, the expulsion of algae — the coral holobiont might adapt not by the coral itself evolving, but by its microbial community shifting toward more heat-tolerant symbiont strains. If true, this predicts a route to environmental resilience that operates on ecological, not genetic-mutation, timescales — a direct test of the hologenome's central claim that community-level flexibility can substitute for host adaptation.

sections.heading: The pushback: does the community actually behave like a genome?
sections.body: Moran and Sloan (2015, PLOS Biology), in 'The Hologenome Concept: Helpful or Hollow?', argued the analogy breaks down at its foundation: unlike chromosomes, most microbial symbionts are not transmitted between host generations with anything close to genomic fidelity — many are reacquired fresh from the environment each generation, so 'coevolved for host benefit' is often really 'ecologically sorted, generation by generation.' They also flagged a conflict-of-interest problem: a microbe under selection to benefit itself is not automatically under selection to benefit the host, so lumping host and microbiome into one selected unit can obscure real competition between them. Douglas and Werren (2016, mBio), in 'Holes in the Hologenome,' pressed the same point further, arguing the label 'holobiont' should be reserved for the minority of associations with genuinely high-fidelity vertical transmission — such as some obligate insect endosymbionts — and not extended to loosely assembled, largely environmentally acquired communities like the human gut microbiome, where host and microbiome are better modeled as evolving under separate, only loosely coupled, selective pressures.

lessons.workedExample: A student presents coral bleaching resistance as proof of hologenome theory: corals with more heat-tolerant bacterial communities survive warming events better, so the coral-microbiome pair is evolving as one unit. A judge who knows Moran and Sloan (2015) asks whether that resident community is passed reliably from parent coral to offspring coral, or reassembled from the surrounding seawater each generation. If it is mostly reacquired from the environment, the observed pattern is ecological sorting within a generation, not the multi-generational co-inheritance that a true unit of selection requires. The stronger project distinguishes the two explicitly: cite the coral probiotic hypothesis as evidence microbial flexibility can buffer environmental stress, while being honest that this is a weaker, ecological claim than the strict hologenome argument that host and microbiome evolve as one selected unit.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the hologenome because it is a genuinely contested theoretical claim, not settled fact dressed up as controversy, and testing whether a student can tell the difference is the point. A weak answer cites the coral probiotic hypothesis as if it proves hologenome theory outright. A strong answer explains the specific evolutionary-biology objection — transmission fidelity — and can state, in their own words, why a community reassembled from the environment each generation is not equivalent to a co-inherited genome, naming Moran and Sloan (2015) or Douglas and Werren (2016) and their proposal to restrict 'holobiont' to high-fidelity vertical-transmission cases rather than every host-microbiome pairing.

questions.prompt: According to Zilber-Rosenberg and Rosenberg's (2008) hologenome theory, why can a holobiont potentially adapt faster than the host genome alone would allow?

options.text: Because host mutation rates are always higher than microbial mutation rates
Because the microbial community can shift composition or acquire genes via rapid reproduction and horizontal gene transfer, on timescales the host's own mutation rate cannot match
Because microbes cannot mutate at all, so only the host genome changes matter
Because host and microbiome genomes physically merge into a single DNA molecule

explanations.a: This reverses the actual comparison; the theory's claim is that microbial change can outpace host genomic change, not the other way around.
explanations.b: Correct — rapid microbial reproduction, mutation, and horizontal gene transfer allow the microbial side of the hologenome to change quickly, a proposed mechanism for faster holobiont-level adaptation.
explanations.c: Microbial mutation and rapid evolution are central to the theory's mechanism, not something the theory denies.
explanations.d: Host and microbial genomes remain physically separate; the hologenome is a conceptual sum of genetic information, not a literal fused molecule.

questions.prompt: What is the core objection Moran and Sloan (2015) raise against treating the holobiont as a straightforward unit of selection?

options.text: Microbes cannot live inside or on host organisms at all
Most microbial symbionts lack the high-fidelity, generation-to-generation transmission that chromosomes have, so many communities are ecologically reassembled rather than co-inherited
Coral bleaching has never been linked to microbial community shifts
Host genomes evolve too slowly to be studied at all

explanations.a: This contradicts the premise of the whole field; symbiosis is not in dispute, only whether it constitutes a unit of selection.
explanations.b: Correct — Moran and Sloan's central point is a transmission-fidelity problem: without reliable co-inheritance across generations, treating host and microbiome as one coevolving selected unit overstates the analogy to a genome.
explanations.c: The coral-bleaching link to microbial shifts is the supporting case for hologenome theory, not something Moran and Sloan denied happens.
explanations.d: Host genome evolution rate is not the objection raised; the issue is specifically about microbial transmission fidelity.

questions.prompt: Order these hologenome-debate milestones chronologically.

items.text: Zilber-Rosenberg and Rosenberg propose the hologenome theory of evolution
Moran and Sloan publish 'The Hologenome Concept: Helpful or Hollow?'
Douglas and Werren propose restricting 'holobiont' to high-fidelity vertical-transmission cases

questions.explanation: The hologenome theory was proposed in 2008; both major critiques followed in 2015 (Moran and Sloan) and 2016 (Douglas and Werren), in that order.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its description.

right.text: A host plus all of its associated microorganisms, treated as a single evolving unit
Corals may resist bleaching by shifting microbial community composition toward heat-tolerant strains rather than the coral itself evolving
Reserve 'holobiont' for associations with genuinely high-fidelity vertical transmission, not loosely-assembled environmentally-acquired communities

questions.explanation: The holobiont is the theory's core unit; the coral probiotic hypothesis is its flagship empirical test case; and Douglas and Werren's proposal is the specific narrowing response to the transmission-fidelity critique.

lessons.label: Founders and Turning Points

sections.heading: Before DNA: culturing the uncultured, on purpose
sections.body: Microbial ecology as a discipline starts with Winogradsky and Beijerinck in the late 1800s, working independently in Russia and the Netherlands. Winogradsky discovered chemolithotrophy — bacteria that get their energy by oxidizing inorganic compounds like sulfur or ammonia instead of eating organic carbon — while studying sulfur and nitrifying bacteria, and built the Winogradsky column, a simple layered mud-and-water setup that still demonstrates microbial stratification by chemistry today. Beijerinck, at Delft, systematized the enrichment culture technique — designing growth conditions that select for a target physiology rather than growing whatever happens to be easiest — and used it to isolate nitrogen-fixing Azotobacter; he is separately credited with the 1898 concept of a 'filterable' infectious agent (tobacco mosaic virus) too small to be bacterial. Enrichment culture stayed the field's dominant method for nearly a century, which also meant the field's picture of microbial life was limited to whatever could be coaxed to grow in a dish.

sections.heading: The molecular pivot: sequences instead of colonies
sections.body: Carl Woese, with George Fox, used comparative ribosomal RNA sequencing in 1977 to show methanogens were as genetically distinct from ordinary bacteria as bacteria are from eukaryotes — the discovery of Archaea, formalized into the three-domain system (Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya) by 1990. Norman Pace then made the pivotal methodological move for ecology specifically: cloning rRNA genes directly out of environmental DNA, bypassing culturing altogether, and using the sequences to survey diversity no dish had ever grown. His 1997 Science review crystallized the resulting picture — that cultured organisms were a small, biased sliver of what was actually out there, the 'uncultured majority.' Mitchell Sogin pushed the resolution further: his 2006 study used massively parallel tag sequencing of 16S hypervariable regions to survey deep-sea samples and revealed a vast 'rare biosphere' — huge numbers of low-abundance taxa invisible to earlier cloning-based surveys, suggesting a seed bank of rare organisms poised to bloom if conditions changed.

sections.heading: From one gene to whole communities, then the whole planet
sections.body: Jo Handelsman coined the term 'metagenomics' in a 1998 paper describing direct cloning of soil DNA into vectors to access the biosynthetic potential of soil microbes that had never been cultured — shifting the unit of study from one marker gene to entire community genomes at once. That toolkit, aimed at humans, defined the field's next era, led by figures like Jeffrey Gordon (pioneering gnotobiotic mouse models linking gut microbiota to host physiology), David Relman (among the first to apply culture-independent methods to human-associated communities), and Rob Knight (building the bioinformatics infrastructure — tools like UniFrac and QIIME — that made large comparative studies practical). That infrastructure scaled to a global turning point: the Earth Microbiome Project, co-founded by Knight, Jack Gilbert, and colleagues, standardized sampling and sequencing protocols across environments worldwide, culminating in Thompson, Gilbert et al. (2017, Nature), which analyzed over 27,000 samples spanning nearly every biome on Earth in one unified framework.

lessons.workedExample: A student running a 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing project on soil samples wants to explain, for a judge, why that method exists at all rather than just describing what the software output shows. Tracing the lineage: the choice of 16S rRNA as the marker gene descends directly from Woese's use of ribosomal RNA to define the domains of life; the decision to sequence DNA straight from soil rather than culturing colonies first descends from Pace's environmental-cloning approach and its 'uncultured majority' finding; and the ability to detect rare, low-abundance taxa in the results at all depends on Sogin's high-throughput tag-sequencing advance. Naming that lineage turns 'I ran a 16S study' into a demonstration that the student understands why the method works, not just how to run it.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the field's history because a student who can trace a modern method back to the innovation that made it possible has a real grasp of the discipline, not just a protocol memorized from a kit manual. A weak answer treats 16S sequencing or metagenomics as though they always existed. A strong answer can name at least the specific pivot relevant to their own project — Woese's rRNA phylogeny, Pace's culture-independent cloning, Sogin's rare-biosphere tag sequencing, or Handelsman's 1998 coinage of 'metagenomics' — and explain concretely what problem that innovation solved, not just recite a name.

questions.prompt: What did Carl Woese and George Fox's 1977 comparative rRNA sequencing work establish?

options.text: That all prokaryotes belong to a single domain of life
That methanogens are genetically distinct enough from ordinary bacteria to represent a separate domain, Archaea
That viruses should be classified as a fourth domain of life
That enrichment culture is the only reliable way to study microbial diversity

explanations.a: The finding split prokaryotes into two distinct domains (Bacteria and Archaea), not one.
explanations.b: Correct — comparative rRNA sequencing showed methanogens were as distinct from bacteria as from eukaryotes, leading to the discovery of Archaea and eventually the three-domain system.
explanations.c: Woese and Fox's work concerned Archaea as a domain, not a viral classification question.
explanations.d: This work was itself a molecular, sequence-based method that moved the field away from reliance on culturing.

questions.prompt: Who coined the term 'metagenomics,' and in what context?

options.text: Norman Pace, describing rRNA gene cloning from environmental DNA
Jo Handelsman, in a 1998 paper on cloning soil DNA to access unculturable microbes' biosynthetic potential
Carl Woese, while defining the three-domain system
Mitchell Sogin, while describing the rare biosphere

explanations.a: Pace pioneered culture-independent rRNA cloning but is not credited with coining 'metagenomics.'
explanations.b: Correct — Handelsman's 1998 paper on cloning soil DNA to access unculturable microbes' chemistry coined the term.
explanations.c: Woese's contribution was rRNA-based domain classification, a separate milestone from the coining of 'metagenomics.'
explanations.d: Sogin's rare-biosphere work used tag sequencing and came later, not the origin of the term 'metagenomics.'

questions.prompt: Order these methodological turning points in microbial ecology chronologically.
