items.text: Winogradsky and Beijerinck develop enrichment culture and discover chemolithotrophy
Woese and Fox discover Archaea via comparative rRNA sequencing
Pace pioneers culture-independent environmental rRNA cloning
Handelsman coins 'metagenomics'
The Earth Microbiome Project publishes its global communal catalogue

questions.explanation: Enrichment culture dates to the late 1800s; Woese and Fox's Archaea discovery came in 1977; Pace's culture-independent cloning approach followed in the 1980s-90s; Handelsman coined 'metagenomics' in 1998; and the Earth Microbiome Project's global synthesis paper appeared in 2017.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher to their specific contribution.

right.text: Revealed the 'rare biosphere' using massively parallel 16S tag sequencing of deep-sea samples
Pioneered gnotobiotic mouse models linking gut microbiota to host physiology
Built bioinformatics infrastructure (e.g., UniFrac, QIIME) and co-founded the Earth Microbiome Project

questions.explanation: Sogin's 2006 tag-sequencing study defined the rare biosphere; Gordon's gnotobiotic mouse work anchored the mechanistic study of gut microbiota and host physiology; Knight's tools and Earth Microbiome Project co-founding scaled comparative microbiome science to a global level.

lessons.label: Four Processes of Community Assembly

sections.heading: Why is this community here, and not some other one?
sections.body: Any patch of habitat, a gut, a soil pore, a lung, ends up with a particular set of microbial taxa at particular abundances. Community ecologists ask why that exact set formed instead of some other set drawn from the same regional pool. Mark Vellend's 2010 synthesis answered by reducing every assembly explanation to four processes: selection, dispersal, drift, and diversification. Selection is deterministic, fitness differences among taxa given the local environment (pH, oxygen, nutrients, host immune pressure) systematically favor some lineages over others. Dispersal is the movement of organisms between sites, it decides which taxa are even present to be selected on. Drift is the stochastic process: random birth, death, and reproduction that shift abundances even when no taxon has a fitness edge, exactly as genetic drift shifts allele frequencies in population genetics. Diversification generates new variants in place via mutation or, in microbes, horizontal gene transfer (HGT) and speciation. HGT is what makes microbial diversification run on a different clock than macrobial diversification: a single conjugative plasmid carrying an antibiotic-resistance gene can move through a bacterial population and hand a new phenotype to millions of cells within days, because it does not require reproduction or vertical inheritance at all, it just needs cell-to-cell contact. Speciation in macrobes, by contrast, accumulates through mutation and reproductive isolation over thousands to millions of years. That difference in tempo is a large part of why a microbial community's functional repertoire can shift dramatically on timescales far too short for classic allopatric speciation to have contributed anything.

sections.heading: Nemergut brings the framework to microbes
sections.body: Diana Nemergut and coauthors (2013, Microbiology and Molecular Biology Reviews) mapped Vellend's four processes onto microbial systems specifically, arguing microbial ecology had been assembling communities without a shared vocabulary for decades. Their key point: microbes make drift and dispersal unusually strong relative to macrobes. Population sizes are enormous, which should dampen drift, but local extinction and colonization happen so fast, and dispersal across microbial passive-mode ranges is so easy, that stochastic turnover can still dominate a signal at small spatial or temporal scales. The question 'which process built this community' is not settled by intuition, deterministic selection and stochastic drift can produce superficially similar patterns, so ecologists need explicit statistical tools, covered in the next lesson, to tell them apart. A community assembled mostly by selection is predictable from the environment; one assembled mostly by drift is not, and that distinction matters for whether restoring a habitat (or a gut) reliably restores its microbiome.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher compares bacterial communities in ten identical artificial ponds, all filled with the same filtered water and left to colonize from the air. If selection dominates, replicate ponds converge on similar taxa because the same environment filters the same winners each time. If drift dominates, replicate ponds diverge randomly, because which rare colonizer arrives first and by chance escapes early extinction differs pond to pond, even though the environment is identical. Nemergut's framework predicts researchers should see a mix: some taxa (say, obligate anaerobes) are selected out everywhere consistently, while rarer, ecologically similar taxa scatter unpredictably across ponds, that specific pattern, selection on some traits plus drift among functionally similar competitors, is what most real microbial datasets show.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'is your community shaped by selection or by chance?' because it is the single question that decides whether a fair project's results will replicate. A weak answer says the sample 'looked different' between conditions without addressing whether that difference could be drift. A strong answer names deterministic selection versus stochastic drift explicitly, states which process the student expected to dominate given their system's spatial scale, and acknowledges dispersal limitation (could the taxa even reach the site?) before claiming selection explains a pattern.

questions.prompt: Which of Vellend's four processes is stochastic rather than deterministic?

options.text: Selection
Drift
Diversification
Dispersal, always

explanations.a: Selection is explicitly the deterministic process in Vellend's framework, fitness differences systematically favor some taxa.
explanations.b: Correct — drift is random birth/death/reproduction that shifts abundances with no fitness advantage involved, the stochastic member of the four.
explanations.c: Diversification generates new variation (mutation, HGT); it is not itself a stochastic sorting process in the same sense as drift.
explanations.d: Dispersal decides which taxa are present to begin with; it can have stochastic elements but is not defined as inherently random the way drift is.

questions.prompt: Match each process to its core definition from Vellend's framework.

right.text: Deterministic fitness differences among taxa
Movement of organisms between sites
Random change in abundance absent fitness differences
Generation of new genetic variation in place

questions.explanation: Selection = deterministic fitness sorting; dispersal = movement between sites; drift = stochastic abundance change; diversification = new variants via mutation/HGT/speciation.

questions.prompt: According to Nemergut et al. (2013), why can drift be unusually influential in microbial communities despite their huge population sizes?

options.text: Microbes cannot undergo natural selection
Rapid local extinction and colonization allow strong stochastic turnover even at large population sizes
Microbial dispersal is always blocked by geographic barriers
Microbes lack any mechanism for diversification

explanations.a: Microbes clearly undergo selection, that is one of the four processes discussed, this option is false.
explanations.b: Correct — fast local extinction/colonization dynamics let drift produce strong stochastic signal at small spatial/temporal scales, even though standing population sizes are enormous.
explanations.c: The opposite is emphasized, easy passive dispersal is one reason microbial assembly differs from macrobial assembly.
explanations.d: Microbes diversify readily via mutation and horizontal gene transfer, this option is false.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in reasoning about which process built a microbial community, from first question asked to last.

items.text: Could the taxa physically reach this site? (dispersal)
Does the local environment systematically favor certain taxa? (selection)
Do replicate communities in identical conditions still diverge unpredictably? (drift)
Are novel variants arising locally via mutation or HGT? (diversification)

questions.explanation: A sensible diagnostic order starts with whether taxa could arrive at all (dispersal), then whether the environment filters them (selection), then whether unpredictable variation remains among replicates (drift), and finally whether new variants are being generated locally (diversification).

lessons.label: Neutral Theory and Null Models

sections.heading: Hubbell's radical simplification
sections.body: Stephen Hubbell's 2001 book The Unified Neutral Theory of Biodiversity and Biogeography proposed something deliberately provocative for tropical forest ecology: assume every individual of every species is functionally equivalent, identical birth, death, and dispersal probabilities, and see how far that assumption gets you toward explaining observed diversity patterns. 'Neutral' does not mean species are identical in traits, it means their per-capita demographic rates are treated as identical for modeling purposes, so community composition drifts randomly (ecological drift) subject only to immigration and speciation, the same logic as the neutral theory of molecular evolution. Hubbell's model reproduced species-abundance curves in real forests strikingly well, which was unsettling to ecologists who assumed niche differences must be doing most of the work.

sections.heading: Sloan's neutral model for microbes, and telling selection from drift
sections.body: Sloan and coauthors (2006, Environmental Microbiology) adapted neutral theory specifically for microbial metacommunities, fitting a neutral community model that predicts a taxon's occurrence frequency across sites from its regional abundance alone, no traits, no environment. When Sloan and coauthors fit the model to real bacterioplankton and activated-sludge communities, it captured the occurrence frequencies of most taxa reasonably well, evidence that pure ecological drift explains a large share of microbial community structure without invoking any environmental filtering at all. But a consistent minority of taxa, disproportionately the rarer ones, fell outside the model's confidence intervals, occurring in far more or far fewer sites than their regional abundance alone would predict. Taxa that fit the neutral prediction are consistent with dispersal and drift; taxa that occur far more or less often than the model predicts are candidates for selection acting on them. This gives a genuinely useful null model: you do not have to assume selection explains a pattern, you first ask whether ecological drift, unweighted by any environmental preference, already explains it. A second, complementary toolkit comes from Stegen and coauthors (2012, ISME Journal), who combined a phylogenetic metric, beta nearest taxon index (betaNTI), with a taxonomic null model, the Raup-Crick metric, to partition community turnover between sites into fractions attributable to selection versus dispersal-plus-drift. Large betaNTI values (beyond +/-2) indicate the phylogenetic turnover between two communities is more or less extreme than a null (drift-only) expectation, signaling selection; values within that range get handed to Raup-Crick to separate dispersal limitation from unconstrained drift.

lessons.workedExample: A student compares gut microbiomes across 20 mice from the same colony. Sequencing shows some bacterial genera present in every mouse and others in only one or two. Rather than assuming presence-everywhere means 'the host selects for it,' the student fits Sloan's neutral model: genera that are regionally abundant across all 20 mice pooled are predicted, under pure neutrality, to show up in most individual mice just by chance dispersal and drift. If a genus sits right on the neutral prediction line, its ubiquity is not evidence of host selection, it is what drift alone predicts. Only genera that fall well above or below the neutral curve, occurring in far more or fewer mice than their regional abundance predicts, are good candidates for a real host-selection story worth investigating further.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes neutral theory to see if a student understands that 'the pattern looks non-random' is not evidence of selection until you have a null model ruling out drift. A weak answer treats any non-uniform abundance distribution as proof of niche differences or host selection. A strong answer names a specific null expectation (a neutral model, or a randomized null distribution) and shows the observed pattern deviates from it before attributing anything to selection, this is the same logic as needing a control group, applied to community structure.

questions.prompt: What does 'neutral' mean in Hubbell's neutral theory of biodiversity?

options.text: All species have identical traits and cannot be told apart
Individuals are treated as having equal per-capita birth, death, and dispersal probabilities regardless of species identity
The environment has no effect on any organism
Species diversity is assumed to be zero

explanations.a: Neutral theory does not claim species are trait-identical, only that their demographic rates are modeled as equivalent.
explanations.b: Correct — this is Hubbell's core simplifying assumption, equal per-capita demographic rates, which lets composition drift stochastically.
explanations.c: Neutral theory is silent on environmental effects on individual organisms; it is a statement about equivalence of per-capita rates, not about the environment being irrelevant to survival generally.
explanations.d: Neutral theory is used to explain how high diversity can arise and persist, not to assume diversity is absent.

questions.prompt: In Sloan et al.'s (2006) neutral community model for microbes, what does it mean when a taxon's observed occurrence frequency closely matches the model's prediction from its regional abundance?

options.text: The taxon is definitely under strong host selection
Its distribution is consistent with dispersal and drift alone, no selection needed to explain it
The taxon is going extinct
The model has failed and should be discarded

explanations.a: The opposite, matching the neutral prediction means selection is not needed to explain the pattern.
explanations.b: Correct — a fit to the neutral model means drift and dispersal, unweighted by environmental preference, already account for the taxon's distribution.
explanations.c: Fitting the model says nothing about extinction trajectory, only about the process shaping current occurrence frequency.
explanations.d: A good fit is a successful, informative outcome of applying the model, not a failure.

questions.prompt: Match each tool or metric to what it is used for.

right.text: Explained tropical forest species-abundance patterns via ecological drift
Predicts microbial taxon occurrence frequency from regional abundance
Detects selection via extreme phylogenetic turnover beyond null expectation
Separates dispersal limitation from pure drift when phylogenetic turnover is within the null range

questions.explanation: Hubbell's original theory targeted forest diversity; Sloan adapted it to predict microbial occurrence frequencies; betaNTI flags selection via extreme phylogenetic turnover; Raup-Crick then splits the remaining (non-selection) turnover into dispersal limitation versus drift.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the Stegen et al. (2012) framework for partitioning community turnover between two sites.

items.text: Compute betaNTI, the phylogenetic turnover relative to a null expectation
If betaNTI is beyond +/-2, classify the turnover as selection-driven
If betaNTI is within +/-2, apply the Raup-Crick metric to the same comparison
Use Raup-Crick's result to distinguish dispersal limitation from unconstrained drift

questions.explanation: betaNTI is computed first; extreme values are attributed to selection; only the remaining, non-extreme comparisons proceed to Raup-Crick, which then separates dispersal limitation from drift.

lessons.label: Succession: Primary, Secondary, and the Infant Gut

sections.heading: Primary succession: colonizing a blank slate
sections.body: Primary succession is community development on a substrate with no prior biological legacy, bare rock exposed by a retreating glacier, or a tooth surface freshly cleaned of biofilm. Glacier forefield studies, notably long-term transects at Alaska's Glacier Bay and Swiss Alpine glaciers, show a predictable early sequence: chemolithotrophic and nitrogen-fixing bacteria arrive first because there is no organic carbon yet, they build the initial nutrient pool that heterotrophs then exploit as plants and their associated fungi establish over subsequent decades. Dental biofilm formation follows an accelerated version of the same logic on a scale of hours to days, early colonizers, chiefly Streptococcus species, adhere directly to the salivary pellicle coating the clean enamel, and their surface receptors then create attachment sites that recruit a second wave of species (coaggregation) that could not have attached to bare enamel. In both systems, the earliest arrivals are not just present, they physically and chemically engineer the conditions the next wave of species depend on, a process called facilitation.

sections.heading: Secondary succession and the infant gut's scripted arrival order
sections.body: Secondary succession happens where a community existed and was disturbed, not annihilated, antibiotics clearing most but not all gut taxa, or a burned forest regrowing from surviving roots and a seed bank. The infant gut is often treated as a hybrid case: a near-sterile system (primary-like) that nonetheless follows a strikingly reproducible order. Yatsunenko and colleagues (2012, Nature), sequencing over 500 individuals across the US, Malawi, and Venezuela, showed infant gut communities are low-diversity and dominated by facultative anaerobes (E. coli-type Proteobacteria) in the first days, these consume residual oxygen and drive the gut anaerobic, which then permits obligate anaerobes to establish. Breastfed infants become dominated by Bifidobacterium, which possesses gene clusters for digesting human milk oligosaccharides that the infant cannot digest itself. Backhed and colleagues (2015, Cell Host & Microbe) tracked this trajectory longitudinally and showed diversification accelerates sharply at weaning, when solid food introduces new fermentable substrates and the community shifts toward an adult-like, Bacteroides- and Firmicutes-rich composition by roughly age three. A community's resistance is how little it changes under a disturbance like antibiotics; its resilience is how fast it returns afterward, and infant communities, being young and low-diversity, tend to have low resistance but often high resilience, while some perturbed adult communities settle into a persistently altered alternative stable state instead of recovering the original configuration.

lessons.workedExample: A student studies gut recovery after a course of amoxicillin in a mouse model, sampling feces before, immediately after, and four weeks after treatment. The 'before' community is diverse and Bacteroides-dominated. Immediately after antibiotics, diversity crashes and facultative anaerobes bloom, structurally similar to the earliest infant-gut stage, because antibiotic killing reopened the oxygen niche the way birth does. At four weeks, if the community returns close to its pre-treatment composition, that is resilience; if it instead settles into a different, stable, Proteobacteria-enriched configuration that persists for months, that is a shift to an alternative stable state, and the student now has a much stronger project because they can name and test which outcome occurred rather than just reporting 'the microbiome changed.'
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about succession and resilience because 'the microbiome changed after X' is a shallow claim, every microbiome changes constantly. What separates weak from strong is whether the student can say what kind of change: transient perturbation with recovery (resilience), permanent shift to a new stable configuration (alternative stable state), or a scripted successional sequence with a mechanistic reason (facilitation, like early anaerobes making the gut hospitable for later colonizers). A strong answer names the mechanism behind the observed order, not just the order itself.

questions.prompt: Why do facultative anaerobes like E. coli-type Proteobacteria typically colonize the infant gut before obligate anaerobes such as Bifidobacterium?

options.text: They are the only bacteria present in breast milk
They consume residual oxygen in the newborn gut, making the environment anaerobic enough for obligate anaerobes to establish
They are resistant to the infant's immune system while obligate anaerobes are not
Obligate anaerobes cannot survive at body temperature until age three

explanations.a: Facultative anaerobes arrive via birth and environmental exposure, not primarily from breast milk composition.
explanations.b: Correct — this is facilitation, early facultative anaerobes deplete oxygen, engineering the anaerobic conditions later obligate-anaerobe colonizers require.
explanations.c: Immune resistance is not the mechanism cited for this successional order; oxygen depletion is.
explanations.d: Obligate anaerobes survive at body temperature throughout infancy; their delayed dominance is about oxygen availability, not temperature.

questions.prompt: A community that is barely disturbed by an antibiotic course, but takes months to return to baseline if it is disturbed, has which combination of properties?

options.text: High resistance, low resilience
Low resistance, high resilience
High resistance, high resilience
An alternative stable state

explanations.a: Correct — resistance is how little the community changes under disturbance (barely disturbed = high resistance), resilience is how fast it recovers if it does change (slow return = low resilience).
explanations.b: This reverses both terms; barely disturbed means high, not low, resistance.
explanations.c: High resilience means fast recovery, but the scenario describes slow recovery, so resilience is low, not high.
explanations.d: An alternative stable state means the community does NOT return to baseline at all; this scenario specifies it does return, just slowly.

questions.prompt: Match each succession concept to its example from the lesson.

right.text: Bare rock exposed by a retreating glacier
Early Streptococcus attachment enabling later coaggregating species on enamel
A perturbed community settling into a new, persistently altered configuration instead of recovering
Introduction of solid food expanding fermentable substrates

questions.explanation: Primary succession = bare glacial rock; facilitation = early Streptococcus enabling later colonizers; alternative stable state = a new persistent configuration after disturbance; weaning introduces solid food as the diversification trigger described by Backhed et al.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of infant gut community development described in the lesson, earliest to latest.

items.text: Low-diversity community dominated by facultative anaerobes consuming residual oxygen
Bifidobacterium dominance in breastfed infants, digesting human milk oligosaccharides
Diversification accelerates as solid food is introduced at weaning
Adult-like, Bacteroides- and Firmicutes-rich composition by roughly age three

questions.explanation: The gut starts near-sterile with facultative anaerobes clearing oxygen, then Bifidobacterium dominates on milk oligosaccharides, then weaning triggers diversification, resulting in an adult-like community by about age three, per Yatsunenko (2012) and Backhed (2015).

lessons.label: Interactions: Cooperation, Competition, and Cross-Feeding

sections.heading: Syntrophy: cooperation forced by thermodynamics
sections.body: Cross-feeding is one organism consuming another's metabolic waste as its own food source, and its strongest form, syntrophy, is cooperation enforced by chemistry rather than choice. Interspecies hydrogen transfer is the classic case: fermenting bacteria breaking down fatty acids to acetate and hydrogen only get a net energy payoff if hydrogen is kept at very low partial pressure, because the reaction is endergonic (energetically unfavorable) unless the products are removed. A methanogenic archaeon consuming that hydrogen to make methane keeps local H2 concentration low enough for the fermenter's reaction to proceed at all, neither organism can do its job alone at meaningful rates, they are metabolically obligate partners. In the gut, a parallel cross-feeding chain runs from complex carbohydrate degraders to butyrate producers: Bacteroides species break dietary fiber down to simple sugars and organic acids, some of which cross-feeding Firmicutes such as Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia convert into butyrate, the short-chain fatty acid that is the primary energy source for colon epithelial cells. Neither step happens without the one before it.

sections.heading: Competition, interference, and losing genes on purpose
sections.body: Where cross-feeding links species, competition and interference actively suppress them. Exploitative competition is indirect, two taxa drawing down the same limiting nutrient. Interference competition is direct chemical warfare: bacteriocins are narrow-spectrum protein toxins, often targeting close relatives competing for the same niche, that many bacteria secrete constitutively or under stress. Type VI secretion systems (T6SS) go further, a contact-dependent, syringe-like nanomachine that punctures a neighboring cell's membrane and injects toxic effector proteins directly, first characterized in detail in Vibrio cholerae and now known across many Gram-negative species as a major driver of interbacterial competition in dense communities like the gut. Set against this competitive picture is the Black Queen hypothesis, proposed by Jeffrey Morris, Richard Lenski, and Erik Zinser (2012, mBio): when a costly metabolic function produces a 'public good' available to the whole neighborhood, for instance an enzyme detoxifying hydrogen peroxide that leaks its benefit to nearby cells, natural selection favors lineages that lose the gene for it and free-ride on neighbors that keep it. Losing the gene saves the metabolic cost of making it, so long as some 'helper' in the community keeps paying that cost, gene loss becomes an adaptive strategy, not decay, explaining why many marine and gut microbes have shed genes for functions their neighbors still supply.

lessons.workedExample: A student sets up a two-species co-culture, a fiber-degrading Bacteroides strain and a butyrate-producing Firmicute, in a minimal medium with fiber as the sole carbon source. The Firmicute alone cannot grow, it lacks the enzymes to break down fiber. The Bacteroides alone grows but its population plateaus at a lower density than in co-culture. Together, both populations reach higher densities than either predicts alone, direct evidence of the cross-feeding chain: Bacteroides breaks fiber into intermediates, and the Firmicute converting those intermediates to butyrate likely also relieves product inhibition on Bacteroides, a textbook syntrophic partnership the student can quantify by measuring short-chain fatty acid concentrations over the growth curve.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing interactions wants to know whether a student can distinguish 'these two species were both present' from a specific, testable mechanism, cross-feeding, exploitative competition, or interference. A weak answer says two taxa 'interacted positively' with no mechanism. A strong answer names the metabolic intermediate being exchanged (or the toxin/system mediating competition) and explains why the interaction is asymmetric or obligate, e.g., that a syntrophic partner cannot survive alone because the reaction is thermodynamically unfavorable without its partner removing the product.

questions.prompt: In interspecies hydrogen transfer, why does the fermenting bacterium need a hydrogen-consuming partner like a methanogen?

options.text: The fermenter cannot survive without hydrogen gas as food
Its fermentation reaction is energetically unfavorable unless hydrogen is kept at low concentration by a partner consuming it
Methanogens produce oxygen the fermenter requires
The partnership is purely social, with no thermodynamic basis

explanations.a: The fermenter produces hydrogen as a waste product, it does not consume it as food.
explanations.b: Correct — the fermentation reaction only becomes energetically favorable when H2 is removed, so the methanogen's consumption of H2 is thermodynamically required for the fermenter's reaction to proceed.
explanations.c: Methanogens are anaerobic and do not supply oxygen; this partnership is unrelated to oxygen.
explanations.d: The partnership is thermodynamically obligate, not merely social, that is the entire point of syntrophy.

questions.prompt: Per the Black Queen hypothesis (Morris, Lenski, and Zinser, 2012), why might a microbe evolve to LOSE a gene for a costly, beneficial enzyme?

options.text: Gene loss is always due to random degenerative mutation with no adaptive value
If the enzyme's benefit is a public good shared by neighbors, losing the gene saves metabolic cost while still receiving the benefit from neighbors that keep it
Losing genes always increases competitive fitness regardless of neighbors
The enzyme becomes toxic once population density rises

explanations.a: The Black Queen hypothesis specifically argues this can be adaptive, not merely degenerative drift.
explanations.b: Correct — free-riding on a neighbor's public good lets a lineage skip the metabolic cost of the function while still benefiting, an adaptive gene-loss strategy.
explanations.c: Fitness gain depends on neighbors continuing to supply the public good; it is conditional, not universal.
explanations.d: Toxicity at high density is not the mechanism described; the mechanism is cost-saving free-riding on a shared benefit.

questions.prompt: Match each interaction mechanism to its description.

right.text: Secreted narrow-spectrum protein toxins targeting close competitors
Contact-dependent nanomachine injecting toxic effectors into neighboring cells
Bacteroides breakdown products feeding Faecalibacterium/Roseburia butyrate production
Adaptive loss of a costly gene whose benefit is supplied as a public good by neighbors

questions.explanation: Bacteriocins are secreted toxins; T6SS is a contact-dependent injection nanomachine; the gut cross-feeding chain runs Bacteroides to butyrate producers; Black Queen dynamics describe adaptive gene loss when neighbors supply a public good.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the gut fiber-to-butyrate cross-feeding chain described in the lesson.

items.text: Dietary fiber enters the colon undigested by the host
Bacteroides species break fiber down into simple sugars and organic acids
Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia convert those intermediates into butyrate
Butyrate is absorbed as the primary energy source for colon epithelial cells

questions.explanation: Fiber first passes undigested to the colon, Bacteroides degrades it to intermediates, butyrate-producing Firmicutes convert those intermediates to butyrate, and the host's colon cells then use that butyrate as fuel.

lessons.label: Biofilms and Spatial Structure

sections.heading: The matrix and the majority mode of microbial life
sections.body: Most microbes on Earth do not live as free-floating (planktonic) single cells suspended in liquid, the way they are usually cultured in a lab flask, they live in biofilms: surface-attached communities encased in a self-produced extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix of polysaccharides, proteins, and extracellular DNA. The matrix is not inert packaging, it retains water against desiccation, binds and concentrates extracellular enzymes near the cells that benefit from them, physically excludes many antibiotics and immune cells, and gives the whole structure mechanical cohesion so it resists being sheared off a surface. Biofilms coordinate their behavior through quorum sensing: cells continuously secrete small diffusible signal molecules (autoinducers), and once cell density, and therefore signal concentration, crosses a threshold, cells collectively switch on density-dependent behaviors such as EPS production, virulence factor release, or bioluminescence, letting a population act coherently only once it is numerous enough for that action to pay off. The core mechanism was first identified in the bioluminescent marine bacterium Vibrio fischeri by Nealson and Hastings in the 1970s and later given the name 'quorum sensing' by Fuqua, Winans, and Greenberg in 1994; Bonnie Bassler and colleagues, starting in the early-to-mid 1990s, extended the picture by discovering a second, interspecies signal (autoinducer-2) in Vibrio harveyi, showing bacteria can eavesdrop on and coordinate with other species, not just their own.

sections.heading: Spatial structure creates niches a flask cannot
sections.body: A well-mixed liquid culture erases spatial structure, every cell experiences roughly the same nutrient and oxygen concentration at any moment, which collapses many niches into one. A biofilm does the opposite: diffusion of oxygen and nutrients from the surrounding fluid creates steep gradients across even a few hundred micrometers of thickness, cells near the biofilm-liquid interface get abundant oxygen and fresh nutrients, while cells deep in the interior experience low oxygen and nutrient depletion, sometimes even dormancy. This gradient structure is precisely what allows the interspecies hydrogen transfer and cross-feeding partnerships from the previous lesson to function efficiently, an aerobe and an obligate anaerobe can coexist within micrometers of each other in a biofilm because the aerobe consumes oxygen fast enough to create an anoxic pocket just behind it, a coexistence impossible in a shaken flask where oxygen is homogenized everywhere. Experiments comparing structured (biofilm or agar-embedded) versus well-mixed liquid cultures of the same synthetic community consistently show that disrupting spatial structure, by vigorous shaking or dispersal, collapses cross-feeding partnerships and often drives the loss of the more fastidious partner, spatial structure is not incidental to these interactions, it is the mechanism that makes them stable. A biofilm also is not a static structure, it runs through a life cycle. Free-swimming cells first attach reversibly to a surface, then commit to irreversible attachment and begin secreting EPS, building through a maturation phase into the three-dimensional, channeled structure with the gradients described above. Once conditions inside the biofilm deteriorate, crowding, nutrient depletion, or a quorum-sensing signal itself can trigger it, a subset of cells actively detach in a regulated dispersal stage, reverting to a motile planktonic state and seeding new biofilms elsewhere, closing the cycle.

lessons.workedExample: A student grows a two-species synthetic community, an aerobic sugar-fermenter and a strictly anaerobic partner it cross-feeds, in two conditions: a static, unshaken flask (which lets a biofilm-like structure and oxygen gradient form at the air-liquid interface) versus a continuously shaken flask. In the static condition, both species persist for weeks, the anaerobe survives in an oxygen-depleted pocket the aerobe creates. In the shaken condition, homogenized oxygen prevents any anoxic niche from forming, and the anaerobe's population crashes within days. The result demonstrates directly that the interaction the student cares about depends on unbroken spatial structure, not just on the two species being present together, a distinction a flask-only experiment without a shaken control would never reveal.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about biofilms and spatial structure because it is where many student projects quietly break their own assumptions, running a 'community' experiment in a shaken flask erases the spatial niches that made the community's interactions possible in the first place. A weak answer treats biofilm and planktonic culture as interchangeable growth formats. A strong answer explains that shaking homogenizes oxygen and nutrient gradients, and predicts, or better, tests, that this should disrupt any interaction relying on those gradients, like an aerobe-anaerobe cross-feeding pair.

questions.prompt: What is the primary functional role of the EPS matrix in a biofilm?

options.text: It has no function beyond visually marking the biofilm's boundary
It retains water, concentrates enzymes near cells, excludes antibiotics and immune cells, and gives mechanical cohesion
It actively pumps oxygen into the deepest layers of the biofilm
It prevents any two species from ever occupying the same biofilm

explanations.a: The matrix is functionally active, not merely a visual marker, it is central to biofilm survival and protection.
explanations.b: Correct — the EPS matrix retains moisture, concentrates enzymes, excludes threats like antibiotics and immune cells, and holds the structure together mechanically.
explanations.c: The matrix does not pump oxygen; in fact oxygen becomes depleted deep in thick biofilms due to diffusion limits, not active transport.
explanations.d: Biofilms are frequently multispecies; the matrix does not prevent coexistence, it can enable it via spatial structure.

questions.prompt: Why does shaking (well-mixing) a synthetic community culture tend to disrupt cross-feeding interactions that depend on oxygen gradients?

options.text: Shaking destroys bacterial DNA directly
Shaking homogenizes oxygen and nutrient concentrations, eliminating the spatial gradients that create separate niches for aerobes and anaerobes
Shaking increases quorum-sensing signal production, which suppresses cross-feeding
Shaking has no measurable effect on spatially dependent interactions

explanations.a: Physical agitation at these scales does not directly damage DNA; the mechanism is about chemical gradients, not genetic damage.
explanations.b: Correct — well-mixing removes the diffusion-limited gradients (oxygen, nutrients) that let spatially separated niches, and the cross-feeding pairs that depend on them, exist.
explanations.c: The lesson does not describe shaking as increasing quorum-sensing signaling; the described effect is gradient homogenization.
explanations.d: The lesson's example shows shaking crashes the anaerobic partner's population, a clear measurable effect.

questions.prompt: Match each biofilm-related term to its description.

right.text: Density-dependent collective behavior switch triggered by autoinducer concentration
Creates distinct aerobic surface and anaerobic interior niches within micrometers
Self-produced polysaccharide/protein/eDNA structure providing protection and cohesion
Discovered interspecies (AI-2) autoinducer signaling, extending quorum sensing beyond a single species

questions.explanation: Quorum sensing is the density-triggered behavior switch; the gradient creates distinct niches; the EPS matrix is the protective structural material; Bassler's work extended the autoinducer mechanism, first identified by Nealson and Hastings and named by Fuqua/Winans/Greenberg, to interspecies (AI-2) signaling.

questions.prompt: Order these events in how a biofilm enables an aerobe-anaerobe cross-feeding partnership, from outermost to innermost spatial position.

items.text: Bulk liquid supplies oxygen and nutrients to the biofilm surface
Aerobic cells at the biofilm-liquid interface consume the incoming oxygen
Oxygen concentration drops steeply with depth, creating an anoxic pocket
An obligate anaerobe occupies the anoxic interior and cross-feeds on the aerobe's byproducts

questions.explanation: Oxygen enters from the bulk liquid, is consumed by surface-dwelling aerobes, creating a gradient that leaves the interior anoxic, which is exactly where the obligate anaerobe partner establishes and cross-feeds.

lessons.label: Biogeochemical Roles: Communities Running Element Cycles

sections.heading: The nitrogen cycle is a relay race between specialists
sections.body: No single organism runs the nitrogen cycle end to end, each transformation is handed off between specialists with distinct metabolisms. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria and archaea (some free-living, some symbiotic, like Rhizobium in legume root nodules) use the nitrogenase enzyme to convert inert atmospheric N2 into ammonia, an energetically expensive reaction that only a narrow set of taxa can perform. Ammonia-oxidizing bacteria and archaea (AOB and AOA) then nitrify it to nitrite, and nitrite-oxidizers finish the job to nitrate, nitrification is aerobic and was long thought entirely bacterial until ammonia-oxidizing archaea were discovered to dominate this step in many soils and oceans. Denitrifiers, working anaerobically, then reduce nitrate stepwise back to N2 gas, closing the loop but also representing the main pathway by which fixed nitrogen (and fertilizer) is lost from agricultural soils. A more recently discovered shortcut, anammox (anaerobic ammonium oxidation), combines ammonium directly with nitrite to produce N2 without ever passing through nitrate, discovered in a wastewater bioreactor in the 1990s and later found to be a major nitrogen-loss pathway in ocean oxygen minimum zones, in some systems responsible for a large fraction of oceanic N2 production.

sections.heading: Sulfur, carbon, and measuring who is actually doing the work
sections.body: The sulfur cycle runs on a parallel relay: sulfate-reducing bacteria and archaea use sulfate as a terminal electron acceptor in anaerobic respiration, producing hydrogen sulfide, while sulfur-oxidizing bacteria (some using light, some chemosynthesis) convert reduced sulfur species back toward sulfate, powering entire hydrothermal-vent food webs with no sunlight involved. In the carbon cycle, methanogenic archaea produce methane as an anaerobic respiration byproduct (recall their role as the hydrogen-consuming partner in syntrophy), while methanotrophic bacteria oxidize methane, often at the oxic-anoxic boundary right above where methanogens work, capturing a large fraction of biologically produced methane before it ever reaches the atmosphere. In every cycle, which process wins in a given patch of soil or water is set by nutrient and electron-acceptor limitation, denitrification only proceeds where oxygen is scarce and nitrate is available, methanogenesis is typically outcompeted by sulfate reduction wherever sulfate is present because sulfate reducers extract more energy per unit of shared substrate like hydrogen. Because these transformations are driven by specific enzymes, ecologists measure who is doing the work using functional-gene markers: nifH quantifies nitrogen-fixation potential, amoA quantifies ammonia-oxidation potential, typically via quantitative PCR that counts gene copies as a proxy for the abundance of organisms capable of that function, alongside direct process-rate measurements like gas-flux chambers or isotope-tracer incubations that measure the reaction actually happening rather than just its genetic potential.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to know whether a constructed wetland is removing nitrate from agricultural runoff, and if so, by which pathway. Measuring nitrate concentration in and out only shows removal happened, not why. The student instead runs an acetylene-inhibition process-rate assay to measure actual denitrification (N2 production) in sediment cores, and separately extracts DNA to quantify nirS or nirK gene copies (denitrification marker genes) by qPCR across sediment depths. If gene abundance and measured process rate both peak in the anoxic sediment layer and track seasonally with nitrate loading, the student has direct evidence the wetland's nitrate removal is driven by microbial denitrification specifically, not, for instance, plant uptake, a distinction that matters enormously for whether the wetland design should be credited for pollution control.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes biogeochemical function because it is the step where students often confuse presence with activity, finding a gene in a metagenome does not mean the reaction is happening at any meaningful rate. A weak answer reports 'we detected nifH' or 'ammonia-oxidizers were present' as if that settles the question of nitrogen fixation or nitrification occurring. A strong answer distinguishes functional-gene potential (who could do it) from a measured process rate (who is doing it, and how much), and explains that gene abundance is only a proxy, ideally paired with a direct rate measurement.

questions.prompt: What does the anammox reaction accomplish that distinguishes it from the classical nitrification-then-denitrification pathway?

options.text: It converts N2 directly into ammonia without any enzymes
It combines ammonium directly with nitrite to produce N2, bypassing the nitrate intermediate entirely
It only occurs in agricultural soils, never in the ocean
It is performed exclusively by plants

explanations.a: Anammox does not fix N2 into ammonia; it does the reverse, converting ammonium and nitrite into N2 gas.
explanations.b: Correct — anammox is a shortcut that skips the nitrate step entirely, combining ammonium and nitrite directly to N2, a discovery from 1990s wastewater bioreactor research later found significant in ocean oxygen minimum zones.
explanations.c: Anammox is notably important in ocean oxygen minimum zones, not restricted to agricultural soils.
explanations.d: Anammox is performed by specific anaerobic bacteria, not plants.

questions.prompt: Why does sulfate reduction typically outcompete methanogenesis for shared substrates like hydrogen when sulfate is present?

options.text: Sulfate reducers are immune to hydrogen toxicity while methanogens are not
Sulfate reducers extract more energy per unit of shared substrate than methanogens can
Methanogens cannot survive in the presence of any sulfur compounds
Sulfate reduction only occurs at temperatures too high for methanogens

explanations.a: Hydrogen toxicity to either group is not the stated mechanism for the competitive outcome.
explanations.b: Correct — the lesson states sulfate reducers extract more energy per unit of shared substrate, which is why they outcompete methanogens for hydrogen wherever sulfate is available.
explanations.c: Methanogens are not universally excluded by sulfur compounds; the mechanism is competitive energetics for a shared substrate, not direct toxicity.
explanations.d: Temperature is not the described mechanism; substrate competition and energy yield are.

questions.prompt: Match each functional-gene marker or process to what it is used to quantify.

right.text: Nitrogen-fixation genetic potential
Ammonia-oxidation genetic potential
Actual process rate as it is currently occurring, not just genetic potential
Oxidize methane at the oxic-anoxic boundary, capturing it before atmospheric release

questions.explanation: nifH and amoA are functional-gene proxies for fixation and nitrification potential respectively; gas-flux/isotope methods measure the actual rate of a process; methanotrophs oxidize methane at the oxic-anoxic interface.

questions.prompt: Order the classical nitrogen cycle steps from atmospheric N2 to N2 gas released back to the atmosphere via denitrification.

items.text: Nitrogen fixation: N2 to ammonia via nitrogenase
Nitrification (ammonia to nitrite) by ammonia-oxidizing bacteria/archaea
Nitrification (nitrite to nitrate) by nitrite-oxidizers
Denitrification: nitrate reduced stepwise back to N2 gas

questions.explanation: The classical relay runs fixation (N2 to ammonia), then nitrification in two steps (ammonia to nitrite to nitrate), then denitrification reduces nitrate back down to N2 gas, closing the loop.

lessons.label: Fecal Microbiota Transplant for C. difficile

sections.heading: Why a single drug keeps failing
sections.body: Clostridioides difficile is an opportunist: it thrives when antibiotics have stripped out the diverse gut community that normally locks up nutrients and bile-acid niches it needs. Treating recurrent C. difficile with more antibiotics — usually vancomycin — cures the acute flare but does nothing to rebuild the community, so up to a quarter of patients relapse, and each relapse raises the odds of the next one. Fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) attacks the actual problem: instead of one compound, it delivers an entire donor community, restoring the metabolic competition (bile-acid conversion, nutrient depletion, direct antagonism) known as colonization resistance that keeps C. difficile from re-establishing.

sections.heading: The trial that changed practice
sections.body: Van Nood et al. (2013, New England Journal of Medicine) ran the first randomized controlled trial comparing donor-feces infusion (via nasoduodenal tube) against standard vancomycin, with and without bowel lavage. The result was so lopsided the data-safety board stopped the trial early: 13 of 16 patients (81%) were cured after a single infusion, rising to 94% after a second infusion for early non-responders, versus roughly 31% cured with vancomycin alone. That gap — one treatment near-total, the other curing well under a third of patients — is what pushed FMT from fringe practice into guideline-recommended therapy almost overnight.

sections.heading: From bedside procedure to regulated product
sections.body: Scaling donor feces safely required infrastructure. OpenBiome, a nonprofit stool bank founded in 2012, began screening donors and shipping frozen, tested material to hospitals so clinicians no longer needed a personal donor for each patient. The FDA treats fecal material as a biological drug requiring an Investigational New Drug application, but exercised enforcement discretion for recurrent C. difficile given the mortality risk of doing nothing. That discretion had limits: in 2019, DeFilipp et al. (New England Journal of Medicine) reported that FMT capsules transmitted an ESBL-producing (extended-spectrum beta-lactamase, drug-resistant) strain of Escherichia coli to two immunocompromised patients, one of whom died of the resulting bloodstream infection. The FDA responded with a safety communication and made screening of donor stool for multidrug-resistant organisms mandatory before further transplants could proceed — a concrete regulatory tightening driven directly by a documented harm, not just a formality. That patchwork gave way to real approvals: Rebyota (RBX2660, a rectally administered donor-derived suspension) was approved in November 2022, and Vowst (SER-109, an oral encapsulated spore product) followed in April 2023 — the first FDA-approved oral fecal microbiota product.

lessons.workedExample: A 68-year-old patient has had three C. difficile recurrences in four months, each time responding to vancomycin and relapsing within weeks after the taper ends. A fourth vancomycin course is unlikely to break the cycle because it re-clears the pathogen without restoring what keeps it cleared. The clinician instead orders a donor stool preparation, screened through a stool bank, delivered via colonoscopy. Within days the patient's stool converts secondary bile acids again — a functional marker that colonization resistance has returned — and at ten-week follow-up there is no relapse, matching the ~81-94% cure pattern seen in the original trial population.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing FMT wants to see that a student understands why swapping a whole community beats swapping in one drug: it is not that donor feces contains a magic antimicrobial, it is that a diverse, metabolically competitive community denies C. difficile the niche it needs. A weak answer says 'FMT puts good bacteria back.' A strong answer names colonization resistance, cites the roughly 81-94% versus 30% contrast from a controlled trial rather than an anecdote, and can explain why the field moved toward standardized, screened products (OpenBiome, Rebyota, Vowst) instead of ad hoc donors — safety and reproducibility, not just efficacy.

questions.prompt: In the van Nood et al. (2013) trial, why was the study stopped early?

options.text: Donor feces infusion caused unacceptable adverse events
An interim analysis showed the infusion group's cure rate was so much higher than vancomycin's that continuing was considered unethical
The vancomycin group had zero relapses, making further comparison pointless
Researchers ran out of screened donor material

explanations.a: The only adverse event was transient diarrhea after infusion; there were no infectious complications.
explanations.b: Correct — the interim cure-rate gap (roughly 81-94% versus about 31%) was large enough that the data-safety board halted enrollment rather than continue randomizing patients to the clearly inferior arm.
explanations.c: The vancomycin-alone arm had a cure rate around 31%, far from zero relapses.
explanations.d: The trial's stoppage was about efficacy data, not a supply shortage.

questions.prompt: What is the core mechanistic reason FMT succeeds where repeated antibiotic courses fail against recurrent C. difficile?

options.text: FMT introduces a stronger antibiotic-producing single species that outcompetes C. difficile
Antibiotics clear the infection but leave the community too depleted to deny C. difficile its niche again, while FMT restores that competitive, colonization-resistant community
FMT works by directly neutralizing the C. difficile toxin
FMT lowers stomach acid so C. difficile spores cannot germinate

explanations.a: FMT's effect comes from a restored diverse community, not one dominant antibiotic-producing organism.
explanations.b: Correct — repeated antibiotics keep re-clearing the pathogen without rebuilding colonization resistance, so relapse continues; FMT restores the whole competitive community.
explanations.c: Toxin neutralization is not the mechanism; it is ecological competition for niches and resources.
explanations.d: This is not how FMT is understood to work; it is not primarily about gastric acid.

questions.prompt: Order these FMT-related developments chronologically.

items.text: OpenBiome founded as a nonprofit stool bank
Van Nood et al. RCT published showing FMT's superiority over vancomycin
Rebyota approved as the first FDA-approved fecal microbiota product
Vowst approved as the first FDA-approved oral fecal microbiota product

questions.explanation: OpenBiome launched in 2012 to supply screened donor material; the landmark RCT was published in 2013; Rebyota was approved November 2022; Vowst, the first oral product, followed in April 2023.

questions.prompt: Match each FMT-related term to its correct description.

right.text: A nonprofit stool bank that screens donors and distributes tested material to hospitals
The ability of an intact gut community to block pathogen establishment through niche and resource competition
The first FDA-approved donor-derived fecal microbiota product, delivered rectally

questions.explanation: Colonization resistance is the ecological mechanism FMT restores; OpenBiome is the infrastructure that scaled safe donor material; Rebyota is the specific approved rectal product.

questions.prompt: Why does the FDA regulate fecal material used for FMT as a biological drug?

options.text: Because it contains synthetic compounds

Because transplanting a live donor microbial community carries risks (infection transmission, unknown long-term effects) that warrant drug-level oversight, though enforcement discretion was used for recurrent C. difficile given the alternative risk
Because Congress passed a law naming feces a controlled substance
Because FMT was invented by a pharmaceutical company

explanations.a: Fecal material is biological, not synthetic; that is not the regulatory rationale.
explanations.b: Correct — live biological material transferred between people carries transmission and safety risks, so it falls under IND requirements, with practical discretion applied given untreated recurrent C. difficile's own risks.
explanations.c: There is no such controlled-substance classification involved.
explanations.d: FMT long predates any single company; the regulatory question is about biological risk, not origin.

lessons.label: Probiotics, Prebiotics, and the Evidence Problem

sections.heading: Two precise definitions, widely blurred in marketing
sections.body: The International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP) fixed working definitions to cut through label noise. Hill et al. (2014) defined a probiotic as 'live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host' — a strain, a dose, and a demonstrated benefit are all required, not just the presence of live bacteria. Gibson et al. (2017) defined a prebiotic as 'a substrate that is selectively utilized by host microorganisms conferring a health benefit' — broadening the older fiber-only definition to include any selectively fermented substrate, provided a benefit is actually shown. Both definitions exist because supplement labels routinely use the words for products that never demonstrated either strain-specific dosing or a measured outcome.

sections.heading: Where the evidence is strong, and where it thins out
sections.body: Evidence quality varies enormously by claim. For antibiotic-associated diarrhea, multiple meta-analyses (including Cochrane reviews) show specific strains — Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG and Saccharomyces boulardii among the best studied — cutting incidence by roughly half, with pooled relative risks in the range of about 0.4 to 0.5 compared to no probiotic, a benefit large and consistent enough to be uncontroversial. Contrast that with the vague 'gut health' or 'boosts immunity' claims stamped on grocery-aisle yogurt: these typically rest on small, unreplicated, or industry-funded trials with no dose-response relationship and no mechanism tied to a measured outcome. The ISAPP definitions exist precisely to separate a therapy tested for a named condition at a named dose, with a specific measured effect size, from a marketing gesture toward the microbiome.

sections.heading: Why most probiotics don't stick around
sections.body: Even effective probiotic strains are usually transient guests, not permanent colonizers. Zmora et al. (2018, Cell) fed a defined probiotic cocktail to volunteers and used endoscopy to sample the actual mucosa, not just stool, finding that colonization was highly individual: some people ('persisters') let the strains establish, while others ('resisters') cleared them, and gut and stool sampling disagreed. In a companion study, Suez et al. (2018, Cell) showed that after antibiotics, generic probiotics could actually delay the native microbiome's return to baseline compared to doing nothing, while autologous FMT (reintroducing a person's own pre-antibiotic stool) restored it fastest. Together the papers argue that colonization resistance from the resident community, not the probiotic strain itself, usually determines whether an add-on microbe takes hold.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to test a claim on a probiotic yogurt label that it 'improves digestive health.' Applying the ISAPP framework, they first ask: does the label name a specific strain and dose, or just 'live active cultures'? It names neither. They then ask what outcome was measured, and find no cited trial at all — just a health claim. Contrast this with an antibiotic-associated-diarrhea study that specifies Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG at a stated CFU dose, given during a defined antibiotic course, with diarrhea incidence as the measured outcome. The student concludes the yogurt claim fails the ISAPP bar on all three counts (strain, dose, demonstrated benefit) while the AAD trial meets it, and frames their science-fair project around testing a specific strain against a specific, measurable outcome rather than a vague wellness claim.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe probiotic and prebiotic claims because this is where consumer science and rigorous science diverge most visibly. A weak answer treats 'probiotic' as a synonym for 'healthy bacteria' and cannot say what strain, dose, or outcome was tested. A strong answer applies the Hill et al. (2014) / Gibson et al. (2017) definitions explicitly, distinguishes evidence tiers (antibiotic-associated diarrhea versus generic gut-health marketing), and can explain — citing Zmora et al. or Suez et al. (2018) — why a probiotic showing up on a label doesn't mean it colonizes, which signals the student understands colonization as a testable, often-failed hypothesis rather than an assumed outcome.

questions.prompt: According to the ISAPP consensus definition (Hill et al. 2014), what three elements must be present for a product to be correctly called a probiotic?

options.text: Any live bacteria, any amount, any claimed benefit
Live microorganisms, administered in adequate amounts, that confer a demonstrated health benefit on the host
Dead or inactivated microorganisms shown to reduce inflammation
A fiber source that feeds resident gut bacteria

explanations.a: The definition specifically requires an adequate, defined amount and a demonstrated benefit, not just any live bacteria in any quantity.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the Hill et al. (2014) ISAPP wording: live organisms, adequate dose, demonstrated benefit.
explanations.c: Probiotics are defined as live organisms, not dead or inactivated ones.
explanations.d: That describes a prebiotic, not a probiotic.

questions.prompt: Which claim category has the strongest supporting evidence base described in this lesson?

options.text: Probiotics for antibiotic-associated diarrhea prevention with specific strains like Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG
Generic 'gut health' claims on grocery-aisle yogurt labels
'Boosts immunity' claims without a named strain or dose
All three have equally strong evidence

explanations.a: Correct — multiple meta-analyses support specific strains reducing antibiotic-associated diarrhea, a much stronger and more consistent evidence base than vague wellness claims.
explanations.b: These claims typically rest on small, unreplicated, or industry-funded studies without a clear mechanism or dose-response.
explanations.c: Without a named strain or dose, such claims cannot be evaluated against the ISAPP framework at all.
explanations.d: Evidence quality varies substantially between these categories; they are not equivalent.

questions.prompt: What did Zmora et al. (2018) find when they used endoscopy to directly sample the gut mucosa of volunteers given a probiotic cocktail?

options.text: All volunteers showed identical, uniform colonization by the probiotic strains
Colonization was highly individual — some people ('persisters') allowed colonization while others ('resisters') cleared the strains, and mucosal sampling disagreed with stool sampling
No volunteers showed any trace of the probiotic strains anywhere
Stool sampling and mucosal sampling always agreed perfectly

explanations.a: The key finding was individual variability, not uniformity, in colonization outcomes.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the persister/resister distinction from Zmora et al. (2018), and the mismatch between stool and mucosal sampling was a central finding.
explanations.c: Some volunteers (persisters) did show colonization; it was not universally absent.
explanations.d: The mucosal and stool results diverged, which was part of why direct mucosal sampling was informative.

questions.prompt: Match each study or definition to what it established.

right.text: ISAPP consensus definition of probiotics
ISAPP consensus definition of prebiotics
Generic probiotics can delay native microbiome recovery after antibiotics compared to autologous FMT

questions.explanation: Hill et al. defined probiotics, Gibson et al. defined prebiotics, and Suez et al. showed post-antibiotic probiotic use could slow the native microbiome's return relative to reintroducing a person's own pre-antibiotic stool.

lessons.label: Designing and Manipulating Communities

sections.heading: Starting from nothing: gnotobiotic mice
sections.body: To learn what a microbial community actually does for a host, ecologists need a blank host to add it to. Germ-free mice, born and raised in sterile isolators with no microbes at all, are that blank slate. Colonizing a germ-free mouse with a known set of organisms produces a gnotobiotic animal — 'known biota' — where every member of the community is identified in advance. Comparing germ-free, gnotobiotic, and conventionally raised (conventionalized) mice given the same diet and environment isolates the community's effect from every other variable: germ-free mice famously show altered immune development, thinner gut mucus, and different fat storage, and conventionalizing a germ-free mouse with a normal community reverses much of that within weeks.

sections.heading: Synthetic communities as a controllable alternative to a whole transplant
sections.body: A whole fecal transplant introduces hundreds of species at once, which is powerful therapeutically but useless for asking which member is doing what. Defined synthetic communities (SynComs) — a curated set of named, cultured strains assembled deliberately — let researchers add or remove one organism at a time and observe the consequence, the same logic as a manipulated-condition experiment in any ecology course. The oldest and most widely used example is the Altered Schaedler Flora (ASF), an eight-member community of named bacterial strains developed in the 1970s that has served as the standard defined flora for gnotobiotic mice ever since — proof that a SynCom doesn't have to be a one-off lab tool but can become a durable, shared reference community other labs reuse. A classic design compares a full SynCom against dropout versions missing one strain, run at multiple doses, with an unconlonized germ-free control and a media-only sham gavage, so any effect can be attributed to the specific organism removed rather than to the act of gavaging itself.

sections.heading: Why the community doesn't just take
sections.body: Assembling a stable engineered community is harder than mixing strains in a tube, because ecological rules govern real gut ecosystems. Priority effects mean the order organisms arrive changes the outcome: an early colonizer can occupy a niche and metabolic byproduct stream before a later, otherwise-competitive strain arrives, locking in a different stable state from the same starting pool. Invasion resistance means an already-established community, even a simple one, can exclude an introduced strain the way an empty gut cannot — which is exactly the colonization resistance mechanism behind FMT's success and behind why so many probiotics fail to persist. Because of this, SynCom experiments must report dose, timing, and order, not just which strains were used, or the result is not reproducible.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher wants to know whether a single bacterial strain, X, is responsible for protecting mice from a pathogen. They cannot just compare mice with strain X to mice without it if the groups were assembled differently. Instead they design four gnotobiotic arms from the same germ-free stock: (1) germ-free control, (2) full ten-member SynCom, (3) the same SynCom with strain X dropped out, (4) media-only sham gavage. All mice are colonized on the same day, at the same dose, then challenged with the pathogen two weeks later. Protection appearing in arm 2 but not arm 3, with arms 1 and 4 both fully susceptible, isolates strain X's contribution from dose, timing, and the general effect of having any community at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe SynCom and gnotobiotic designs because they reveal whether a student understands manipulated experiments versus mere observation. A weak answer says 'we added bacteria and measured what happened' with no dropout, dose, or timing control. A strong answer explicitly names the confound structure — germ-free baseline, full community, single-member dropout, sham gavage — and can explain priority effects: that assembly order, not just membership, can change which stable state a community reaches, so a single successful colonization doesn't prove the strain would work if introduced later or in a different order.

questions.prompt: What is a gnotobiotic mouse?

options.text: A wild-caught mouse with an unknown, natural microbiome
A germ-free mouse colonized with a specific, known set of microorganisms
A mouse raised on a special antibiotic-laden diet
A mouse whose genome has been edited to remove immune genes

explanations.a: A wild-caught mouse's microbiome is unknown, the opposite of gnotobiotic.
explanations.b: Correct — 'gnotobiotic' means known biota: a germ-free animal deliberately colonized with an identified community.
explanations.c: Diet manipulation alone does not make an animal gnotobiotic; it is about a defined microbial community.
explanations.d: Gnotobiotic status concerns the microbial community present, not genetic editing of the host.

questions.prompt: In a SynCom dropout experiment testing whether strain X protects against a pathogen, why is a media-only sham gavage control necessary in addition to a germ-free control?

options.text: It isn't necessary; the germ-free control alone is sufficient
It controls for any effect of the gavage procedure itself, separating handling stress or procedural artifacts from the biological effect of the community
It replaces the need for a full SynCom arm
It tests whether the pathogen can survive in media alone

explanations.a: Without a sham gavage, any difference between germ-free and colonized mice could be partly attributable to the act of gavaging rather than the microbes themselves.
explanations.b: Correct — the sham control isolates procedural effects (handling, gavage stress) from the biological effect of the introduced community.
explanations.c: The sham control and full SynCom arm test different things and both are needed.
explanations.d: The sham gavage tests the effect of the procedure on the host, not pathogen survival in media.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in setting up a rigorous SynCom dropout experiment, from first to last.

items.text: Obtain germ-free mice from sterile isolators
Randomly assign mice to full-SynCom, dropout-SynCom, sham, and germ-free arms
Gavage each arm on the same day at a matched dose
Challenge all arms with the pathogen after a fixed colonization period

questions.explanation: Rigor requires starting from a common germ-free stock, randomizing arm assignment before any treatment, colonizing all arms simultaneously at a matched dose, and only then applying the pathogen challenge so timing cannot confound the result.

questions.prompt: Match each ecological concept to its description in engineered-community experiments.

right.text: The order in which strains arrive changes which stable community state results
An established community can exclude a newly introduced strain
A curated, defined set of named cultured strains assembled deliberately for controlled manipulation

questions.explanation: Priority effects concern arrival order changing outcomes, invasion resistance concerns established communities resisting newcomers, and a SynCom is the defined-strain tool used to test both under controlled conditions.

lessons.label: Environmental Bioremediation

sections.heading: A deep-sea community that bloomed on oil
sections.body: When the Deepwater Horizon well ruptured in April 2010, roughly a fifth of the released oil and gas formed an invisible plume drifting about 1,100 meters deep in the Gulf of Mexico, far from sunlight and oxygen-poor. Hazen et al. (2010, Science) sampled more than 200 locations across 17 sites in the plume and found it dominated by a single, previously uncharacterized group of cold-adapted, hydrocarbon-degrading bacteria in the order Oceanospirillales, present at roughly double the cell density found outside the plume. The community had shifted, in effect, to specialize almost entirely on consuming the spilled hydrocarbons, degrading alkane compounds with estimated half-lives on the order of days despite the near-freezing deep-water temperatures that were expected to slow microbial activity substantially — a striking contrast with typical cold, open-ocean background hydrocarbon degradation, which without a concentrated, adapted community to drive it can take weeks to months to achieve comparable breakdown.

sections.heading: Biostimulation versus bioaugmentation
sections.body: Two contrasting strategies exist for accelerating microbial cleanup. Biostimulation adds nutrients — typically nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizers — to a site where degrading organisms are already present but nutrient-limited, letting the existing community scale up its own activity; this was the dominant approach after the 1989 Exxon Valdez spill, where fertilizer application on Alaskan shorelines measurably sped oil breakdown by resident bacteria. Bioaugmentation instead introduces new, often non-native, degrader strains or consortia into a site that lacks them. The Deepwater Horizon plume response leaned toward the biostimulation logic in the sense that the ecosystem's own indigenous Oceanospirillales bloom did most of the degrading work once nutrients and oxygen dynamics allowed it, without needing engineered organisms added from outside.

sections.heading: Engineered ecosystems built for a single ecological job
sections.body: Some of the largest deliberately managed microbial communities on Earth run inside wastewater treatment plants. Activated sludge systems cultivate a mixed aerobic floc of bacteria and protozoa that consume organic waste and clump into settleable particles, a design essentially unchanged in principle since the early 20th century. A more recently engineered addition is the anammox (anaerobic ammonium oxidation) process, discovered in Delft, Netherlands in the 1990s: bacteria related to the genus Brocadia oxidize ammonium using nitrite instead of oxygen, converting it directly to nitrogen gas. Anammox-based reactors now remove nitrogen from wastewater with a fraction of the aeration energy and no added carbon source that conventional nitrification-denitrification requires, making it one of the clearest cases of a microbial-ecology discovery becoming an industrial-scale engineered community.

lessons.workedExample: An environmental science student is designing a bench-scale experiment to compare cleanup strategies for a soil sample contaminated with diesel. They set up three microcosms: (1) untreated contaminated soil, (2) contaminated soil plus nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizer (biostimulation), (3) contaminated soil plus fertilizer and an added commercial hydrocarbon-degrader inoculum (bioaugmentation). After four weeks they measure residual hydrocarbon concentration in each. If soil microbial counts show the site already has degrading organisms present, the biostimulation arm often matches or approaches the bioaugmentation arm's performance at lower cost and complexity — mirroring how the indigenous Oceanospirillales bloom in the Deepwater Horizon plume did substantial degrading work once conditions favored it, without externally added microbes.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing bioremediation wants a student who can name the actual mechanism and case study, not just say 'bacteria eat the oil.' A weak answer cannot distinguish biostimulation from bioaugmentation or say which one a given site needs. A strong answer explains that the choice depends on whether capable degraders are already present (favoring biostimulation, cheaper and lower-risk) versus absent (requiring bioaugmentation, which risks introducing organisms that fail to establish or disrupt existing structure), and can cite the Deepwater Horizon Oceanospirillales bloom or the anammox reactor as a concrete example of communities doing engineered ecological work.

questions.prompt: What did Hazen et al. (2010) find dominating the deep-sea hydrocarbon plume after the Deepwater Horizon spill?

options.text: A diverse, evenly distributed mix of dozens of common soil bacteria
A previously uncharacterized, cold-adapted group of hydrocarbon-degrading bacteria in the order Oceanospirillales, at roughly double the cell density found outside the plume
Almost no detectable microbial activity due to the cold, oxygen-poor depth
A community entirely of introduced, engineered bacteria added for cleanup

explanations.a: The plume was dominated by one specialized group, not an even mix of many common species.
explanations.b: Correct — this Oceanospirillales-related group specialized on the hydrocarbons and was found at markedly elevated density within the plume.
explanations.c: Despite cold temperatures, degradation rates were surprisingly rapid, not absent.
explanations.d: The dominant degraders were indigenous, naturally occurring organisms, not introduced ones.

questions.prompt: A contaminated site already has native hydrocarbon-degrading bacteria present but growth is limited by low nitrogen and phosphorus. Which strategy directly addresses this limitation?

options.text: Bioaugmentation, by adding new degrader strains
Biostimulation, by adding nutrients so the existing degraders can grow faster
Sterilizing the site and starting over
Removing oxygen to force anaerobic degradation

explanations.a: Adding new strains doesn't address the actual bottleneck, which is nutrient limitation on organisms already present.
explanations.b: Correct — biostimulation adds the limiting nutrients (commonly nitrogen and phosphorus) so the indigenous, already-present degraders can scale up activity, as done after the Exxon Valdez spill.
explanations.c: Sterilizing would remove the very degraders capable of doing the cleanup work.
explanations.d: Removing oxygen isn't indicated when the limitation described is nutrients, not electron acceptor availability.

questions.prompt: Match each engineered or observed microbial system to its description.

right.text: A mixed aerobic bacterial-protozoan floc that consumes organic waste in wastewater treatment
Bacteria related to Brocadia that oxidize ammonium using nitrite, producing nitrogen gas without added carbon or heavy aeration
A deep, cold, oxygen-poor hydrocarbon cloud dominated by an indigenous Oceanospirillales-related bloom

questions.explanation: Activated sludge is the classic aerobic floc treatment system, anammox is the nitrogen-removal process discovered in Delft that bypasses conventional nitrification-denitrification, and the Deepwater Horizon plume is the natural case of an indigenous degrader bloom.

questions.prompt: Order these events related to microbial oil degradation from earliest to most recent.

items.text: Exxon Valdez spill and fertilizer-based biostimulation cleanup (1989)
Anammox process discovered in Delft, Netherlands (1990s)
Deepwater Horizon well rupture (April 2010)
Hazen et al. publish deep plume Oceanospirillales findings in Science (2010)
