questions.explanation: The Exxon Valdez spill and its fertilizer-based response came in 1989; anammox was discovered in the 1990s; the Deepwater Horizon rupture occurred in April 2010, with the Hazen et al. plume study published later that same year.

lessons.label: Food and Fermentation Microbiomes

sections.heading: Cheese rinds as a reproducible model ecosystem
sections.body: Fermented foods are attractive to ecologists for the same reason gnotobiotic mice are: they are small, fast, and tractable communities that still show real ecological structure. Wolfe, Button, Santarelli, and Dutton (2014, Cell) surveyed 137 cheese rind communities from ten countries and found that despite wildly different geographic origins, rinds converged on a small number of reproducible community types built from about two dozen widely shared bacterial and fungal genera. Critically, they then reconstructed these communities in vitro on cheese-curd agar in the lab and watched the same succession patterns and species interactions recur, turning cheese rinds into one of the few natural microbial communities where in situ patterns and in vitro experiments can be directly cross-checked against each other.

sections.heading: Lactic-acid succession in vegetable ferments
sections.body: Kimchi and sauerkraut follow a well-documented successional sequence driven by the vegetable's own resident microbes plus the salt brine environment. Leuconostoc mesenteroides, a heterofermentative lactic acid bacterium, typically dominates first: it tolerates the initial salt and oxygen conditions, produces carbon dioxide that helps drive out oxygen, and lowers the pH just enough to disadvantage spoilage organisms. As acidity increases, more acid-tolerant homofermentative species — commonly Lactobacillus plantarum and related lactobacilli — take over and finish the fermentation at a lower pH than Leuconostoc can tolerate — typically stabilizing the finished kimchi or sauerkraut in the pH 3.5-4.0 range, low enough to keep most spoilage and pathogenic organisms from re-establishing. This is priority-effect ecology in miniature: the early colonizer's own activity remodels the environment in a way that hands the niche to its successor, a predictable, temperature- and salt-concentration-dependent handoff rather than a random mix.

sections.heading: Kombucha SCOBYs and spoilage as community shift
sections.body: A kombucha SCOBY ('symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast') is a self-organized partnership: yeasts such as Saccharomyces and Brettanomyces ferment sugar to ethanol and carbon dioxide, and acetic acid bacteria, chiefly Acetobacter, oxidize that ethanol to acetic acid while secreting the cellulose that forms the SCOBY's floating pellicle — each group's byproduct is the other's substrate, a cross-feeding relationship rather than simple coexistence. Food spoilage, by contrast, is what happens when an intended fermentation community loses control of the niche: if salt, acidity, or temperature conditions favor an unwanted organism early, that organism can seize the priority-effect advantage instead, producing off-flavors, gas, or pathogens rather than the target ferment — the same successional logic that builds a good kimchi can just as easily build a spoiled batch.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to test whether starting salt concentration changes which bacterium dominates a cabbage ferment. They prepare batches at 2%, 3%, and 5% salt by weight, sample each at day 1, 3, 7, and 14, and plate onto media selective for lactic acid bacteria while tracking pH. At low salt they expect Leuconostoc to dominate briefly before Lactobacillus plantarum takes over as pH drops, matching the standard succession; at high salt they predict a slower, more Lactobacillus-dominated trajectory since high salt disadvantages some early colonizers. This design turns a kitchen ferment into a genuine manipulated-condition ecology experiment: one variable (salt), a measured successional outcome (which genus dominates over time), and a mechanism (priority effects driven by pH and salt tolerance) tying the numbers to the biology.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing a fermentation project wants to see the student treat the ferment as an ecosystem with succession, not a single-organism process. A weak answer says 'good bacteria ferment the food.' A strong answer names the specific successional handoff — Leuconostoc mesenteroides to Lactobacillus plantarum in kimchi or sauerkraut, or the yeast-to-acetic-acid-bacteria cross-feeding in a kombucha SCOBY — and can explain why an early colonizer's own metabolic byproducts (acid, CO2, ethanol) reshape the environment for whoever comes next, which is exactly the priority-effect logic covered elsewhere in this unit.

questions.prompt: What made the Wolfe, Button, Santarelli, and Dutton (2014) cheese rind study notable as a model system for microbial ecology?

options.text: It was the first study to sequence a single cheese sample's genome
It surveyed 137 rind communities across ten countries, found convergent reproducible community types, and successfully reconstructed the same succession patterns in vitro on cheese-curd agar
It showed that cheese rinds contain no bacteria, only fungi
It proved that geography is the only factor determining rind community composition

explanations.a: The study surveyed many rind communities broadly, not a single genome sequencing effort.
explanations.b: Correct — the large cross-country survey plus successful in vitro reconstruction is what made cheese rinds a tractable, cross-checkable model system.
explanations.c: Rinds host both bacteria and fungi as dominant community members.
explanations.d: The notable finding was that communities converged on similar types despite different geographic origins, the opposite of geography being the sole determinant.

questions.prompt: Order the typical successional stages of a salt-brine vegetable ferment like kimchi or sauerkraut.

items.text: Leuconostoc mesenteroides dominates, tolerating initial salt/oxygen and producing CO2 and mild acid
Rising acidity begins to disadvantage Leuconostoc
More acid-tolerant Lactobacillus plantarum and related species take over
Fermentation stabilizes at a lower pH than Leuconostoc could tolerate

questions.explanation: Leuconostoc's own early activity lowers pH and depletes oxygen, which eventually disadvantages itself and hands the niche to more acid-tolerant Lactobacillus species, stabilizing the ferment at a lower final pH.

questions.prompt: Match each fermentation system or organism group to its ecological role.

right.text: Ferments sugar to ethanol and CO2, providing the substrate the next group consumes
Oxidizes ethanol to acetic acid and secretes the cellulose pellicle
Early salt- and oxygen-tolerant colonizer of vegetable ferments that lowers pH via CO2 and mild acid production

questions.explanation: Leuconostoc plays the early-colonizer role in vegetable ferments; kombucha yeasts produce ethanol that acetic acid bacteria then oxidize, a cross-feeding relationship that also builds the SCOBY's cellulose pellicle.

questions.prompt: Why can the same successional logic that produces a good kimchi also produce a spoiled ferment?

options.text: Spoilage always requires a completely different set of organisms unrelated to fermentation microbes
If early conditions (salt, acidity, temperature) favor an unwanted organism instead of the intended starter, that organism can seize the same priority-effect advantage and dominate the succession
Spoilage only happens when no microorganisms are present at all
Fermentation and spoilage are unrelated processes governed by entirely different physical laws

explanations.a: Spoilage organisms often come from the same general microbial pool present on the raw ingredients; it's the conditions that determine who wins.
explanations.b: Correct — priority effects are conditional: whichever organism the starting conditions favor gets a head start and reshapes the environment, for better or worse.
explanations.c: Spoilage requires organisms to be present and active, not absent.
explanations.d: Both are succession processes governed by the same ecological principles, just with different favored organisms.

lessons.label: Soil, Plant, and One-Health Microbiomes

sections.heading: The rhizosphere as a plant-recruited community
sections.body: The rhizosphere is the thin zone of soil immediately surrounding plant roots, and it is not a passive neighborhood — plants actively shape it by exuding sugars, organic acids, and signaling compounds through their roots, selectively feeding and recruiting microbes that benefit them. Plant-growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR), including many Pseudomonas, Bacillus, and Azospirillum species, fix nitrogen, solubilize phosphorus, or produce hormones like auxin that stimulate root growth, while mycorrhizal fungi extend a plant's effective root surface area in exchange for sugars. This is the same ecological logic as colonization resistance in the gut: a plant that recruits and maintains a dense, competitive rhizosphere community leaves less room and fewer nutrients for pathogens trying to invade the root zone.

sections.heading: Disease-suppressive soils: a documented, mechanistic case
sections.body: Some soils actively suppress plant disease even when the pathogen is present, and the best-studied example is take-all decline in wheat. After a severe outbreak of the fungal pathogen Gaeumannomyces graminis (which causes take-all disease), continuous wheat monoculture in the same field often leads to disease severity spontaneously dropping over several years. Research led by Weller and Thomashow traced this to a buildup of specific Pseudomonas fluorescens genotypes in the rhizosphere that produce the antibiotic compound 2,4-diacetylphloroglucinol (DAPG), which directly inhibits the pathogen. The mechanism matters because it shows suppression isn't vague 'healthy soil' — it is a traceable buildup of a specific antibiotic-producing bacterial population, reproducible enough that transferring suppressive soil to a conducive field can transfer the suppression.

sections.heading: Commercial inoculants and the One Health frame
sections.body: Commercial soil inoculants marketed to farmers and gardeners promise PGPR or mycorrhizal benefits, but field performance is notoriously inconsistent: an inoculant strain that helped in a controlled greenhouse trial often fails to establish against the resident soil community outdoors, since invasion resistance applies to soil just as it does to the gut. Effects depend heavily on soil type, existing microbial density, and crop, so a product proven at one farm cannot be assumed to work at another without testing. This connects to One Health, the framework recognizing that soil, plant, animal, and human microbiomes are linked rather than separate systems — antibiotic residues and resistance genes move from agricultural soil into water and food, and soil microbial diversity loss has been linked to reduced diversity in the microbiomes of animals and people living nearby, making soil an entry point for cross-system microbiome questions, not an isolated compartment.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants a defensible BSL-1 science-fair project on soil microbiome shifts. Rather than testing a commercial inoculant's marketing claim directly (hard to control outdoors), they design a manipulated pot experiment: identical sterilized potting soil, split into pots that receive (1) no inoculant, (2) a commercial PGPR inoculant, (3) a compost-tea community from a local disease-suppressive-associated field, each with the same seedling species, watering, and light. They measure a defined outcome — root length and a simple culturable-colony count on selective media at day 14 and day 28 — rather than eyeballing plant 'health.' This keeps the project within BSL-1 safety limits (no known pathogens introduced deliberately), gives a measurable community-shift outcome, and lets them discuss invasion resistance honestly if the inoculant fails to outperform the untreated control, which is itself a valid, explainable result.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing a soil or One Health project wants evidence the student understands soil communities as competitive ecosystems, not a bag of beneficial microbes to sprinkle on. A weak answer claims an inoculant simply 'adds good bacteria' and reports only anecdotal plant appearance. A strong answer names a mechanism — DAPG-producing Pseudomonas in take-all decline, or PGPR nutrient/hormone effects — explains why inoculant establishment is not guaranteed (invasion resistance from the resident community), and can connect the soil-level finding to the One Health frame: why soil microbiome shifts are not confined to soil.

questions.prompt: In take-all decline, what is the documented mechanism by which continuous wheat monoculture leads to reduced disease severity over time?

options.text: The wheat plants evolve genetic resistance within a few growing seasons
A buildup of specific DAPG-producing Pseudomonas fluorescens genotypes in the rhizosphere directly inhibits the take-all pathogen
Repeated tilling physically destroys the pathogen's spores
The soil becomes too nutrient-poor to support any microbial life, including the pathogen

explanations.a: Take-all decline occurs on a timescale and through a mechanism inconsistent with rapid host genetic evolution; it is a soil microbial community shift.
explanations.b: Correct — research led by Weller and Thomashow traced take-all decline to a buildup of DAPG-producing Pseudomonas fluorescens genotypes that antagonize Gaeumannomyces graminis.
explanations.c: Tilling is not the documented mechanism; the suppression is microbially mediated and transferable via soil transfer, which physical disruption would not explain.
explanations.d: Suppressive soils remain microbially active; the suppression is due to an antagonistic population increasing, not overall biological depletion.

questions.prompt: Why do commercial soil inoculants often underperform in the field compared to controlled greenhouse trials?

options.text: Because greenhouse soil is always sterile and field soil never is

Because an introduced strain faces invasion resistance from the resident soil community, and outcomes depend heavily on soil type, microbial density, and crop, none of which transfer automatically between sites
Because inoculants are illegal to use outdoors
Because field soil contains no plants for the inoculant to associate with

explanations.a: Greenhouse soil is not necessarily sterile; the key issue is competition from an established resident community outdoors.
explanations.b: Correct — this mirrors gut colonization resistance: an established community can exclude a newcomer, and site-specific variables mean results don't generalize automatically.
explanations.c: There is no such legal restriction described; this is an ecological establishment problem.
explanations.d: Field soil obviously contains crop plants; the issue is microbial competition, not absence of a host.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in rhizosphere and soil microbiome ecology.

right.text: An antibiotic compound produced by specific Pseudomonas fluorescens genotypes that suppresses a fungal pathogen
Bacteria that fix nitrogen, solubilize phosphorus, or produce growth hormones to benefit the plant
A framework recognizing soil, plant, animal, and human microbiomes as linked rather than separate systems

questions.explanation: PGPR directly benefit plant growth through nutrient and hormone effects, DAPG is the specific antibiotic mechanism behind take-all decline, and One Health is the cross-system framework linking soil to animal and human health.

questions.prompt: Order the events of take-all decline in a wheat field from first to last.

items.text: A severe outbreak of Gaeumannomyces graminis (take-all disease) occurs
Wheat is grown continuously (monoculture) in the same field over subsequent seasons
DAPG-producing Pseudomonas fluorescens genotypes build up in the rhizosphere
Disease severity spontaneously declines despite the pathogen still being present

questions.explanation: Take-all decline begins with a severe outbreak, is followed by continuous monoculture that favors the buildup of antagonistic DAPG-producing Pseudomonas genotypes, and results in a spontaneous drop in disease severity even though the pathogen remains present.

questions.prompt: A student wants to design a BSL-1-safe science-fair project testing a soil inoculant. Which design best isolates the inoculant's effect from other variables?

options.text: Compare one inoculated plant on a windowsill to a photo of a plant from a magazine advertisement

Use identical sterilized potting soil split into replicate pots (no inoculant, commercial inoculant, and a comparison community), same seedling species, watering, and light, with a measured outcome like root length or colony counts at fixed timepoints
Add the inoculant to random soil samples collected from different parts of town and see which grows best
Skip the untreated control since the inoculant is 'supposed to help' anyway

explanations.a: Comparing to an unrelated photo provides no controlled data at all.
explanations.b: Correct — matched starting soil, replicate pots, controlled conditions, and a defined measurable outcome isolate the inoculant's effect from confounds and stay within BSL-1 limits.
explanations.c: Random soil samples from different locations introduce uncontrolled variation in existing microbial community and soil type, confounding the inoculant's effect.
explanations.d: Without an untreated control, there is no baseline to know whether the inoculant did anything at all.
